name: Kishōtenketsu narrative (起承転結)
description: The canonical 4-beat East Asian narrative form. Tells a story without conflict by introducing an unrelated element in the third beat, then revealing its hidden coherence in the fourth. Use when the story should land through recognition rather than resolution.
exemplars: Sazae-san 4-koma; Murakami short stories; My Neighbor Totoro.

name: Noh play (能 / 五段)
description: Classical Japanese masked theater in 5 dan following the jo-ha-kyū rhythmic principle. Use when the story requires sustained meditative pace before a concentrated payoff — appropriate for ghost-story, dream-narrative, and mystic-suggestion forms.
exemplars: Zeami's Atsumori; Hagoromo; Dōjōji.

name: Sewamono / Domestic tragedy (世話物)
description: Edo-period bunraku/kabuki domestic tragedy featuring merchant-class lovers caught between giri (duty) and ninjō (feeling), often resolved through love-suicide. Use when the protagonist must be destroyed by impossibility of choosing between duty and feeling.
exemplars: Chikamatsu's Love Suicides at Sonezaki; Love Suicides at Amijima.

name: Rakugo (落語)
description: Classical Japanese comic monologue. A single seated storyteller performs a comic narrative ending in a punchline. Use when the story is dialogue-heavy and turns on a final wordplay or twist.
exemplars: Jugemu; Manjū Kowai; Toki-Soba.

name: Haibun travel narrative (俳文紀行)
beats: Onward movement to the next place
description: Hybrid prose-and-haiku travel form where each location's experience crystallizes in a haiku. Use when the narrative is journey-shaped and emotionally compressed.
exemplars: Bashō's Oku no Hosomichi; Yosa Buson's haibun.

name: Kaidan / Japanese ghost story (怪談)
beats: Slow, deliberate mood-setting in everyday life
Recognition of poignant impermanence as residue
description: Japanese supernatural tale whose horror operates through quiet intrusion. The uncanny enters everyday life calmly and is rarely defeated, instead absorbed with the residue of impermanence.
exemplars: Hearn's Yuki-onna and Mujina; Ueda Akinari's Ugetsu Monogatari; Kurosawa's Pulse.

name: Iyashikei / Healing slice-of-life (癒し系)
beats: Quiet pause as the disturbance is sat with
description: Gentle low-stakes narrative form in which small disturbances are absorbed back into a slightly-evolved equilibrium. Use when the story should soothe rather than excite.
exemplars: Aria; Yokohama Kaidashi Kikō; Mushishi.

name: Mono no aware narrative (物の哀れ)
beats: A moment of beauty, presence, or attachment is established
The fleeting nature of the moment is recognized
description: A narrative whose entire arc bends toward the recognition that something beautiful is fleeting — the bittersweet awareness of impermanence. Use when the payoff is recognition without resolution.
exemplars: The Tale of Genji; Kawabata's Snow Country; Ozu's Tokyo Story.

name: Wabi-sabi narrative (侘寂)
beats: An imperfect, flawed, or incomplete object/situation is presented
The reader's expectation that this is "broken" is allowed to settle
The imperfection is reframed as the source of the beauty
The new relationship to imperfection is held
description: Narrative whose central reframe is the reinterpretation of imperfection as essential rather than broken. Use when the story should invert the reader's relationship to flawed things.
exemplars: Sōetsu Yanagi's writings; Tanizaki's In Praise of Shadows; the kintsugi essay form.

name: Mu-ending narrative (無の物語)
description: Narrative that ends in deliberate emptiness, silence, or absence. The void is not interpretation-pending — it IS the resolved state.
exemplars: Akutagawa's "The Life of a Stupid Man"; Ozu's Tokyo Story (final shot); Teshigahara's Woman in the Dunes.

name: Yūgen narrative (幽玄)
description: Narrative whose payoff is an intimation — never a statement — of something profound and unsayable beneath the surface. The unsaid is the point.
exemplars: Zeami's mugen-Noh dream plays; Akutagawa's "In a Grove"; Ozu's late films.

name: Watakushi-shōsetsu / I-novel (私小説)
beats: The narrator establishes their compromised circumstance
A moral or social pressure presses on the narrator
The narrator fails or acts shamefully
The narrator records the failure without redemption
description: Distinctly Japanese confessional autobiographical fiction. The narrator-protagonist is barely fictionalized; the moral register is unflinching self-exposure without redemptive shape.
exemplars: Tayama Katai's Futon; Dazai's No Longer Human; Naoya Shiga.

name: Gi-seung-jeon-gyeol narrative (기승전결)
description: Korean reading of the East Asian 4-beat form. Same structure as kishōtenketsu, used distinctly in Korean essays, sijo poetry, and modern literary fiction.
exemplars: Classical sijo poems; Yi Sang's modernist essays; Han Kang short pieces.

name: Sijo poetry-narrative (시조)
description: 3-line classical Korean poetic form (~43-45 syllables) compressing an entire narrative arc into three movements. The third line characteristically introduces a sharp turn.
exemplars: Hwang Jini's classical sijo; Yun Seon-do's Eobu Sasi-sa.

name: Pansori narrative (판소리)
beats: Storyteller's spoken opening sets the scene (Aniri)
Sung passage carries the emotional state (Sori)
Sung climactic passage delivers the emotional peak (Sori)
description: Classical Korean epic-song form. A single sorikkun carries the narrative through alternating spoken (aniri) and sung (sori) passages, with audience cries (chuimsae) as structural punctuation.
exemplars: Chunhyang-ga; Simcheong-ga; Heungbu-ga; Jeokbyeok-ga.

name: Han narrative (한 서사)
beats: Accumulated grievance held in the body
description: Narrative whose engine is han — accumulated, inherited, or unspoken sorrow. The payoff is a release that acknowledges rather than erases the wound. The Korean tragic form.
exemplars: Min Jin Lee's Pachinko; Im Kwon-taek's Sopyonje; Memories of Murder.

name: Jeong narrative (정 서사)
description: Narrative whose payoff is recognition of a deep, unspoken affectionate bond that was always there. Jeong is built through accumulation, not declaration.
exemplars: Lee Isaac Chung's Minari; Reply 1988; Park Wan-suh stories.

name: Sageuk / Korean historical court drama (사극)
beats: Court setting and protagonist's place established
Court intrigue tightens around the protagonist
Duty conflicts with feeling, family, or truth
New order emerges or protagonist falls
description: Korean historical narrative set in the Joseon court. Indirection is structural — every action must occur within yangban propriety.
exemplars: Jewel in the Palace; Six Flying Dragons; Mr. Sunshine.

name: Hyo / Filial-piety narrative (효 서사)
beats: Filial relationship and parent's need established
Quiet deepening of bond and obligation
Filial duty is tested by impossible demand
description: Narrative built around a child's extreme sacrifice for a parent. The genre's force is in the completeness of acceptance, not internal struggle.
exemplars: Simcheong-ga; Cheong (1972 film); My Mother, the Mermaid.

name: Heungbu-style folk tale (흥부형 민담)
beats: Two siblings introduced with contrasting moral characters
Each sibling encounters a creature in distress
Kind sibling helps; cruel sibling exploits
Cruel sibling attempts to copy and is punished
description: Two-sibling Korean folk tale where moral character is revealed through how each treats the weak. The agent of justice is nature, not human authority.
exemplars: Heungbu and Nolbu; Kongjwi and Patjwi; The Tiger and the Persimmon.

name: Sin-myeong shamanic narrative (신명 서사 / 굿)
beats: Accumulated grievance or longing held in the community
Spirits invoked through music and movement
description: Narrative culminating in collective ecstatic release — kut shamanic ritual, mask-dance climax. Resolution is experiential and ecstatic rather than logical.
exemplars: The Wailing's kut sequence; Sopyonje's climactic sori; talchum mask-dance.

name: Qǐ-chéng-zhuǎn-hé narrative (起承轉合)
description: Original Tang-dynasty 4-beat structure that gave rise to kishōtenketsu and gi-seung-jeon-gyeol. Foundational to classical Chinese poetry, especially jueju.
exemplars: Du Fu and Li Bai jueju poems; Lu Xun short essays.

name: Wuxia / Martial-hero narrative (武俠)
description: Narrative of a martial-arts protagonist navigating the jianghu — the underworld of rival sects, sworn brotherhoods, and unwritten honor codes. Defining tension is conflict between feeling, code, and political duty.
exemplars: Jin Yong's Legend of the Condor Heroes; Gu Long's Chu Liuxiang; King Hu films.

name: Xianxia / Cultivation-fantasy narrative (仙俠)
beats: Cultivation path begins under master or scripture
Heavenly tribulation descends and is survived
Final ascension to immortality or sovereignty
description: Narrative of a cultivator's ascent through measurable tiers of spiritual/martial advancement. The structural payoff is advancement itself; each breakthrough is a beat.
exemplars: Investiture of the Gods; I Shall Seal the Heavens; The Untamed.

name: Sanguo-style strategic narrative (三國演義式)
beats: Stratagem laid quietly across many scenes
Reversal of fortune through superior planning
description: Historical-strategic narrative whose payoff is the disclosure of long-laid plans. The strategist's perspective is foregrounded, not the spy/detective's discovery.
exemplars: Romance of the Three Kingdoms; Records of the Grand Historian.

name: Daoist sage parable (道家寓言)
description: Short philosophical narrative whose payoff is the Dào revelation — non-conceptual insight via paradox, animal-fable, or skilled artisan. Resolves through wuwei.
exemplars: Zhuangzi's "Cook Ding Cuts Up an Ox"; "The Useless Tree"; "The Butterfly Dream".

name: Confucian moral exemplum (儒家典範故事)
beats: Protagonist's filial or moral situation established
Heaven, parent, or community recognizes the virtue
description: Short didactic narrative built to demonstrate a Confucian virtue through a single exemplary action. Force comes from the completeness of acceptance.
exemplars: 24 Filial Exemplars (二十四孝); didactic episodes in Three Kingdoms.

name: Chuanqi / Tang marvelous tale (傳奇)
beats: Scholar or young man encountered in mortal circumstances
Bond forms across the supernatural divide
Karma returns across lives or reveals true identity
description: Short literary tale mixing strange (foxes, ghosts, immortals) with the human (love, examinations, journeys). The supernatural is moral mirror.
exemplars: "The Story of Yingying" (Yuan Zhen); "Du Zichun"; Taiping Guangji.

name: Zhiguai / Anomaly record (志怪)
beats: A factual-register opening: name, date, place
Brief reflection or moral, often understated
description: Short tale recording a strange event in documentary register, as if reporting fact. Distinct from chuanqi by being shorter and more cataloging.
exemplars: Pu Songling's Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio; Gan Bao's In Search of the Supernatural.

name: Caizi-jiaren / Scholar-and-beauty romance (才子佳人)
beats: Scholar and beauty introduced separately, both exceptional
Familial, political, or social obstacle separates them
Reunion and union, often sanctioned by the emperor
description: Ming-Qing romance pairing scholar with talented young woman, overcoming social obstacles toward happy union. Lovers court through composed verse.
exemplars: Wang Shifu's Story of the Western Wing; Tang Xianzu's Peony Pavilion.

name: Shenmo / Gods-and-demons fantasy (神魔)
beats: Cosmic order established (Heaven, mortal realm, demonic realm)
Episodic encounters with demons, gods, and trials
Protagonist's own cultivation across the journey
description: Long-form fantasy where a mortal protagonist traverses a cosmology of gods, demons, immortals. Signature: cosmic, picaresque, episodic scale.
exemplars: Wu Cheng'en's Journey to the West; Investiture of the Gods.

name: Pinghua / Oral storytelling chapter-novel (評話 / 說書)
beats: Recap or resumption from prior chapter
description: Long narrative composed for oral performance, structured around chapter-end cliffhangers. Audience-aware pacing built into the form.
exemplars: Water Margin; Three Kingdoms in oral form; Yangzhou pinghua.

name: Pañca-Sandhi drama (पञ्चसन्धि)
description: 5-juncture structure of Sanskrit drama from Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra. Use when the story should have classical formal symmetry with a deliberate pause before final movement.
exemplars: Kalidasa's Abhijñānaśākuntalam; Bhasa's Svapnavāsavadattam; Shudraka's Mṛcchakaṭika.

name: Navarasa-driven narrative (नवरस)
beats: Contrasting rasas introduced for relief and depth
Emotional intensification toward the dominant rasa
Climactic full expression of the dominant rasa
Settling into the dominant flavor's afterglow
description: Narrative organized to evoke the nine rasas systematically — śṛṅgāra, hāsya, karuṇā, raudra, vīra, bhayānaka, bībhatsa, adbhuta, śānta. Use when the structural ambition is emotional.
exemplars: Kalidasa's Meghadūta; Tagore's Gitanjali; Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali.

name: Itihasa epic / Ramayana 7-kāṇḍa (इतिहास)
beats: Court life and the just-before crisis (Ayodhyā-kāṇḍa)
description: Classical Indian historical-mythical epic. Vast, multi-generational, with frame narrators and explicit didactic interludes. Use when narrative requires civilizational scope.
exemplars: Valmiki's Rāmāyaṇa; Vyasa's Mahābhārata (18-parva variant); Tulsidas's Rāmcaritmānas.

name: Jataka tale (जातक)
beats: Present-day occasion that prompts the telling
Karmic outcome resolves the past-life tale
Moral identification of present-day characters with past-life ones
description: Buddhist birth-story: a present situation explained by a past life of the Bodhisattva, illustrating karmic root of present circumstance. 547 canonical Jatakas in Pali.
exemplars: The Monkey King Jataka; The Hare in the Moon; Vessantara Jātaka.

name: Pañchatantra fable (पञ्चतन्त्र)
beats: Frame question or dilemma is posed
Nested fable inside the first if relevant
Outcome of the fable demonstrates the principle
description: Nested-frame collection of moral animal fables organized into five books, each demonstrating a principle of practical wisdom (nīti).
exemplars: Vishnu Sharma's Pañcatantra; Arabic Kalīla wa Dimna; Hitopadeśa.

name: Kāvya / Refined poetic narrative (काव्य)
beats: Description of city, season, and beauty
Love or quest establishes the action
description: Classical Sanskrit refined literary narrative — ornate description, elaborate similes, attention to figures of sound and sense. Mahākāvya canonical structure.
exemplars: Kalidasa's Raghuvaṃśa; Bharavi's Kirātārjunīya; Sri Harsha's Naiṣadhīyacarita.

name: Champu / Mixed prose-verse (चम्पू)
beats: Verse intensifies a key image or emotion
description: Classical Indian narrative form combining prose and verse passages — prose for action, verse for emotional intensification. Oscillates between fast prose movement and lyrical lingering.
exemplars: Trivikrama Bhaṭṭa's Nalacampū; Bhoja's Rāmāyaṇacampū.

name: Sangam Akam / Interior love-narrative (அகம்)
beats: Emotional situation unfolds within the tiṇai's logic
description: Classical Tamil love-poetry-narrative classified by tiṇai (landscape-mood). Mountain (kuṟiñci) for union, forest (mullai) for separation, etc. The landscape IS the emotional state.
exemplars: Kuṟuntokai; Akanāṉūṟu; Naṟṟiṇai.

name: Sangam Puram / Exterior heroic narrative (புறம்)
beats: Hero or king introduced in public role
Hero acts according to aṟam (righteous duty)
description: Classical Tamil exterior-life narrative: war, kings, gifts, public death, the ethics of the warrior. Counterpart to akam.
exemplars: Puṟanāṉūṟu; Patiṟṟuppattu; Sangam bardic praise-poems.

name: Bhakti devotional narrative (भक्ति)
beats: Memory or vision of the divine beloved
description: Devotional poem-narrative whose engine is the lover-devotee's longing for the divine beloved. The relationship between human and divine is structured as romance.
exemplars: Mirabai's bhajans; Andal's Tiruppāvai; Surdas; Kabir; Tagore's Gitanjali.

name: Maqama / Rhymed-prose picaresque (مقامة)
beats: Narrator places himself in a particular city
Stranger delivers an extraordinary verbal performance
Narrator recognizes the stranger as the recurring rogue
description: Short rhymed-prose tale featuring a recurring eloquent rogue who deceives through dazzling display of language. Episodic; collections of 50-100 maqamat per author.
exemplars: Al-Hamadhani's Maqamat (the original 51); al-Hariri's Maqamat (50); Andalusian imitations.

name: Dastan / Oral epic (داستان)
beats: Hero ventures into the world; first adventures
Encounter with the tilism (enchanted realm) or supernatural antagonist
description: Long oral epic narrative shared across Persian, Arabic, Turkic, Urdu, and South Asian Muslim cultures. Performed by professional dastango.
exemplars: Dāstān-e Amir Hamza (the Hamzanama); Tilism-e Hoshruba; Persian Shāhnāma.

name: Mathnawi / Sufi narrative poem (مثنوی)
beats: Digression into a related tale or parable
Resolution that leaves the spiritual point as residue
description: Long narrative poem in rhyming couplets, often loosely-structured as chain of stories illustrating Sufi teaching. Stories teach by accumulation rather than direct moral.
exemplars: Rumi's Masnavi-i Ma'navi; Attar's Conference of the Birds; Sanai's Hadiqat al-Haqiqa.

name: Frame-tale / Thousand and One Nights (ألف ليلة وليلة)
beats: Frame situation established (the king and Scheherazade)
Outer-frame story begins for the night
Sometimes a doubly-nested tale inside that
Return to frame; cliffhanger holds for next night
description: Frame-narrative form where outer story (Scheherazade) contains hundreds of nested tales. The frame's tension (death deferred by storytelling) saturates every sub-tale.
exemplars: One Thousand and One Nights; Tūṭīnāma; Sindbad-nāma.

name: Sufi parable (حكمة)
description: Short illustrative tale delivering Sufi spiritual point through paradox, reversal, or apparent foolishness — often featuring a wise fool. Surface absurdity is the door to deeper truth.
exemplars: Mulla Nasruddin tales; Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliyā; Idries Shah collections.

name: Marsiya / Karbala elegy (مرثیة)
beats: Companions one by one approach martyrdom
Final battle and death of the Imam
description: Shi'a Islamic elegiac narrative retelling Husayn's martyrdom at Karbala, performed during Muharram. Communal sacred grief; collective re-living of originating martyrdom.
exemplars: Anis's Marsiya-e Anis; Dabir's marsiyas; Lucknow school marsiya recitations.

name: Sirah / Prophetic biography (سيرة)
description: Biographical narrative of the Prophet Muhammad assembled from hadith and chains of transmission. Citation-chains ground every event.
exemplars: Ibn Ishaq's Sīrat Rasūl Allāh; al-Tabari's history; Martin Lings's Muhammad.

name: Adab essay-narrative (أدب)
description: Refined essayistic prose tradition combining ethical instruction, historical anecdote, witty dialogue, poetry, and personal observation. Cultivated worldliness.
exemplars: al-Jahiz's Kitab al-Bukhalaʾ; al-Tanukhi; Ibn Qutayba.

name: Griot epic / Sundiata model
beats: Genealogy and praise of the lineage opens
Hero overcomes the deficiency through trial
Closing praise that ties hero to present audience
description: Long oral epic performed by hereditary jeli/griot, recounting the founding figure of an empire or lineage. Integrates praise-song, history, genealogy, proverbs, kora/balafon.
exemplars: Sundiata: An Epic of Old Mali; the Sunjata Epic in multiple griot lineages.

name: Anansi trickster cycle
beats: Anansi covets something he hasn't earned
Larger or stronger figure is targeted
Outcome is celebrated or used to explain how something came to be
description: Akan trickster tales featuring Anansi the spider outwitting stronger animals through cunning. Carried to Caribbean and Americas via slave trade.
exemplars: How Anansi Got the Stories; Anansi and the Sky-God; Anansi and Turtle.

name: Ifá ese / Divination story
beats: The diviner gives a prescription (often a sacrifice, ebo)
Lesson applies to the present consultation
description: Yoruba divination narrative attached to one of the 256 odu. When a babalawo casts and an odu emerges, its corresponding ese is recited. Prescriptive-prophetic function.
exemplars: Ese attached to Eji-Ogbe, Oyeku-Meji, Iwori-Meji; collected in Wande Abimbola's Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá.

name: Yoruba oriki praise-narrative (Oríkì)
beats: Historic deeds compressed into vivid epithets
Praise of physical or spiritual qualities
Closing that ties subject to audience or community
description: Yoruba praise-narrative composed of densely-packed honorifics, historical references, and metaphoric epithets. Identity-establishing rather than progressive.
exemplars: Oriki of the orisha Shango, Ogun, Yemoja; Karin Barber's I Could Speak Until Tomorrow.

name: Dilemma tale
beats: Setup with a problem requiring multiple actors
Tale ends with "Who deserves the most credit?"
description: Short folk tale ending in an open question rather than resolution. The community discussion IS the form's completion. Provokes moral debate.
exemplars: Tales in Bascom's African Dilemma Tales; Yoruba, Akan, Bamana, Hausa, and Limba traditions.

name: Pourquoi tale / Why-story
beats: Long-ago state of the world established
A character acts in a way that disrupts the original state
Closing etiological tag ("and that is why...")
description: Short folk tale explaining why some natural feature is the way it is. Common across West African traditions and globally.
exemplars: Why the Tortoise Has a Cracked Shell (Igbo); Why the Sky Is Far Away; Bantu origin tales.

name: Funeral praise-oration / Akan funeral
beats: Recognition of the deceased's joining the ancestors
description: Funeral praise-narrative integrating biography, lineage praise, ancestral invocation. The deceased is being escorted into the community of ancestors.
exemplars: Akan funeral orations; Yoruba ancestral oriki; Igbo ikwa ozu narratives.

name: Call-and-response narrative
description: Communal narrative form where leader recites and audience responds. Co-produced; foundational to spirituals, gospel, blues, hip-hop.
exemplars: West African work-song narratives; spirituals; jeli call-response within Sundiata.

name: Diné Hózhǫ́jí / Beauty Way ceremony-narrative
beats: Opening — the disruption that requires restoration
East movement — dawn, white shell, beginning
Closing — Hózhǫ́ náhásdlį́į́ ("It has become beauty again")
description: Ceremonial narrative structured around restoration of hózhǫ́ (balance, beauty, harmony) through four directional movements. The story returns disrupted person, family, or world to balance.
exemplars: Beautyway; Blessingway (Hózhǫ́ǫ́jí); Diné oral ceremonial narratives.

name: Coyote trickster cycle
beats: Coyote becomes hungry, lustful, or jealous
World is changed by the disaster (sometimes etiologically)
description: Widely-distributed trickster cycle across Plains, Southwest, Plateau Indigenous traditions. Coyote as both creator and fool. Morally complex and funny.
exemplars: Coyote tales across Diné, Hopi, Apache, Nez Perce, Salish, Crow, Lakota.

name: Popol Vuh creation cycle
beats: Primordial state — water and sky, before time
First attempts at creating humans (mud, wood) fail
Hero Twins introduced; their father defeated in Xibalba
Twins descend into Xibalba and undergo trials
Twins defeat the Lords of Death through trickery
Twins ascend; sun and moon emerge
description: K'iche' Maya creation narrative — origin of world, multiple creation-failures, Hero Twins' descent into Xibalba, emergence of present world.
exemplars: Popol Vuh (transcribed 16th c.); Dennis Tedlock's English translation.

name: Lakota star-knowledge cycle
beats: Corresponding earthly journey or ceremony begins
Mid-cycle — story enters its central event
Stars shift; earthly events shift in parallel
Closing — stars and ceremony align in completion
description: Lakota narrative cycle in which sacred stories are mapped onto stars and constellations, with corresponding earthly events following seasonal star movements.
exemplars: Lakota cycles connected to the Pte San Win story; Goodman's Lakota Star Knowledge.

name: Iroquois Great Law origin narrative (Kayanerenkó:wa)
beats: Hiawatha's daughters die; he is shattered by grief
Peacemaker meets Hiawatha and consoles him through ceremony
They travel together to convert each nation
Five Nations united under the Great Law
description: Haudenosaunee origin narrative of the Great Law of Peace — founding of the Confederacy by the Peacemaker and Hiawatha. Collective political form emerges from individual mourning.
exemplars: The Great Law of Peace (Haudenosaunee oral and wampum-recorded tradition); Arthur Parker's rendering.

name: Inuit Sedna narrative
beats: She is tricked or forced into a bad marriage
Father throws Sedna into the sea; she clings to the gunwale
Her fingers are cut; each finger becomes a marine animal
She descends to the bottom of the sea, becoming its mother
Ongoing relationship — humans must propitiate her
description: Inuit narrative cycle of Sedna (Nuliajuk) — sea-mother whose body parts become marine animals. Encodes ethical relationships with hunted animals.
exemplars: Sedna narratives across Inuit communities (Greenland, Nunavut, Alaska); Knud Rasmussen's recordings.

name: Nanabozho trickster-creator cycle
beats: Nanabozho desires something or feels a lack
Feature of the present landscape or animal-world results
description: Anishinaabe narrative cycle of Nanabozho — culture-hero, trickster, creator. World-shaping is byproduct of foolish appetite rather than divine intention.
exemplars: Nanabozho cycles across Ojibwe, Odawa, Potawatomi traditions; Basil Johnston's Ojibway Heritage.

name: Haudenosaunee Thanksgiving Address (Ohén:ton Karihwatéhkwen)
description: Haudenosaunee opening prayer-narrative recited before all gatherings. Each beat: "We give thanks to [X]; now our minds are one." Gratitude as cosmology.
exemplars: Living Haudenosaunee tradition; recited before councils, ceremonies, schools; Robin Wall Kimmerer's Braiding Sweetgrass.

name: Icelandic family saga (Íslendingasögur)
beats: Genealogical opening — settlers and farms introduced
Killing or wrongdoing escalates the feud
Chain of killings extends across generations
description: Icelandic family saga: prose narrative of multi-generational feuds in Iceland's settlement period, composed in 13th-14th c. with restrained, almost documentary register.
exemplars: Njáls saga; Egils saga; Laxdœla saga; Grettis saga; Gísla saga.

name: Echtrae / Irish otherworld adventure
beats: Otherworld figure (often a fairy woman) arrives with invitation
Hero returns, often warned not to touch mortal soil
Return reveals mortal time has passed; transformation or death follows
description: Early Irish narrative form — hero is invited to the Otherworld, returns to find mortal world transformed or aged. Dangerous porousness between worlds.
exemplars: Echtrae Conli; Echtrae Cormaic; Echtrae Bran.

name: Immram / Irish sea-voyage
beats: Departure from Ireland for a holy or driven reason
First island — wonder, ordeal, or temptation
Subsequent islands, each with its own meaning
Encounter with the Earthly Paradise or sacred destination
Survivor returns transformed; many companions lost
description: Early Irish sea-voyage narrative through sequence of strange islands, each with its own marvel or ordeal. Episodic-allegorical journey.
exemplars: Immram Brain; Immram Curaig Maíle Dúin; Navigatio Sancti Brendani.

name: Táin / Cattle-raid epic (Táin Bó Cúailnge)
beats: Pillow talk — Medb and Ailill argue who is wealthier
Ulstermen incapacitated by curse — Cú Chulainn alone defends
Sequence of single combats at fords
Death of Cú Chulainn's foster-brother Ferdiad in single combat
Bull captured, fights and kills the rival bull, dies
description: Central narrative of the Irish Ulster Cycle. Queen Medb raids Ulster for the great brown bull; Cú Chulainn alone defends through single combats.
exemplars: Táin Bó Cúailnge (Old Irish, 11th-12th c.); Thomas Kinsella's modern translation.

name: Mabinogi / Welsh Four Branches (Pedair Cainc y Mabinogi)
beats: Protagonist established in a particular kingdom
Encounter with the otherworld or marvel
description: Four Branches of the Welsh Mabinogi — structurally interlinked sequence of medieval Welsh prose narratives following different but connected protagonists.
exemplars: The Mabinogion (Sioned Davies trans.); the Four Branches: Pwyll, Branwen, Manawydan, Math.

name: Eddic mythological poem (Eddukvæði)
beats: Invocation or framing voice (often a völva)
Mythic situation established (often cosmic origin or impending crisis)
Decisive action — battle, transformation, knowledge gained
description: Norse mythological poetry in alliterative meter — cosmogony, wisdom-dialogue, heroic-legendary, god-narratives. Mythologically dense rather than character-interior.
exemplars: Völuspá; Hávamál; Þrymskviða; Atlakviða; Vafþrúðnismál.

name: Aisling / Irish vision-poem
beats: Poet wandering or asleep in Irish landscape
She names herself — Ireland under various names — and laments her enslavement
She prophesies the return of the rightful king or liberation
description: Irish form: a poet falls asleep and is visited by a spéirbhean ("sky-woman") personifying Ireland. Highly conventionalized political-allegorical bardic form.
exemplars: Aogán Ó Rathaille's Gile na Gile; Eoghan Rua Ó Súilleabháin's aislings.

name: Þáttr / Norse short tale
beats: Icelander or stranger arrives at the Norwegian court
Stranger demonstrates unexpected skill or character
description: Short Norse tale, often embedded in king's-saga, where Icelander visits Norwegian court, is initially dismissed, then proves himself.
exemplars: Auðunar þáttr Vestfirzka; Þorsteins þáttr stangarhöggs.

name: Magical realism (Realismo mágico)
beats: Everyday Latin American setting established in realist register
Characters receive the marvel as ordinary
Cumulative weight of marvels reframes the realist surface
Closing — often circular, mythic, or generational
description: Narrative mode where fantastic events occur within otherwise realistic settings and are received by characters as ordinary. The supernatural is woven into daily life's texture.
exemplars: García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude; Allende's House of the Spirits; Rulfo's Pedro Páramo.

name: Lo Real Maravilloso / The marvelous real
beats: Specific Latin American historical or geographic situation
Reality of the situation reveals its own intrinsic marvel
Narrator notes that no European frame fits
Marvel is shown to be the actual character of this reality
Closing in the marvelous as a fact, not a flourish
description: Carpentier's term: where magical realism inserts the marvelous into the real, lo real maravilloso asserts that Latin American reality itself is already marvelous.
exemplars: Carpentier's El reino de este mundo; Los pasos perdidos; Carpentier's 1949 prologue.

name: Testimonio
beats: Witness establishes who they are and the community they speak for
Onset of state, paramilitary, or systemic violence
Address to the reader: "this happened, and it must be known"
description: First-person witness narrative, often spoken by a marginalized person and edited by another. Bearing witness on behalf of a community.
exemplars: Rigoberta Menchú's Me llamo Rigoberta Menchú; Domitila Barrios; Esteban Montejo (Barnet).

name: Crónica / Latin American chronicle
beats: Specific situation, scene, or person observed
Reflective turn — what does this scene mean
Wider implication or quiet closing image
description: Literary-journalistic narrative form blending essay, reportage, and short story. The narrator's voice is essayistic; events are real but rendered with literary attention.
exemplars: Pedro Lemebel's Pinochet-era crónicas; Carlos Monsiváis on Mexico City; Elena Poniatowska.

name: Boom novel / Multi-perspective complexity
beats: Personal stories and political histories intersect
Closing that may circle back to opening, transformed
description: Latin American Boom novelistic form — structurally complex, multi-perspective, time-fragmented, politically engaged. Formal experimentation mirrors political-historical complexity.
exemplars: Vargas Llosa's Conversation in the Cathedral; Cortázar's Hopscotch; Fuentes's Death of Artemio Cruz.

name: Gauchesque narrative (Literatura gauchesca)
beats: Conflict — gaucho violates state law (often justifiably)
Confrontation, often with another gaucho or state agent
Resolution — exile, death, or return on his own terms
description: Argentine-Uruguayan narrative featuring the gaucho — pampas horseman — as protagonist. Frontier-pastoral with state-conflict undertone.
exemplars: Hernández's Martín Fierro; Güiraldes's Don Segundo Sombra; Borges's gauchesque stories.

name: Indigenismo narrative
beats: Indigenous community established in its own terms
Encounter with mestizo or criollo state, hacienda, or church
Indigenous resistance — often communal, sometimes spiritual
Outcome — endurance, defeat, or transformation, on Indigenous terms
description: Narrative form (primarily Andean and Mesoamerican) that places Indigenous experience and worldview at the center, critiquing the criollo state's ongoing dispossession.
exemplars: Icaza's Huasipungo; Alegría's Broad and Alien Is the World; Arguedas's Deep Rivers; Castellanos's Balún Canán.

name: Costumbrismo / Manners narrative
beats: Detailed observation of a representative scene
Type or character emerges from the scene
Narrator's reflection — affectionate, satirical, or melancholy
description: 19th-c. literary form focused on close observation of regional customs, types, manners, folk life. Anthropological in eye, literary in voice.
exemplars: Ricardo Palma's Tradiciones peruanas; Esteban Echeverría's "El matadero"; cuadros de costumbres.

name: Aristotelian three-act structure
beats: End — resolution that follows necessarily from the middle
description: Foundational Western dramatic structure. Every action has a beginning, middle, and end. Most modern story structures elaborate this base.
exemplars: Sophocles' Oedipus Rex; most Western feature films at macro level; Hamlet; Pride and Prejudice.

name: Freytag's Pyramid / 5-act structure
beats: Rising action — complication and tension build
Climax — peak of tension; protagonist's fortune turns
Falling action — consequences of the climax unfold
description: Gustav Freytag's 5-act model derived from Greek and Shakespearean tragedy. The pyramid reflects rise toward climax and fall after.
exemplars: Shakespeare's Macbeth, Othello, Romeo and Juliet; Sophocles' Antigone.

name: Overcoming the Monster (Booker)
beats: Anticipation — hero learns of the monster
Final escape and reversal — monster destroyed; hero returns
description: Booker's plot 1: protagonist learns of great evil, prepares, faces apparent defeat, then defeats the monster. Use when threat is singular, embodied, must be confronted directly.
exemplars: Beowulf; Dracula; Jaws; Star Wars: A New Hope; Alien.

name: Rags to Riches (Booker)
beats: Out into the world; initial success
description: Booker's plot 2: poor figure rises to wealth, falls back into adversity, then rises permanently with mature self-knowledge. Deserved elevation tested by reversal.
exemplars: Cinderella; David Copperfield; Aladdin; Jane Eyre; Slumdog Millionaire.

name: The Quest (Booker)
beats: The call — goal revealed; hero accepts
Arrival and frustration — goal in sight but blocked
Final ordeals — last and worst trials
Goal — object obtained or place reached
description: Booker's plot 3: hero learns of precious object/place, journeys with companions, faces ordeals, obtains the goal. External-goal-oriented.
exemplars: The Odyssey; The Lord of the Rings; Watership Down; Indiana Jones and the Raiders of the Lost Ark.

name: Voyage and Return (Booker)
beats: Anticipation and fall into the other world
Initial fascination — the new world is wondrous
Frustration — the new world becomes threatening
Thrilling escape and return — homeward, changed
description: Booker's plot 4: protagonist travels into strange world, has wondrous and threatening experiences, escapes home transformed. No specific goal — the journey IS the structure.
exemplars: Alice in Wonderland; Gulliver's Travels; The Wizard of Oz; Gone with the Wind.

name: Comedy (Booker)
beats: A small, tightly-knit world fallen under shadow of confusion
Recognition — true identities and feelings revealed
Restoration — new community formed; often weddings
description: Booker's plot 5: society in confusion deepens to apparent impasse, resolved with everyone reconciled. Confusion resolved into community.
exemplars: Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, Twelfth Night; Austen's novels; Bringing Up Baby.

name: Tragedy (Booker)
beats: Anticipation — protagonist drawn toward fateful course
Dream — initial commitment; success seems possible
Nightmare — situation spirals out of control
description: Booker's plot 6: protagonist commits to a course driven by ego-attachment that gradually consumes them, leading inevitably to their destruction.
exemplars: Macbeth; Anna Karenina; Death of a Salesman; Breaking Bad; Citizen Kane.

name: Rebirth (Booker)
beats: Falling under shadow — protagonist enters dark state
State seems to ease — false reprieve
Threat of doom returns and intensifies
Imprisonment — completely under the dark power
Redemption — love or sacrifice breaks the spell
description: Booker's plot 7: protagonist falls under dark power, is gradually swallowed, then redeemed by love or sacrifice that breaks the spell.
exemplars: A Christmas Carol; Beauty and the Beast; Crime and Punishment; Groundhog Day.

name: Quest (Tobias)
beats: Hero in unsatisfied state; receives the call
Series of trials, each revealing something about the hero
Discovery that the real quest is internal
Achievement of the goal — transformed in self
description: Tobias's character-focused quest: external goal is placeholder for self-discovery. Use when external goal is secondary to internal transformation.
exemplars: Don Quixote; The Alchemist; Eat, Pray, Love; Wild (Strayed).

name: Adventure (Tobias)
beats: Inciting event sends hero into action
Travel to new locations; obstacles encountered
Each location adds excitement and stakes
description: Tobias's action-focused adventure: series of incidents drives protagonist forward. Action, novelty, travel for their own sake.
exemplars: Treasure Island; Jurassic Park; Indiana Jones; The Hobbit.

name: Pursuit (Tobias)
beats: Reversal — pursued may turn or pursuer may falter
Capture or escape resolves the pursuit
description: One character pursues another. The chase IS the plot. Tension from physical or strategic pursuit.
exemplars: Les Misérables; The Fugitive; Mad Max: Fury Road; Heat.

name: Rescue (Tobias)
beats: Hero pursues villain to recover victim
description: Hero must save a victim from a villain. Three-cornered structure: hero, villain, victim. Moral clarity of "save the innocent from the wicked."
exemplars: The Searchers; Taken; Saving Private Ryan; Princess Bride.

name: Escape (Tobias)
beats: Capture or imprisonment establishes the trap
description: Protagonist is trapped and must escape. The protagonist saves themselves. Self-liberation under constraint.
exemplars: The Count of Monte Cristo; The Shawshank Redemption; The Great Escape; Papillon.

name: Revenge (Tobias)
beats: Consequences of revenge — vindication or hollowness
description: Protagonist is wronged and seeks retribution. The genre's question is whether revenge will satisfy or destroy.
exemplars: The Count of Monte Cristo; Hamlet; Kill Bill; Oldboy; Gladiator.

name: The Riddle (Tobias)
description: Puzzle at the heart of the narrative; reader and protagonist work together to solve it. The pleasure is the deduction.
exemplars: The Murders in the Rue Morgue; The Da Vinci Code; The Name of the Rose; Christie generally.

name: Rivalry (Tobias)
beats: Two rivals introduced — equally matched, opposed in goal
Each rival escalates; each gains and loses
Resolution — one wins, one falls; or both transformed
description: Two protagonists locked in opposition, each defined by the other. Symmetrical — both characters are full agents.
exemplars: Amadeus; The Social Network; The Prestige; Ben-Hur.

name: Underdog (Tobias)
description: Sustained narrative of unlikely hero rising against more powerful opposition. Disadvantage as the fuel for an extended arc.
exemplars: Rocky; Karate Kid; Slumdog Millionaire; The Pursuit of Happyness.

name: Temptation (Tobias)
description: Protagonist faces moral test in the form of attractive but forbidden choice. Internal struggle is the center.
exemplars: Faust; The Picture of Dorian Gray; Wall Street; The Talented Mr. Ripley.

name: Metamorphosis (Tobias)
beats: Crisis brought on by the transformation
description: Character undergoes literal physical or supernatural transformation. Distinct from internal Transformation: this is external/visible.
exemplars: Kafka's The Metamorphosis; The Fly; Beauty and the Beast (Beast's perspective); The Shape of Water.

name: Transformation (Tobias)
description: Internal transformation arc. Character is fundamentally changed by experience. Payoff is who the protagonist becomes.
exemplars: A Christmas Carol; Groundhog Day; Eat, Pray, Love; The King's Speech.

name: Maturation (Tobias)
beats: Young protagonist in protected or limited world
Confrontation with adult complications and disillusionment
description: Coming-of-age plot. Young protagonist confronts adult world and matures through hardship. The bildungsroman shape.
exemplars: The Catcher in the Rye; To Kill a Mockingbird; Stand by Me; Boyhood.

name: Love (Tobias)
description: Two people meet, kept apart by obstacle, come together. Classical love-plot in simplest form. Desire crossing obstacle.
exemplars: Pride and Prejudice; When Harry Met Sally; Romeo and Juliet; Notting Hill.

name: Forbidden Love (Tobias)
beats: Lovers must choose: defy or conform
description: Love is forbidden by society, family, or moral law — and that prohibition IS the plot. Love against social structure.
exemplars: Romeo and Juliet; Tristan and Iseult; Brokeback Mountain; The English Patient.

name: Sacrifice (Tobias)
beats: Choice between self and greater good crystallizes
Greater good preserved; protagonist's loss honored
description: Protagonist must give up something dear to achieve a greater good. Climax is the sacrifice itself.
exemplars: A Tale of Two Cities; Casablanca; Saving Private Ryan; Schindler's List.

name: Discovery (Tobias)
beats: Reorganization of self around the new knowledge
description: Character uncovers truth about themselves — identity, origins, or past. Investigation is biographical-internal.
exemplars: Oedipus Rex; Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back; Atonement; The Sixth Sense.

name: Wretched Excess (Tobias)
beats: Moment of clarity — refused or accepted too late
description: Protagonist destroyed by their own appetites — gluttony, lust, ambition, addiction. Excess of a single drive consuming its host.
exemplars: Requiem for a Dream; Leaving Las Vegas; Citizen Kane; The Wolf of Wall Street.

name: Ascension (Tobias)
beats: Character in modest position with potential
description: Character rises to greatness — moral, social, or accomplishment-based. Upward-arc; climax is achievement of stature.
exemplars: Lincoln; Joan of Arc; Gandhi (Attenborough); Lawrence of Arabia.

name: Descension (Tobias)
beats: Character at heights — power, prestige, security
First crack — small loss or mistake
Bottom — sometimes with possibility of rebirth
description: Character falls from great position. Fall-arc; gradual loss of stature, position, or self.
exemplars: King Lear; Sunset Boulevard; There Will Be Blood; The Godfather Part II.

name: Polti's 36 Dramatic Situations (taxonomic)
beats: Supplication, 2. Deliverance, 3. Crime pursued by vengeance, 4. Vengeance for kin, 5. Pursuit, 6. Disaster, 7. Falling prey to cruelty, 8. Revolt, 9. Daring enterprise, 10. Abduction, 11. The enigma, 12. Obtaining, 13. Enmity of kinsmen, 14. Rivalry of kinsmen, 15. Murderous adultery, 16. Madness, 17. Fatal imprudence, 18. Involuntary crimes of love, 19. Slaying of unrecognized kinsman, 20. Self-sacrifice for ideal, 21. Self-sacrifice for kindred, 22. All sacrificed for passion, 23. Necessity of sacrificing loved ones, 24. Rivalry superior/inferior, 25. Adultery, 26. Crimes of love, 27. Discovery of dishonor of loved one, 28. Obstacles to love, 29. An enemy loved, 30. Ambition, 31. Conflict with a god, 32. Mistaken jealousy, 33. Erroneous judgment, 34. Remorse, 35. Recovery of lost one, 36. Loss of loved ones
description: Polti's exhaustive catalog of every dramatic situation. NOT a sequential beat structure but a taxonomy of situational primitives that deploy within other structural genres. Use as scene-design vocabulary.
exemplars: Polti's foundational 1895 work uses Greek, French, Goethe drama for each.

name: Campbell's Monomyth / Hero's Journey
description: Joseph Campbell's seventeen-stage cyclical structure from cross-cultural mythological analysis. Departure, Initiation, Return.
exemplars: The Odyssey; Star Wars; The Matrix; The Lion King; Harry Potter.

name: Vogler's Writer's Journey (12-stage)
description: Christopher Vogler's screenwriting-friendly distillation of Campbell's Monomyth into 12 stages, designed for Hollywood film structure.
exemplars: Star Wars: A New Hope; The Matrix; Finding Nemo; The Lion King.

name: Harmon's Story Circle (8-stage)
beats: A character is in a zone of comfort
Pay a heavy price for it
description: Dan Harmon's compressed 8-step Hero's Journey, used in TV writing (Community, Rick and Morty). Emphasizes return-to-changed-self.
exemplars: Most Rick and Morty episodes; Community ("Remedial Chaos Theory"); many The Simpsons episodes.

name: Save the Cat (15-beat)
description: Blake Snyder's 15-beat screenplay structure, with each beat assigned to a specific page range in a 110-page screenplay. Highly prescriptive Hollywood feature standard.
exemplars: Miss Congeniality; Legally Blonde; most modern Hollywood mid-budget films.

name: Truby's 22-Step Anatomy
beats: First revelation and decision: changed desire and motive
description: John Truby's 22-step structure: built around moral premise, ghost (past wound), desire, opponent, plan, battle, self-revelation. Story as organic moral argument.
exemplars: The Godfather; Casablanca; Tootsie; L.A. Confidential.

name: Propp's 31 Folktale Functions
beats: Absentation, 2. Interdiction, 3. Violation, 4. Reconnaissance, 5. Delivery, 6. Trickery, 7. Complicity, 8. Villainy or Lack, 9. Mediation, 10. Beginning Counteraction, 11. Departure, 12. First Function of the Donor, 13. Hero's Reaction, 14. Receipt of a Magical Agent, 15. Guidance, 16. Struggle, 17. Branding, 18. Victory, 19. Liquidation, 20. Return, 21. Pursuit, 22. Rescue, 23. Unrecognized Arrival, 24. Unfounded Claims, 25. Difficult Task, 26. Solution, 27. Recognition, 28. Exposure, 29. Transfiguration, 30. Punishment, 31. Wedding
description: Vladimir Propp's structural analysis of 100 Russian folk tales yielded 31 narrative functions in fixed order. Foundational to structuralist narratology.
exemplars: Russian folktales; The Frog Prince; Cinderella (in Propp's analysis); European folktale corpus.

name: In medias res / Homeric epic structure
beats: Opening in medias res — reader dropped into a charged scene
Frame device or character begins flashback
Backstory unfolds, building toward the opening scene
Catch-up to the opening; narrative continues forward
description: Classical epic structural convention: narrative begins in middle of action (typically near climax), uses flashback or framed retelling for earlier events.
exemplars: The Iliad; The Odyssey; Paradise Lost; The Sound and the Fury; Pulp Fiction.

name: Murdock's Heroine's Journey
beats: Awakening to feelings of spiritual aridity
Initiation and descent to the goddess
Urgent yearning to reconnect with the feminine
description: Maureen Murdock's 10-stage cyclical journey: separation from feminine, identification with masculine, eventual disillusionment, reintegration with wounded feminine self.
exemplars: Eat Pray Love; Wild (Strayed); Frozen (Anna's arc); The Devil Wears Prada.

name: Hudson's Virgin's Promise
beats: Gives up what kept her stuck
description: Kim Hudson's 13-stage feminine creative-emergence journey. Protagonist begins in suppressive community, secretly cultivates her gift, is exposed, ultimately transforms her community.
exemplars: Brave (Pixar); Mulan; Moana; Billy Elliot; Whale Rider.

name: Vonnegut's Six Story Shapes (taxonomic)
beats: Man in a Hole — falls into trouble, climbs out
Boy Meets Girl — finds, loses, regains something wonderful
From Bad to Worse — steady descent
Which Way is Up — ambiguous oscillation
Creation Story — steady rise from nothing
Cinderella — small rise, sudden fall, sudden greater rise
description: Kurt Vonnegut's emotional-arc taxonomy. Stories plotted on good fortune/ill fortune over time yield one of six recurring shapes.
exemplars: Vonnegut illustrated each with classics — Cinderella, The Metamorphosis (Bad-to-Worse), biblical narratives (Creation).

name: Expository documentary
description: Voice-of-God narration directly addresses viewer to convey information, building an argument supported by visual evidence. Most traditional documentary mode.
exemplars: The Civil War (Burns); Cosmos (Sagan); Attenborough nature documentaries.

name: Observational documentary
beats: Subject's life or event begins without framing
Camera leaves; closure is what was witnessed
description: Fly-on-the-wall mode. Camera observes events without narration, interviews, or apparent intervention. Viewer positioned as witness.
exemplars: Frederick Wiseman (Titicut Follies, High School); Maysles brothers (Salesman, Grey Gardens); Hoop Dreams.

name: Participatory documentary
beats: Reflection on what the encounter has revealed
description: Filmmaker is visibly present, interacting with subjects. The documentary's truth comes from the encounter between filmmaker and subject.
exemplars: Michael Moore's films; Werner Herzog's documentaries; Nick Broomfield.

name: Reflexive documentary
beats: Construction of the documentary made visible
description: Documentary that draws attention to its own constructedness — to the conventions, the politics of representation, the impossibility of pure objectivity.
exemplars: Man with a Movie Camera (Vertov); Sans Soleil (Marker); F for Fake (Welles); The Act of Killing.

name: Performative documentary
description: Foregrounds filmmaker's subjective experience and emotional truth — personal essay, autobiography, embodied perspective. Rejects objectivity in favor of "what this means to me."
exemplars: Marlon Riggs's Tongues Untied; Sarah Polley's Stories We Tell; Agnès Varda's The Beaches of Agnès.

name: Poetic documentary
description: Privileges mood, rhythm, visual association over linear argument. Often non-narrative, organized by visual/aural patterns.
exemplars: Ruttmann's Berlin: Symphony of a Great City; Reggio's Koyaanisqatsi; Fricke's Baraka, Samsara.

name: Monroe's Motivated Sequence
beats: Need — establish a problem or unmet need
Visualization — paint the future with/without the solution
description: Alan Monroe's 5-step persuasive speech structure (1935). Specifically engineered for behavior change — not just informing but motivating action.
exemplars: Most TED Talks; nonprofit fundraising appeals; Steve Jobs's iPhone keynote.

name: Toulmin Argument Model
beats: Warrant — the principle that connects grounds to claim
Backing — support for the warrant itself
Rebuttal — circumstances under which the claim does not hold
description: Stephen Toulmin's 6-component model of practical argument. Distinguishes from formal logic by acknowledging probability and qualification.
exemplars: Most academic argumentation; legal briefs; well-constructed op-eds; policy white papers.

name: Rogerian Argument
beats: State the opposing view fairly and accurately
Acknowledge contexts in which the opposing view is valid
Show contexts in which your view is valid
Propose a synthesis or shared higher principle
description: Carl Rogers-influenced argumentative form built around establishing common ground before advancing one's position. Use when audience holds opposing views and adversarial rhetoric would harden positions.
exemplars: Conflict-resolution writing; The Atlantic's "I Used to Believe" series; mediation literature.

name: Socratic Dialogue
beats: Recognition of what the interlocutor did not know
description: Plato's didactic dialogue form. Teacher leads interlocutor through questions that expose confused premises. Teaching is in the questioning, not the assertion.
exemplars: Plato's dialogues (Meno, Republic, Euthyphro); Socratic-method legal education; Hofstadter's Gödel, Escher, Bach.

name: Aristotelian Triple Appeal (Ethos/Pathos/Logos)
beats: Logos — argument's logical structure and evidence
description: Aristotle's three modes of persuasion. Not a sequential beat structure but a triad of registers any persuasive text combines.
exemplars: Lincoln's Gettysburg Address; MLK's "I Have a Dream"; great political speeches generally.

name: Inverted Pyramid (journalism)
beats: Lead — who, what, when, where, why, how
description: Defining structure of news writing — most important information first, supporting details next, background last. Designed for telegraph-era news.
exemplars: Wire-service news (AP, Reuters); breaking news in major newspapers; NYT front-page hard news.

name: Nut-graf feature lead
beats: Nut graf — "this story is about [larger phenomenon]"
description: Feature-style structure: anecdotal opening followed by paragraph explaining why the story matters. The reader is invited in by scene before being told the stakes.
exemplars: WSJ front-page features (canonical); New Yorker reportage; long-form magazine journalism.

name: Tick-Tock
beats: Climactic event reached at its actual chronological point
description: Reconstructed-chronology narrative. A major event retold beat-by-beat in real time, often using interviews and documents.
exemplars: WaPo tick-tocks of 9/11, Capitol riot, election nights; Politico post-election reconstructions.

name: Profile / Portrait
beats: Opening scene — subject in characteristic action
Current situation; what is at stake now
Defining encounter or moment with the writer
Closing image that crystallizes the subject
description: Journalistic biographical narrative of a single person. Present scene → backstory → present significance. Tied to a present news peg.
exemplars: Talese's "Frank Sinatra Has a Cold"; New Yorker profiles; Esquire profiles; Vanity Fair features.

name: Long-form literary journalism
beats: Scene that opens with vivid specificity
Multiple scenes build the narrative arc
Closing scene that returns or transforms the opening
description: Extended reported nonfiction using techniques of fiction — scene-by-scene, full dialogue, interior perspective, status detail — to render real events.
exemplars: Capote's In Cold Blood; Didion's Slouching Towards Bethlehem; Wolfe's The Right Stuff; Orlean's The Orchid Thief.

name: Investigative narrative
beats: Documents and sources break the story open
description: Reported narrative whose engine is the journalist's investigation itself — gradual uncovering of hidden facts, often involving institutional wrongdoing.
exemplars: All the President's Men (Woodward-Bernstein); Spotlight (Boston Globe); Farrow's Catch and Kill; ProPublica.

name: Case Study
beats: Decision point — what choice was faced
Analysis — what made it work or fail
description: Structured narrative of specific business situation, decision, and outcome. Used in education, consulting, B2B marketing. Analytic register; narrative serves transferable lessons.
exemplars: Harvard Business School cases; McKinsey case studies; HubSpot customer cases; HBR case features.

name: Pitch Deck Story
description: Narrative arc of a startup investor pitch. Engineered for 10-15 slides and 15 minutes. Establishes need and offer in tight time.
exemplars: YC pitch deck template; Sequoia template; Airbnb's 2008 pitch deck.

name: Brand Origin Story
beats: Specific moment of insight or unmet need
description: Company's foundational narrative — founder's moment of insight, unmet need perceived, early struggle, present significance. Creates emotional attachment to brand.
exemplars: Nike (Phil Knight's car); Apple's garage; Patagonia's Yvon Chouinard; Airbnb's air mattresses.

name: Customer Success Story
description: Narrative of specific customer's transformation through using a product. Before-state → catalyst → after-state, with measurable outcomes.
exemplars: Salesforce customer cases; nonprofit impact reports; HBR customer features.

name: Crisis Communication
beats: Acknowledge the situation immediately and specifically
Explain what is being done now
description: Structured corporate response to scandal, accident, or public failure. Acknowledge harm, accept responsibility, articulate corrective action, restore trust.
exemplars: J&J Tylenol response (1982 gold standard); Domino's 2009 video response; Boeing 737 MAX (negative example).

name: Disruption Narrative
beats: Disruptor enters with seemingly inferior product
Disruptor improves rapidly along an unexpected dimension
description: Christensen's framing as public narrative: incumbent industry leader overtaken by smaller competitor offering "worse" product that redefines market.
exemplars: Netflix vs Blockbuster; Tesla vs legacy auto; Uber vs taxis; Airbnb vs hotels; Christensen's The Innovator's Dilemma.

name: White Paper
beats: Current state of solutions and their limitations
description: Long-form authoritative document defining a problem, examining existing solutions, advocating a specific approach. Used in B2B marketing, policy advocacy.
exemplars: Government policy white papers; Bitcoin whitepaper (Satoshi 2008); enterprise software vendor whitepapers.

name: IMRAD Research Paper
beats: Methods — how the research was conducted
Discussion — what the results mean, limitations, implications
description: Standard structure of empirical scientific papers. Designed for reproducibility and rapid expert reading.
exemplars: Most empirical scientific papers since mid-20th c.; Nature, Science, biomedical journals.

name: Literature Review
description: Academic synthesis of existing research — a structured map of the field. Identifies major findings, contested questions, methodological approaches, gaps.
exemplars: Annual Review articles; doctoral dissertation literature-review chapters; systematic reviews in medicine.

name: Position Paper / Op-Ed
beats: Hook — a vivid case or news peg
description: Short-to-medium argumentative essay advocating a specific position. Compressed for journalistic or institutional reading.
exemplars: NYT op-eds; Atlantic essays; institutional position papers; academic policy essays.

name: Grant Proposal
description: Structured request for funding research, programs, or projects. Distinguished by dual audience: program officers and reviewers.
exemplars: NIH R01 grants; NSF proposals; foundation grants (Ford, MacArthur, Gates); humanities NEH grants.

name: Opening Statement (legal)
beats: Theme of the case stated in one sentence
Identification of key witnesses and what they will say
Promise of what the evidence will show
What the lawyer will ask the jury to find
description: First address by lawyer to jury, previewing the case. Strictly bounded — must be roadmap, not argument; promises evidence rather than asserting conclusions.
exemplars: Iconic opening statements: O.J. Simpson trial; Atticus Finch in To Kill a Mockingbird; A Few Good Men.

name: Closing Argument (legal)
beats: Story of what happened, now with evidentiary backing
Why the evidence proves the claim
Anticipation and rebuttal of opposing argument
description: Lawyer's final address to jury, connecting evidence to verdict requested. Argument is permitted; lawyer is now persuading rather than previewing.
exemplars: Atticus Finch's closing in To Kill a Mockingbird; Clarence Darrow's closings; 12 Angry Men.

name: Stump Speech
beats: Personal story that grounds the candidate
Call to action — vote, volunteer, donate
description: Repeated political speech delivered across many campaign stops. Modular and emotionally consistent — same emotional arc through varying details.
exemplars: Obama's 2008 campaign stump; Bernie Sanders 2016/2020; classical campaign speeches.

name: Inaugural Address
beats: Acknowledgment of the moment and predecessors
Naming of the historical challenge or opportunity
Vision and call to collective effort
Ceremonial close — often invoking divine or historical witness
description: Ceremonial speech by incoming head of state. Distinguished by move from contested partisanship to symbolic unity.
exemplars: Lincoln's Second Inaugural; FDR's First Inaugural; JFK's "ask not"; Obama 2009.

name: Concession Speech
description: Speech of defeated candidate acknowledging loss and legitimacy of opponent's victory. The transfer of legitimacy IS the engine.
exemplars: Al Gore 2000; John McCain 2008; Hillary Clinton 2016.

name: Manifesto
beats: Identification of the responsible parties or systems
Call to immediate action or alignment
description: Declarative public statement of intent or principles by a movement. Designed to provoke alignment and rupture. Galvanizes rather than persuades.
exemplars: Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto; Futurist Manifesto (Marinetti); Port Huron Statement; Haraway's Cyborg Manifesto.

name: Whistleblower Narrative
beats: Insider's position and initial belief in the institution
Implications for the institution and the public
description: First-person account of insider exposing institutional wrongdoing, often at personal cost. Authority comes from inside position.
exemplars: Snowden's Permanent Record; Ellsberg's Secrets; Frances Haugen; Wigand (basis for The Insider).

name: Cosmic Horror (Lovecraftian)
beats: Scholar or investigator encounters disturbing artifact or text
Investigation reveals fragments of cosmic truth
Each new revelation is worse than the last
Glimpse of the actual cosmic horror
Investigator's mind cracks under the truth
Closing — suggestion that the horror persists
description: Horror based on smallness of human consciousness against indifferent or malevolent cosmos. The threat is ontological, not personal.
exemplars: Lovecraft's "Call of Cthulhu," "At the Mountains of Madness"; Blackwood's "The Willows"; True Detective S1; Annihilation (VanderMeer).

name: Gothic Horror
beats: Innocent protagonist arrives at gloomy ancestral place
House or estate destroyed or transformed
description: Horror anchored in atmospheric place — haunted house, ruined castle, decaying estate — and family secrets, suppressed sexuality, return of the buried past.
exemplars: Walpole's Castle of Otranto; Wuthering Heights; Jane Eyre; Rebecca; The Haunting of Hill House; Crimson Peak.

name: Whodunit
beats: Murder discovered in a contained setting
Reveal of the true murderer with reasoning
description: Puzzle-mystery in which detective gathers clues to identify killer from closed cast of suspects. The pleasure is the deduction; clues are fairly available to careful reader.
exemplars: Christie's And Then There Were None, Murder on the Orient Express; Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes; Knives Out; Glass Onion.

name: Hardboiled Detective
beats: Detective hired for a seemingly small case
First-person narrator establishes voice and city
Case opens up — wider corruption hinted
Resolution that does not restore order — corruption persists
description: Detective story rooted in urban realism, moral ambiguity, cynical first-person narrator. The puzzle is secondary to atmosphere and detective's character.
exemplars: Hammett's The Maltese Falcon; Chandler's The Big Sleep; Mosley's Easy Rawlins; Chinatown; Mystic River.

name: Cozy Mystery
beats: Detective uses local knowledge to solve
description: Puzzle-mystery in low-violence pastoral or small-town setting with amateur detective. The world is one the reader wants to return to.
exemplars: Christie's Miss Marple; Murder, She Wrote; Hamish Macbeth; Only Murders in the Building.

name: Bildungsroman
beats: Departure from home into wider world
Sequence of formative encounters and lessons
Re-orientation and decision about life path
description: European novel of formation. Young protagonist's psychological and moral development from naïve youth through formative trials to mature adulthood.
exemplars: Goethe's Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship; David Copperfield; Great Expectations; Portrait of the Artist; To Kill a Mockingbird.

name: Picaresque
beats: Pícaro introduced as low-born and resourceful
Picaresque journey begins — series of episodic encounters
Each episode exposes a different social stratum's hypocrisy
Pícaro's wits are tested and survive
description: Satirical episodic novel following low-born rogue through adventures across various social strata, exposing each through the rogue's wits. Pícaro does NOT mature — they survive.
exemplars: Lazarillo de Tormes; Don Quixote (in part); Tom Jones; Huckleberry Finn; Augie March; Catch-22.

name: Refusal-of-the-Easy
beats: Quiet refusal that needs no defense
Cost of refusal absorbed without complaint
description: Short narrative whose entire arc is the protagonist's deliberate refusal of an obviously beneficial choice — not because they fail to see its value, but because accepting would betray something they refuse to name. Quiet sovereignty as the resolution.
exemplars: Cincinnatus narratives; Washington stepping down after two terms; Bartleby's "I would prefer not to" extended into a structural arc.

name: The Inversion of Care
beats: Devoted care established as a relationship's defining trait
The care, taken to an extreme or wrong shape, harms its object
Recognition that the love and the harm cannot be separated
description: Narrative in which the act of caring for someone causes the harm it sought to prevent. Captures the loving harmer — good intentions becoming the wound.
exemplars: Lady Bird (mother's love as criticism); helicopter-parenting narratives; over-protection that accelerates decline.

name: Witness-Without-Intervention
beats: Protagonist arrives in position to witness
Sustained, attentive observation of what unfolds
Departure — what was seen is now carried by the witness
description: Narrative in which the protagonist is positioned as witness to something significant — usually injustice or beauty — and the structural payoff is the quality of the witnessing itself, not action taken.
exemplars: Travel writing; quieter wartime journalism; Didion's California essays; certain photography essays (Salgado).

name: Slow-Yes
beats: Series of small offerings absorbed without acknowledgment
Yes arrives quietly, almost without ceremony
description: Narrative whose entire arc is the gradual softening of a no into a yes — across many small moments rather than a single decisive turn. Cumulative arrival without obstacle.
exemplars: Late-life-romance narratives; mentor/student arcs; The Remains of the Day (in some readings); Lost in Translation.

name: Ledger-Closes
beats: Old, unsettled obligation established as background
Quiet decision and movement to settle it now
description: Narrative whose engine is settling a long-standing moral debt — not revenge (hot, proportional), but cool deliberate return of what was owed, after many years.
exemplars: Restitution narratives in post-war fiction; The Reader (Schlink); Ishiguro's The Buried Giant; estate-and-inheritance dramas.

name: The Held Question
beats: Partial answers and complications deepen the question
Question articulated more precisely; resolution declined
description: Narrative whose payoff is the deepening of a question rather than its resolution. The question itself ripens. Reader leaves more curious, more precisely uncertain.
exemplars: Borges's "The Library of Babel"; Anne Carson's The Glass Essay; The Crying of Lot 49 (Pynchon); some W.G. Sebald.

name: Chosen One narrative
beats: Prophecy or sign reveals the chosen status
Trials that prove or threaten the chosenness
Final confrontation only the chosen can face
description: Protagonist singled out by prophecy, birth, or supernatural sign as uniquely fated. Distinct from Hero's Journey by its external selection — the call is not refuseable in any meaningful way.
exemplars: Harry Potter; The Matrix (Neo); Star Wars (Anakin/Luke); Dune (Paul Atreides); Buffy the Vampire Slayer.

name: Fish Out of Water
beats: Protagonist established in their native element
Failures of adaptation produce comedy or trouble
Resolution — protagonist either adapts or returns transformed
description: Protagonist placed in environment radically alien to their habits and competencies; the friction between protagonist and setting drives both comedy and growth.
exemplars: Crocodile Dundee; Coming to America; Lost in Translation; Schitt's Creek.

name: Mentor and Pupil
beats: Pupil's trial (with or without mentor present)
Pupil surpasses, honors, or buries the mentor
description: Narrative centered on relationship between experienced master and inexperienced student. The mentor's wisdom is tested as much as the pupil's capacity. Story is about transmission across generations.
exemplars: Star Wars (Yoda/Luke); Karate Kid; Good Will Hunting; Dead Poets Society; Whiplash.

name: Buddy narrative
beats: Both characters established in their distinct modes
description: Two protagonists with contrasting temperaments, methods, or backgrounds paired (often forced together). Pleasure is the friction-and-bond between mismatched partners.
exemplars: Lethal Weapon; Rush Hour; Toy Story; Pulp Fiction (Vincent and Jules); 48 Hrs.

name: Ensemble narrative
beats: Cast introduced in their network of relations
Lines of conflict and alliance form
Climactic event involves the whole group
description: Narrative organized around a group of roughly equal-weight characters whose intersecting arcs constitute the story. The cast IS the story.
exemplars: The Big Chill; Magnolia; Crash; Love Actually; Friends; The Office.

name: Stranger Comes to Town
beats: Hidden tensions in the community surface
Confrontation with what the stranger represents
description: One of John Gardner's two foundational stories. Outsider's arrival disrupts static order of a community, exposing tensions and forcing reconfiguration.
exemplars: Shane; High Noon; The Stranger (Camus); Chocolat; Pale Rider.

name: Hero Goes on a Journey
description: Gardner's other foundational story. Protagonist leaves the familiar and travels into the unknown. The journey is the form, not necessarily a search.
exemplars: On the Road; The Wizard of Oz; Wild (Strayed); The Odyssey; many road-movie narratives.

name: Sacrificial Lamb
beats: Innocent figure introduced as community's hope or treasure
description: Innocent character must die or suffer to redeem or save a community, often without their full understanding of why. The lamb may not even understand the role.
exemplars: The Lottery (Jackson); Sophie's Choice; certain biblical narratives; Of Mice and Men (Lennie).

name: Riches to Rags
beats: First crack — error, betrayal, or external shock
Decline accelerates; possessions and status stripped
description: Mirror of Booker's Rags-to-Riches. Character begins in wealth, status, or comfort and falls — through error, betrayal, or systemic collapse — into deprivation.
exemplars: King Lear; Joseph Roth's Job; Margin Call (corporate variant); Great Depression narratives; Falling Down.

name: Round Robin / Interlocking narrative
beats: Second story-arc with passing reference to the first
Third arc — pattern of connection emerges
description: Narrative composed of multiple discrete stories that connect through shared characters, locations, themes, or coincidences. The reader's pleasure is recognition of connections.
exemplars: Pulp Fiction; Magnolia; Cloud Atlas; A Visit from the Goon Squad (Egan); Olive Kitteridge.

name: Narration mode
section: CLASSICAL RHETORICAL MODES (the 9 modes of discourse)
description: Telling a story — sequential events arranged in time. The fundamental rhetorical mode. Use when the goal is to recount what happened.
exemplars: Most fiction; personal essays; news reports.

name: Description mode
section: CLASSICAL RHETORICAL MODES (the 9 modes of discourse)
description: Detailed sensory rendering of a person, place, object, or scene. The goal is to make the reader perceive. Use when content is what something is like rather than what happens.
exemplars: Travel writing; nature writing (Annie Dillard); descriptive passages in literary fiction.

name: Exposition mode
section: CLASSICAL RHETORICAL MODES (the 9 modes of discourse)
description: Explanation of an idea, concept, or process. The goal is to make the reader understand. Use when content is informational and the reader needs to grasp how something works.
exemplars: Most explanatory journalism; textbook prose; Wikipedia articles; popular-science writing.

name: Argumentation mode
section: CLASSICAL RHETORICAL MODES (the 9 modes of discourse)
description: Reasoning to convince. The mode designed for changing minds. Use when the goal is to advance a contested claim with evidence and reasoning.
exemplars: Op-eds; legal briefs; academic argumentative essays.

name: Comparison and Contrast
section: CLASSICAL RHETORICAL MODES (the 9 modes of discourse)
description: Structure organized around the systematic juxtaposition of two or more subjects. Use when understanding comes through what is like and what is unlike.
exemplars: "X vs Y" essays; product comparisons; literary criticism comparing authors.

name: Cause and Effect
section: CLASSICAL RHETORICAL MODES (the 9 modes of discourse)
description: Structure tracing causal chains — what produces what, and why. Use when content is why something happened or what something will produce.
exemplars: Historical analysis; epidemiological reports; many Atlantic explanatory features.

name: Process Analysis
section: CLASSICAL RHETORICAL MODES (the 9 modes of discourse)
beats: Goal or end-state of the process named
description: Step-by-step explanation of how something is done or how something happens. Two sub-modes: directive (instructions) and informative. Use when content is procedural.
exemplars: Recipes; instructional manuals; Wikihow articles; how-to journalism.

name: Definition mode
section: CLASSICAL RHETORICAL MODES (the 9 modes of discourse)
beats: Differentia (what distinguishes it from others in the genus)
description: Establishing precisely what a term, concept, or category means — by genus, by negation, by example, by etymology. Use when content's success depends on a term being shared.
exemplars: Dictionary entries; philosophical essays defining terms; scientific definitions.

name: Classification and Division
section: CLASSICAL RHETORICAL MODES (the 9 modes of discourse)
description: Organizing a complex domain into categories (classification) or breaking a single thing into its parts (division). Use when content is taxonomic.
exemplars: Linnaean biological taxonomy; this very catalog; diagnostic frameworks (DSM-5).

name: Syllogism
description: Aristotle's three-part deductive argument. The foundational form of formal reasoning.
exemplars: "All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal."

name: Enthymeme
description: Syllogism with one premise unstated — assumed shared with the audience. The most common form of real-world persuasive reasoning.
exemplars: "He's a politician — of course he's lying"; most editorial argumentation.

name: Argument by Analogy
beats: Case B (the one in question) described
Conclusion: what holds in A likely holds in B
description: Reasoning that two cases share enough relevant features that what is true of one is likely true of the other. Use when direct evidence is absent but a comparable case can be invoked.
exemplars: Legal precedent argument; "Inviting them is like inviting a fox into the henhouse"; many policy debates.

name: Confirmation-Refutation
beats: Confirmation — positive arguments for your view
description: Classical rhetorical structure: first establish your own arguments positively, then dismantle the opposing view. Use when audience is mixed and both sides need addressing.
exemplars: Cicero's speeches; classical legal argumentation; many traditional sermons.

name: Concession-and-Counter
beats: Acknowledge the opposing point as valid
Specify the limits of that validity
description: A move within argument: explicitly grant a point to the opposing view, then redirect to a stronger point that holds despite the concession. Honest acknowledgment of partial agreement strengthens credibility.
exemplars: "Yes, the policy has costs — but the costs of inaction are higher"; common in skilled op-eds.

name: Reductio ad Absurdum
description: Showing that an opponent's premise leads to absurd or contradictory consequences, thereby disproving the premise.
exemplars: Plato's dialogues; satirical essays (Swift's "A Modest Proposal"); legal argument.

name: Bandwagon
section: PROPAGANDA / INFLUENCE FORMS (Institute for Propaganda Analysis, 1937)
beats: Implication that joining is natural or inevitable
Call to align with the majority
description: Persuasion arguing "everyone is doing it / believes it / supports it" — therefore you should join. Exploits social proof.
exemplars: Election advertising; consumer marketing ("Join the millions...").

name: Glittering Generality
section: PROPAGANDA / INFLUENCE FORMS (Institute for Propaganda Analysis, 1937)
description: Use of vague, virtuous-sounding terms (freedom, justice, family values) without specific content — letting the audience fill in their own meaning.
exemplars: Most political speech; brand slogans; nationalist rhetoric.

name: Card Stacking
section: PROPAGANDA / INFLUENCE FORMS (Institute for Propaganda Analysis, 1937)
beats: Position presented as if comprehensively supported
description: Selective presentation of evidence — only the facts that support the position, omitting contradictory evidence.
exemplars: Advertising; tendentious journalism; legal briefs (within ethical bounds).

name: Plain Folks appeal
section: PROPAGANDA / INFLUENCE FORMS (Institute for Propaganda Analysis, 1937)
beats: Speaker's elite or unusual status known
Speaker performs ordinary register and concerns
description: Speaker positions themselves as ordinary, just-like-you, to bypass elite-skepticism in the audience.
exemplars: Political speeches by candidates of privilege; folksy CEO messaging; populist communication.

name: Testimonial appeal
section: PROPAGANDA / INFLUENCE FORMS (Institute for Propaganda Analysis, 1937)
description: A respected or admired figure endorses the position or product. Audience trust in a third party transfers to the proposition.
exemplars: Celebrity ads; expert endorsements; political endorsements.

name: Transfer
section: PROPAGANDA / INFLUENCE FORMS (Institute for Propaganda Analysis, 1937)
description: Associating the proposition with a symbol, image, or institution that the audience already values (flag, religion, family) — transferring positive feeling.
exemplars: Patriotic political ads; brand storytelling that invokes religious imagery; nostalgic marketing.

name: Name Calling
section: PROPAGANDA / INFLUENCE FORMS (Institute for Propaganda Analysis, 1937)
beats: Audience encouraged to dismiss without examining
