description: Discrediting the opposing position by attaching pejorative labels — without engaging the substance. Recognized propaganda technique; ethically loaded.
exemplars: Political mudslinging; ad hominem attacks; ideological labeling.

name: Fear Appeal
section: PROPAGANDA / INFLUENCE FORMS (Institute for Propaganda Analysis, 1937)
description: Persuasion grounded in arousing fear of consequences if audience does not adopt the position. Powerful and ethically heavy.
exemplars: Public-health campaigns (smoking, drunk driving); insurance ads; political fear campaigns.

name: Editorial (institutional voice)
description: Unsigned argumentative piece representing the position of a publication's editorial board. Distinguished from op-eds by institutional weight.
exemplars: New York Times editorials; Wall Street Journal editorials; The Economist leaders.

name: Letter to the Editor
beats: Closing return to the larger stake
description: Short, signed reader response to previous coverage. 200-400 words. Conversational claim on shared readership.
exemplars: Daily newspaper letters pages; London Review of Books letters; New York Review of Books letters.

name: Obituary
description: Biographical narrative of a recently-deceased person. Valedictory mode — what was this life for.
exemplars: New York Times obituaries; The Economist's Monday obit; Telegraph's eccentric obituaries.

name: Sports Feature
beats: What the result means beyond sport
description: Long-form sports narrative going beyond game results to character, context, and meaning. The sports event or athlete carries broader human or cultural weight.
exemplars: Sports Illustrated features; The Players' Tribune; W.C. Heinz; Gary Smith.

name: Service Journalism / How-to
description: Practical instructional content presented in journalistic form. Blends process analysis with editorial selection.
exemplars: Wirecutter product guides; Lifehacker how-tos; women's-magazine service features.

name: News Analysis
description: Signed journalist's interpretation of news events — distinguishing implications, providing context, identifying stakes. Distinct from news (reports) and op-ed (argues): analysis explains and frames.
exemplars: NYT "News Analysis" pieces; Politico analysis pieces; Atlantic explanatory journalism.

name: Listicle
description: Information presented as a numbered list with brief descriptions. Scannable structure: each item is self-contained.
exemplars: BuzzFeed lists; Cracked features; many magazine year-end lists.

name: Annual Letter to Shareholders
description: CEO's signed reflection on the year's performance, strategy, and vision. Hybrid: financial accountability + brand storytelling + strategic communication.
exemplars: Warren Buffett's Berkshire letters; Jeff Bezos's Amazon shareholder letters; Howard Schultz's Starbucks letters.

name: Quarterly Earnings Call narrative
description: Structured corporate narrative delivered to analysts and investors quarterly. Engineered for credibility under scrutiny.
exemplars: Apple, Microsoft, Tesla earnings calls; SEC-required communications.

name: SWOT-Style Strategic Narrative
description: Strategic analysis organized as Strengths / Weaknesses / Opportunities / Threats — internal and external, positive and negative.
exemplars: Business school cases; consulting deliverables; corporate strategy reviews.

name: OKR Story
description: Strategic narrative organized around Objectives (qualitative goals) and Key Results (quantitative measures). Used at Intel, Google, and across modern tech.
exemplars: Google internal reviews; modern tech company quarterly reviews; Measure What Matters (Doerr).

name: Post-Mortem / Retrospective
description: Structured analysis of a project, incident, or failure after the fact, with the explicit goal of organizational learning rather than blame.
exemplars: Engineering post-mortems (Google SRE tradition); aviation incident reports; agile retrospectives.

name: Conference Paper / Talk
description: Short academic presentation (typically 15-20 minutes) at a conference. Compressed argument oriented toward in-room peer scrutiny.
exemplars: Most academic conference talks; AAAS, AMA, MLA conferences; academic colloquia.

name: Dissertation Defense
description: Doctoral candidate's oral defense of their dissertation before a committee. High-stakes mastery demonstration under expert challenge.
exemplars: PhD dissertation defenses across disciplines; standard academic credentialing.

name: Academic Book Review
description: Scholarly review of an academic book, situating it within a field and assessing contributions. Emphasizes disciplinary conversation.
exemplars: American Historical Review book reviews; Journal of Philosophy reviews; field-specific academic journals.

name: Creation myth (cosmogony)
description: Narrative explaining how the world, universe, or fundamental order came to be. Establishes the most basic terms of reality.
exemplars: Genesis 1-2; Enuma Elish (Babylonian); Hesiod's Theogony; Diné creation; Yoruba Olódùmarè narratives.

name: Flood myth
description: Widely-distributed narrative type. Divine displeasure leads to a great flood; chosen few survive to rebuild. Found in Mesopotamian, Hebrew, Greek, Hindu, Aztec traditions.
exemplars: Genesis 6-9 (Noah); Epic of Gilgamesh (Utnapishtim); Greek Deucalion; Hindu Manu; Aztec Coxcoxtli.

name: Theogony
beats: Conflict between generations (often: child overthrows parent)
description: Narrative of the origin and genealogy of the gods. Distinguished from cosmogony by its specific concern with how the divine pantheon came into being and stratified.
exemplars: Hesiod's Theogony; Norse Eddic god-genealogies; Hurrian-Hittite Kumarbi cycle; Sumerian Enuma Elish.

name: Hero-Birth narrative
beats: Prophecy of greatness or threat to authority
description: Otto Rank's identified pattern. Hero's birth involves miraculous circumstances, attempt to destroy infant, exposure, rescue and raising by humble or animal foster-parents, eventual recognition.
exemplars: Moses; Romulus and Remus; Oedipus; Krishna; Sargon of Akkad; Cyrus the Great.

name: Trickster Origin Cycle
description: Pan-cultural narrative pattern. Trickster figure (Coyote, Anansi, Loki, Maui, Hermes, Eshu) wanders early world breaking rules; byproduct of misadventures is origin of present-world features.
exemplars: Anansi tales (Akan); Coyote tales (Plains/Southwest); Maui tales (Polynesian); Loki tales (Norse); Hermes (Greek).

name: Apocalyptic / End-Times narrative
beats: New order or rebirth (in some traditions)
description: Narrative of the foretold or imminent end of an era, world, or order — often involving cosmic battle, judgment, and renewal. Ultimate stakes; structural payoff is reckoning.
exemplars: Book of Revelation; Norse Ragnarök; Hindu Kali Yuga / Kalki; Aztec Five Suns; Daniel and 2 Esdras.

name: Anecdote
description: Short narrative of a single incident, usually personal, recounted to make a point, illustrate a character, or generate laughter. The shortest narrative form.
exemplars: Conversational storytelling; speeches that hinge on a single illustrating tale; many social-media micro-stories.

name: Joke (3-beat)
beats: Build — second iteration that confirms expectation
Punchline — third iteration that subverts expectation
description: Setup, escalation, punchline. The classical compressed comedy form. Use when laughter is the entire purpose and structural economy is key.
exemplars: "A priest, a rabbi, and a minister walk into a bar..."; standup comedy; rule-of-three jokes.

name: Tall Tale
description: Story whose comedy comes from progressive exaggeration — each detail more impossibly large than the last. Often featuring legendary folk heroes (Paul Bunyan, Pecos Bill).
exemplars: Paul Bunyan tales; Pecos Bill; American frontier tall tales; Mark Twain's Roughing It.

name: Urban Legend
beats: "This happened to a friend of a friend"
description: Modern folk-narrative presented as having happened to a friend-of-a-friend, typically with horror, ironic, or cautionary twist. Perpetual "almost-true" claim.
exemplars: "The Hook"; "The Vanishing Hitchhiker"; "Bloody Mary"; collected by Jan Harold Brunvand.

name: Cautionary Tale (general)
description: Narrative whose primary function is warning — depicting a character's poor choice and consequences, so audience may avoid the same fate. Moral instruction through negative example.
exemplars: Little Red Riding Hood; Pinocchio; Reefer Madness; Requiem for a Dream.

name: Riddle-Narrative
description: Narrative organized around the posing of a riddle whose solution is the climax. Reader/listener invited to solve along with characters. Intellectual play as the structural pleasure.
exemplars: Oedipus and the Sphinx; Bilbo and Gollum; Anglo-Saxon Exeter Book riddles; Turandot.

name: Proverb-Narrative
beats: Situation that will exemplify the proverb
description: Short narrative whose closing line is a proverb or saying that crystallizes the tale's meaning. The story exists to ground and authenticate the proverb. Condensed wisdom validated by example.
exemplars: Aesop's fables; West African Akan proverb stories; Yoruba proverb-narratives; Chinese chengyu origin tales.

name: Sermon
description: Religious address — typically based on scripture — combining exegesis, moral exhortation, and pastoral application. Interpretive spiritual instruction with explicit application.
exemplars: Augustine's sermons; Jonathan Edwards's "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God"; MLK sermons; Islamic khutbah; Jewish drash.

name: Parable
beats: Outcome that exceeds or inverts expectation
description: Short illustrative story in which surface narrative carries spiritual or moral teaching. Distinguished from fable by human characters and religious context. Spiritual truth approached obliquely.
exemplars: Parables of Jesus (Good Samaritan, Prodigal Son, Sower); rabbinic mashal; Sufi parables (Rumi, Attar); Buddhist parables.

name: Prayer
description: Direct address to the divine, usually with structured movement: invocation, acknowledgment, petition, thanksgiving, closing. Speaker-to-divine address across traditions.
exemplars: The Lord's Prayer; Islamic Salah; Hindu Sandhyavandanam; Buddhist refuge formulas; secular prayer-shaped meditations.

name: Confession narrative
description: First-person narrative of moral failure and acknowledgment, often within a religious frame seeking forgiveness. Honest accounting before God or community.
exemplars: Augustine's Confessions; Tolstoy's A Confession; Rousseau's Confessions; AA / 12-step testimonies.

name: Conversion testimony
description: First-person narrative of religious conversion. Pre-conversion life, awakening or crisis, decision, transformed post-conversion life. The moment of changed allegiance.
exemplars: Paul's Damascus account (Acts 9); John Newton's "Amazing Grace" backstory; Augustine's Confessions; modern evangelical testimony.

name: Hagiography (saint's life)
beats: Birth and early signs of holiness
description: Biographical narrative of a holy figure — saint, mystic, religious founder — emphasizing miraculous events, exemplary virtue, and posthumous influence. Devotional register.
exemplars: Athanasius's Life of Anthony; Sufi tadhkirat al-awliya (Attar); Hindu Bhakti hagiographies; Catholic saints' lives.

name: Mystical Vision narrative
beats: The experience itself (rendered in the limits of language)
Reflection on what was seen and what cannot be said
description: First-person account of direct religious experience — vision, ecstasy, union with the divine. Centered on the experience itself, not its conditions.
exemplars: Teresa of Ávila's Interior Castle; Julian of Norwich's Revelations; Cloud of Unknowing; Rumi's ecstatic poems; Hildegard of Bingen.

name: Eulogy
beats: Acknowledgment of the gathering and shared loss
Specific stories that embody the deceased
What we lose and what they leave
description: Speech delivered in honor of a recently-deceased person, typically at the funeral. Holds collective grief while honoring the individual.
exemplars: Pericles's funeral oration (Thucydides); famous eulogies in modern public life; family eulogies generally.

name: Toast
beats: Greeting and acknowledgment of the moment
Brief story or reflection on the honoree
description: Short speech offered at a celebratory gathering, raising a glass in honor of a person, occasion, or shared value. Brevity, public address, ceremonial close.
exemplars: Wedding toasts; retirement toasts; New Year's Eve toasts; many cultural toast traditions.

name: Wedding Speech (Best Man / Maid of Honor)
beats: How the speaker knows the couple
Sincere observation about the couple's bond
description: Toast-extension delivered at a wedding by a chosen friend. Mixed tonal register: comedy, sentiment, ceremonial witnessing all in one.
exemplars: Wedding speech traditions across cultures; comedy films featuring famous wedding-speech scenes (Four Weddings and a Funeral).

name: Roast
beats: Setup — speaker positioned as "rougher" than usual
description: Comic ceremonial speech where a person is teased through pointed insults understood as affectionate. The ceremony's structure protects the honoree; affection is underneath the cruelty.
exemplars: Friars Club roasts; Comedy Central roasts; Dean Martin's celebrity roasts; modern televised roast formats.

name: Acceptance Speech
beats: Brief reflection on what the work means
Closing — often a call or a wish
description: Speech delivered upon receiving an award or honor. Hybrid: gratitude + brief vision + acknowledgment of others. Engineered for brevity under emotional pressure.
exemplars: Oscar acceptance speeches; Nobel Prize lectures; honorary doctorate addresses.

name: Commencement Address
beats: Personal story or memory from the speaker's own life at this stage
Direct address to graduates' fears and hopes
description: Speech delivered at graduation ceremony, typically by outside speaker. Engineered for an audience facing transition. Moves from acknowledging the moment to offering wisdom for what comes next.
exemplars: David Foster Wallace's "This Is Water"; Steve Jobs's Stanford 2005 address; J.K. Rowling at Harvard; Toni Morrison's commencement addresses.

name: Social Realism
beats: Pressures of economic / political structure shown
Implicit or explicit call for change
description: Fiction depicting working-class life, social conditions, and economic structures, typically with reformist intent. Politically-reformist register.
exemplars: Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath; Sinclair's The Jungle; Richard Wright's Native Son; Sembène's films and novels.

name: Naturalism
beats: Character's inherited and environmental conditions established
Closing acknowledgment of the deterministic frame
description: Fiction grounded in assumption that human behavior is determined by environment, heredity, and circumstance. Quasi-scientific determinism.
exemplars: Zola's Rougon-Macquart cycle; Crane's Maggie: A Girl of the Streets; Dreiser's Sister Carrie; Frank Norris's McTeague.

name: Kitchen-Sink Realism
description: Mid-20th-c. British genre depicting working-class domestic life with unflinching ordinariness, typically in industrial-Northern settings. Granular texture of working-class home and pub.
exemplars: Osborne's Look Back in Anger; Sillitoe's Saturday Night and Sunday Morning; Mike Leigh's films; Ken Loach's films.

name: Dirty Realism
beats: Small action with large emotional weight
description: Late-20th-c. American minimalist fiction depicting the underside of American life — trailer parks, motels, ordinary failures — with stripped-down prose and unsentimental detail.
exemplars: Carver's What We Talk About When We Talk About Love; Richard Ford's Rock Springs; Tobias Wolff; Bobbie Ann Mason.

name: Greek Tragedy (proper Aristotelian)
description: Classical Athenian drama as theorized by Aristotle: noble protagonist's reversal through hamartia, evoking pity and fear, achieving catharsis. Fated structure with choral commentary.
exemplars: Sophocles' Oedipus Rex; Euripides' Medea; Aeschylus' Oresteia; Sophocles' Antigone.

name: Senecan Tragedy
beats: Rising action with ghost or supernatural figure
description: Roman tragedy in style of Seneca — five acts, rhetorical heightening, ghosts, on-stage violence, declamation over action. Closet-drama orientation. Heightened rhetoric and macabre intensity.
exemplars: Seneca's Thyestes, Medea, Phaedra; influenced Renaissance Revenge Tragedy.

name: Revenge Tragedy
beats: Murder discovered or revealed (often by ghost)
description: Renaissance English subgenre. Protagonist seeks revenge for kinsman's murder, undergoes moral degradation, dies with antagonists. Moral consumption through revenge.
exemplars: Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy; Shakespeare's Hamlet; Webster's The Duchess of Malfi; Tourneur's The Revenger's Tragedy.

name: Domestic Tragedy
description: Tragedy set in middle- or working-class domestic life rather than royal settings. Democratization of tragic stature. Ordinary life under tragic pressure.
exemplars: Miller's Death of a Salesman; O'Neill's Long Day's Journey Into Night; Williams's A Streetcar Named Desire; Ibsen's A Doll's House.

name: Comedy of Manners
beats: Social setting and its conventions established
description: Satirical comedy that mocks the affectations, etiquette, and pretensions of a specific social class. The gap between manners and reality.
exemplars: Congreve's The Way of the World; Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest; Noel Coward's plays; Jane Austen's novels.

name: Farce
beats: First mistaken identity or unlikely circumstance
Resolution — often by exhaustion rather than logic
description: Comedy built on improbable situations, mistaken identities, slamming doors, and accelerating chaos. Physical and situational comedy as escalating impossibility.
exemplars: Feydeau's farces; Frayn's Noises Off; A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum; Marx Brothers films.

name: Satire
beats: Pretension destroyed by its own logic
description: Comedy with critical intent — exposing folly, hypocrisy, or vice through ridicule. Two main modes: Horatian (gentle) and Juvenalian (savage). Moral-political target.
exemplars: Swift's A Modest Proposal; Gulliver's Travels; Catch-22; Dr. Strangelove; Animal Farm.

name: Black / Dark Comedy
beats: Audience's discomfort and laughter both engaged
Escalation — situation gets worse and funnier
description: Comedy that finds humor in subjects normally treated with seriousness or horror — death, disease, war, atrocity. Uncomfortable laughter; grim reality is funny.
exemplars: Dr. Strangelove; MASH; Heller's Catch-22; The Death of Stalin; Fargo; Martin McDonagh's plays.

name: Slapstick
description: Physical comedy based on broad, exaggerated, body-based humor — pratfalls, pies in faces, chase sequences. Pure body-driven, language-free comedy.
exemplars: Charlie Chaplin's films; Buster Keaton; Three Stooges; Looney Tunes; Mr. Bean.

name: Parody
beats: Target genre or work invoked through stylistic imitation
Pleasure of recognition for the audience
description: Comedy that imitates the style and conventions of a specific work or genre to comic effect. The formal target is what's being mocked.
exemplars: Mel Brooks's Young Frankenstein, Spaceballs; Airplane!; This Is Spinal Tap; Galaxy Quest; Cervantes's Don Quixote.

name: Opera narrative
beats: Act 1 — situation, principals introduced through arias
Final act — death, reunion, or transformation
description: Sung-through dramatic narrative combining music, poetry, and theater. 3-4 acts with arias for character interiority, ensembles for conflict. Heightened emotion sustainable only through music.
exemplars: Verdi's La Traviata; Puccini's La Bohème; Mozart's Don Giovanni; Wagner's Ring Cycle; Adams's Nixon in China.

name: Broadway Musical
beats: Series of book scenes alternating with songs
Act 1 close — usually a high-energy ensemble
description: American musical-theater form combining book (spoken scenes), songs, and dance. English vernacular and integrated book-songs structure.
exemplars: West Side Story; Hamilton; Les Misérables; Chicago; Sweeney Todd; Wicked.

name: Ballet narrative
beats: Principal characters introduced through pas de deux
description: Narrative dance work, typically without text, communicating story through choreography, music, costume, and staging. Body-narrative — story through bodies in motion.
exemplars: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake, The Nutcracker, Sleeping Beauty; Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring; Giselle.

name: Testimonial Ad
description: Advertising in which a real (or plausible) customer narrates their experience with the product. Peer credibility rather than authority endorsement.
exemplars: Most consumer-product advertising; "real people, not actors" campaigns; modern Instagram ad creator content.

name: Comparison Ad
description: Advertising that explicitly compares the product to a competitor's, highlighting advantages. Named adversarial structure.
exemplars: Apple's "Mac vs. PC" campaign; Pepsi Challenge; Tesla's silent-comparison-with-gas-cars marketing.

name: Lifestyle Ad
beats: Product as natural part of the scene
Implication: this is who you could be
description: Advertising that sells the product through association with an aspirational way of life rather than functional features. Identity-coded value.
exemplars: Ralph Lauren campaigns; Apple's "Shot on iPhone"; Patagonia's outdoor narratives; luxury-goods advertising.

name: Before / After Ad
description: Advertising that shows the subject's state before using the product and after, with the product as transformative agent. Direct, conversion-focused.
exemplars: Weight-loss ads; home-renovation shows; before-and-after marketing across industries.

name: Product Launch Story
description: Narrative announcing a new product, woven around the problem the product solves, the insight that produced it, and the future it makes possible.
exemplars: Apple keynote launches (Steve Jobs's iPhone, 2007); Tesla unveilings; SaaS-product launch posts.

name: Filibuster narrative
beats: Substantive content (often reading from prepared materials)
description: Extended speech delivered to delay legislative action — the act of speaking is itself the political move. Hybrid: substantive content + procedural function.
exemplars: Strom Thurmond's 24-hour filibuster (1957); Wendy Davis's Texas filibuster (2013); Bernie Sanders 2010; Mr. Smith Goes to Washington.

name: Town Hall Address
description: Politician's direct engagement with constituents, structured as remarks followed by Q&A. Semi-improvised middle and accountability-under-pressure tenor.
exemplars: Modern American town halls; British MP constituency surgeries; presidential town hall debates.

name: Debate format
description: Structured public confrontation between candidates or positions, governed by formal rules of time, response, and rebuttal. Contest visible to voters.
exemplars: Lincoln-Douglas debates (1858); Kennedy-Nixon (1960); modern presidential debates; British Question Time.

name: Pilgrimage Memoir
beats: Stages of the journey, each with a lesson
description: First-person narrative of a religious or spiritual pilgrimage — Mecca, Jerusalem, Camino, Varanasi, Mount Kailash. The journey is interior as well as exterior.
exemplars: Bashō's Oku no Hosomichi; Cheryl Strayed's Wild (secular); The Way of a Pilgrim; Robert Macfarlane's The Old Ways.

name: Spiritual Autobiography
description: Long-form first-person account of a life's spiritual development. Distinct from secular autobiography by emphasis on the soul's journey.
exemplars: Augustine's Confessions; Teresa of Ávila's Life; Merton's The Seven Storey Mountain; Yogananda's The Autobiography of a Yogi; C.S. Lewis's Surprised by Joy.

name: Allegorical Religious Narrative
beats: Protagonist sets out on figural journey
Each encounter represents a spiritual challenge
description: Narrative whose surface story figures a deeper spiritual journey — characters, places, and events stand for spiritual states or lessons. Spiritual content encountered through story rather than argument.
exemplars: Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress; Everyman; Spenser's The Faerie Queene; Hesse's Siddhartha; Coelho's The Alchemist.

name: Lecture
description: Structured oral presentation of a topic by an expert to learners, typically 30-60 minutes. Pedagogical (not peer-review) audience.
exemplars: University lectures; MOOC video lectures; Great Courses productions; classical vorlesungen.

name: Tutorial / How-To Lesson
description: Step-by-step instructional content designed to teach a specific skill or process. Operational aim: learner can DO something at the end.
exemplars: Instructional videos; cooking shows; technical tutorials; coding bootcamp lessons.

name: Textbook Chapter
description: Structured educational chapter combining exposition, examples, and review questions. Engineered for systematic curriculum coverage.
exemplars: University-level textbooks; K-12 textbooks; standard educational publishing.

name: TED Talk format
description: Short (5-18 minute) talk format engineered for memorability and viral sharing. Combines personal story, big idea, and call to action. One big idea worth spreading.
exemplars: Brené Brown's "Power of Vulnerability"; Sir Ken Robinson's "Do Schools Kill Creativity?"; Hans Rosling; Simon Sinek's "Start With Why."

name: Khan Academy / Video Tutorial
description: Short, screen-captured video lesson explaining a single concept with examples — common in modern online education. Specific compressed-video format.
exemplars: Khan Academy videos; 3Blue1Brown's math videos; Crash Course; Veritasium; Numberphile.

name: MOOC Module
description: Self-paced online course unit combining video lecture, readings, quizzes, and discussion. Asynchronous remote-pedagogy structure.
exemplars: Coursera, edX, Udacity courses; Stanford Online; MITx.

name: Coaching / Mentorship Conversation
description: Structured developmental conversation between mentor and mentee — questions, reflection, accountability. Specific developmental-relationship register.
exemplars: Executive coaching conversations; ICF coaching framework; modern mentorship programs.

name: Apprenticeship / Master Class
description: Direct skill-transmission from master practitioner to learner — through demonstration, critique, and supervised practice. Embodied, master-led register.
exemplars: Traditional craft apprenticeships; medical residency; MasterClass platform; conservatory-style music training.

name: Hard Science Fiction
beats: Conflict turns on understanding the science correctly
description: SF grounded in scientifically plausible extrapolation — physics, chemistry, biology as known are respected. The pleasure is in rigorous extrapolation.
exemplars: Arthur C. Clarke's Rendezvous with Rama; Andy Weir's The Martian; Kim Stanley Robinson's Mars trilogy; Greg Egan.

name: Space Opera
beats: Stable cosmic order restored or transformed
description: Large-scale science fiction featuring interstellar adventure, romance, and conflict — often soft on scientific plausibility, strong on adventure. Epic scale.
exemplars: Star Wars; Iain M. Banks's Culture novels; Lois McMaster Bujold's Vorkosigan saga; Frank Herbert's Dune.

name: Time Travel narrative
description: Narrative in which characters travel between time periods. Sub-types: closed-loop, branching, free-will. Time itself as a medium.
exemplars: H.G. Wells's The Time Machine; Back to the Future; La Jetée / 12 Monkeys; Looper; Connie Willis.

name: First Contact narrative
beats: Resolution — relationship established or contact lost
description: Narrative centered on humanity's first encounter with an alien intelligence. Core question: understanding across radical difference.
exemplars: Lem's Solaris; Ted Chiang's "Story of Your Life" (Arrival); Sagan's Contact; Liu Cixin's The Three-Body Problem.

name: Dystopian narrative
beats: Quiet rebellion or attempt to escape
description: Narrative set in future or alternate society organized around oppressive principles — typically projected from author's present. Warning through extrapolation.
exemplars: Zamyatin's We; Orwell's 1984; Huxley's Brave New World; Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale.

name: Utopian narrative
beats: Visitor or narrator arrives in or describes the utopia
Tour of its features and principles
Comparison to the broken outside world
description: Narrative depicting an idealized society — explicitly imagined as better than the present. Less narratively dramatic than dystopian; more politically prescriptive.
exemplars: Thomas More's Utopia; Bellamy's Looking Backward; Morris's News from Nowhere; Le Guin's The Dispossessed.

name: Post-apocalyptic narrative
beats: Threat from human or environmental forces
Choice that reveals what is being preserved or rebuilt
description: Narrative set after civilizational collapse — nuclear, viral, environmental, supernatural. What survives, what is rebuilt, what is lost.
exemplars: McCarthy's The Road; Miller's A Canticle for Leibowitz; Mandel's Station Eleven; King's The Stand.

name: Alternate History
beats: Point of divergence ("what if X happened differently?") established
Resolution that comments on the actual history
description: Narrative set in a world where history diverged at a specific point — Hitler won, the Confederacy survived, the Roman Empire didn't fall. Counterfactual exploration of consequence.
exemplars: Dick's The Man in the High Castle; Harris's Fatherland; Robinson's The Years of Rice and Salt; Harry Turtledove.

name: Cyberpunk
beats: Outsider protagonist with specific technical skill
Encounter with corporate or AI antagonist
Confrontation through the network and the body
description: Near-future SF combining "high tech and low life" — corporate-dominated dystopias, pervasive networked technology, hardboiled outsider protagonists. Established literary genre since 1984.
exemplars: William Gibson's Neuromancer; Blade Runner; Ghost in the Shell; Snow Crash (Stephenson); Altered Carbon.

name: Steampunk
beats: Protagonist on quest tied to that tech
Encounters with social classes and machinery
Resolution with implications for the alt-history
description: Speculative fiction set in alternate Victorian-era past where steam-power technology has advanced — airships, mechanical computers, brass-and-leather aesthetics. Historical-fantasy hybrid.
exemplars: Gibson and Sterling's The Difference Engine; Philip Reeve's Mortal Engines; The Wild Wild West; Steamboy.

name: Solarpunk
description: Speculative fiction depicting hopeful, ecologically-integrated futures — renewable energy, biomimetic architecture, post-scarcity local economies. Counter-genre to dystopia and cyberpunk pessimism.
exemplars: Becky Chambers's Monk and Robot; Robinson's The Ministry for the Future; Sunvault anthology.

name: Climate Fiction (Cli-Fi)
description: Fiction grappling explicitly with climate change — its causes, ongoing consequences, possible futures. Spans dystopia, near-future realism, post-apocalyptic.
exemplars: Robinson's New York 2140; Octavia Butler's Parable of the Sower; Atwood's MaddAddam trilogy; The Overstory (Powers).

name: Military Science Fiction
description: SF foregrounding military structure, combat, and command — often in interstellar conflicts. Chain-of-command, tactics, experience of soldiering.
exemplars: Heinlein's Starship Troopers; Haldeman's The Forever War; David Drake's Hammer's Slammers; The Expanse.

name: Generation Ship narrative
beats: Current generation's relation to original purpose
Conflict between traditional and revisionist factions
description: SF set aboard slower-than-light spaceship whose journey takes generations. Generational drift and societal evolution within the ship are core content.
exemplars: Heinlein's Orphans of the Sky; Robinson's Aurora; Aldiss's Non-Stop; Le Guin's "Paradises Lost."

name: AI / Robot Narrative
beats: Resolution about AI's nature and rights
description: SF featuring artificial intelligence or robots as protagonists or central agents — exploring consciousness, autonomy, and the line between human and machine.
exemplars: Asimov's I, Robot and The Bicentennial Man; Ex Machina; Her; Westworld; Becky Chambers's Monk and Robot.

name: Singularity narrative
description: SF set around the moment when AI surpasses human cognition — the technological singularity. Focus on the transformation event itself and its civilizational consequences.
exemplars: Vernor Vinge's Marooned in Realtime; Charles Stross's Accelerando; Hannu Rajaniemi's The Quantum Thief; Transcendence.

name: Mind Upload narrative
beats: Resolution about which version is "really" the protagonist
description: SF in which consciousness is digitized, transferred, or copied — exploring identity, mortality, and the meaning of self when continuity is decoupled from a single body.
exemplars: Greg Egan's Permutation City and Diaspora; Iain M. Banks's Culture novels; Black Mirror's "San Junipero"; Altered Carbon.

name: Virtual Reality narrative
beats: Stakes from VR bleed into real world (or vice versa)
Resolution about which reality is primary
description: SF set within or around immersive virtual environments — the relationship between real and simulated reality is central. Sub-form of cyberpunk but distinct.
exemplars: Stephenson's Snow Crash and Reamde; Cline's Ready Player One; The Matrix; Sword Art Online.

name: Apocalypse-in-Progress (slow apocalypse)
description: SF depicting civilization's collapse not as cataclysm but as gradual unraveling — degradation, abandonment, slow decay observed across time. Mid-apocalyptic rather than post-apocalyptic.
exemplars: Octavia Butler's Parable of the Sower; Kim Stanley Robinson's 2312 (in part); Children of Men; The Road (in retrospect).

name: Time Loop
description: Narrative in which the protagonist relives the same period of time repeatedly — usually until they figure out how to escape. Repetition itself as structural device.
exemplars: Groundhog Day; Edge of Tomorrow; Russian Doll; Palm Springs; Looper (variant).

name: Alien Invasion narrative
description: SF in which Earth is attacked by extraterrestrial forces; humanity must resist, survive, or comprehend the invader. Distinguished from First Contact by its hostile-encounter premise.
exemplars: H.G. Wells's The War of the Worlds; Independence Day; War of the Worlds (Spielberg); V; Edge of Tomorrow.

name: Pandemic / Outbreak narrative
beats: Resolution at population scale, with reckoning
description: Narrative of a disease outbreak — its origin, spread, response, and consequences. Spans medical thriller, science fiction, and post-apocalyptic. Biology against civilization.
exemplars: Crichton's The Andromeda Strain; Preston's The Hot Zone; Contagion (2011); King's The Stand; Mandel's Station Eleven.

name: Dystopian YA
beats: Teen protagonist's family or community threatened
description: Young-adult fiction set in dystopian futures, with adolescent protagonists. YA conventions: chosen-one, romantic triangle, clear good-and-evil.
exemplars: Collins's The Hunger Games; Roth's Divergent; Lowry's The Giver; Dashner's The Maze Runner.

name: Robinsonade (castaway narrative)
beats: Construction of shelter, tools, food supply
Encounter with environment or other people
Rescue or final acceptance of the island
description: Narrative of person stranded in isolation — typically on an island — who must survive and create order from scratch. Civilization-building from nothing.
exemplars: Defoe's Robinson Crusoe; Verne's The Mysterious Island; Cast Away; Andy Weir's The Martian; Lord of the Flies.

name: Lost World narrative
beats: Encounter with its creatures or peoples
Return — sometimes with souvenir or warning
description: Adventure fiction in which an isolated location preserves an ancient or otherwise lost ecosystem — dinosaurs, prehistoric peoples, forgotten civilizations.
exemplars: Doyle's The Lost World; Haggard's She; Burroughs's The Land That Time Forgot; Jurassic Park; King Kong.

name: Dieselpunk
beats: War, crime, or political intrigue tied to the tech
description: Speculative fiction set in alternate 1920s-1950s timelines with diesel-era technology aesthetics — propeller-driven aircraft, art deco, two-stroke industrial.
exemplars: Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow; The Iron Dream (Spinrad); BioShock aesthetic.

name: Slipstream / Weird Fiction
description: Fiction that exists between genres — neither fully realist, fully fantastic, nor fully horror — using estrangement and dream-logic. Refusal of clean genre placement.
exemplars: Kelly Link's stories; Karen Russell; George Saunders; Aimee Bender; Kafka (proto-slipstream).

name: New Weird
beats: Protagonist with unusual skill or stigma
Confrontation with bodily or political horror
description: Late-20th/early-21st-c. literary movement combining weird fiction, fantasy, horror, SF — often urban-decay settings, biological-grotesque imagery, political weight.
exemplars: China Miéville's Perdido Street Station; Jeff VanderMeer's Annihilation; M. John Harrison's Light; The Etched City (Bishop).

name: Hopepunk
beats: Protagonist commits a small kind act
Compounding kindnesses build a small space
Survival of the kindness, even partial
description: Reaction against grimdark — fiction insisting that hope, kindness, and small acts of decency are forms of rebellion against darkness. Defiance through goodness.
exemplars: Becky Chambers's Wayfarers series; Ted Lasso; The Good Place; Cory Doctorow's Walkaway.

name: Generation-Skip Future History
description: SF that traces a civilization across centuries, jumping between generations — future-history form. Planetary or interstellar civilization, not single ship.
exemplars: Olaf Stapledon's Last and First Men; Asimov's Foundation; Robinson's Mars trilogy; Vinge's A Deepness in the Sky.

name: Anthropological SF
beats: Insight about what makes the society work
description: SF whose primary interest is the imagined social structure, language, and cosmology of a fictional society — often through visitor-anthropologist protagonist.
exemplars: Le Guin's The Left Hand of Darkness, The Dispossessed; Sheri Tepper; Mary Doria Russell's The Sparrow.

name: Hard Cyberpunk / Post-cyberpunk
beats: Networked society established with sociological depth
Investigation through technical and political means
description: Cyberpunk that takes the sociology and politics of network society as central — less neon-noir, more institutional analysis. Surveillance, capital, labor.
exemplars: Stephenson's The Diamond Age and Cryptonomicon; Doctorow's Little Brother and Walkaway; Gibson's Pattern Recognition.

name: Wuxia-Influenced Fantasy (Western adaptation)
description: Western fantasy drawing structural elements from Chinese wuxia — martial-honor codes, qi-energy systems, jianghu-like underworlds. Distinct from native wuxia by being non-Chinese-cultural.
exemplars: Fonda Lee's Jade City; Saladin Ahmed's Throne of the Crescent Moon.

name: LitRPG (Literary Role-Playing Game)
beats: Protagonist enters game-world or wakes with game-rules
description: Speculative fiction that incorporates explicit RPG mechanics — leveling up, stats, classes — into the narrative. Diegetic game-system.
exemplars: Dungeon Crawler Carl (Dinniman); He Who Fights with Monsters; Andrew Rowe's Arcane Ascension; Russian Play to Live series.

name: Police Procedural
description: Crime narrative following methodical investigation by police — emphasizing routines, hierarchies, and frustrations of professional detective work. Institutional, multi-actor focus.
exemplars: Hill Street Blues; Law & Order; The Wire; Ed McBain's 87th Precinct novels.

name: Locked Room Mystery
description: Mystery in which a crime appears physically impossible — committed in a sealed environment with no apparent way for the perpetrator to enter or exit. The puzzle is the mechanism.
exemplars: Poe's "The Murders in the Rue Morgue"; John Dickson Carr's The Hollow Man; Christie's And Then There Were None; Knives Out.

name: Howcatchem (Inverted Detective Story)
beats: Final confrontation with the criminal trapped
description: Inverted from whodunit — audience knows from beginning who committed the crime, and the pleasure is watching the detective methodically catch the criminal.
exemplars: Columbo; R. Austin Freeman's Dr. Thorndyke stories; Highsmith's Ripley novels (variant).

name: Forensic Procedural
description: Crime narrative centered on forensic science — DNA, ballistics, autopsy, toxicology — as the detective's primary tool. Foregrounds the laboratory.
exemplars: CSI franchise; Bones; Patricia Cornwell's Kay Scarpetta novels; Kathy Reichs's Tempe Brennan.

name: Cold Case Narrative
description: Old, unsolved crime is reopened — typically because of new evidence, new technology, or persistent investigators. Archaeology-of-crime register.
exemplars: Cold Case (TV); Mindhunter; Michelle McNamara's I'll Be Gone in the Dark; true-crime podcasts.

name: True Crime narrative
description: Non-fiction account of an actual crime, typically a murder, told with novelistic technique. Distinct from journalism by literary scope; from fiction by documentary grounding.
exemplars: Capote's In Cold Blood; Ann Rule's The Stranger Beside Me; Helter Skelter (Bugliosi); Serial podcast.

name: Caper / Comic Heist
description: Lighter, comedic variant of the heist. The team is more eccentric, stakes more whimsical, tone playful. Heist that entertains rather than menaces.
exemplars: The Sting; Snatch; The Italian Job; Logan Lucky; Going in Style.

name: Noir
beats: Cynical protagonist drawn into a case
Tragic close — protagonist destroyed or diminished
description: Crime narrative steeped in moral ambiguity, urban decay, fatalism, shadowed visual register. Pervasive philosophical despair — protagonist is doomed, system corrupt.
exemplars: Double Indemnity; Out of the Past; Sunset Boulevard; James M. Cain's The Postman Always Rings Twice; Cornell Woolrich.

name: Scandinavian Noir (Nordic Noir)
beats: Critique of Nordic society's hidden failures
description: Crime fiction from Nordic countries combining bleak landscapes, social-democratic critique, morally complex investigators. Sociological depth — crime as symptom of societal disease.
exemplars: Stieg Larsson's Millennium trilogy; Henning Mankell's Wallander; Jo Nesbø's Harry Hole; The Killing; The Bridge.

name: Tartan Noir
beats: Crime tied to local class or political fault line
description: Scottish crime fiction characterized by working-class urban settings (Glasgow, Edinburgh), dark humor, political-social grit. Crime, place-specificity, and Celtic darkness.
exemplars: Ian Rankin's Rebus; William McIlvanney's Laidlaw; Val McDermid; Denise Mina.

name: Conspiracy Thriller
beats: Protagonist stumbles into a small wrongness
description: Narrative in which protagonist gradually uncovers a vast hidden plot — typically governmental, corporate, or institutional — that threatens to destroy them. Paranoia-driven.
exemplars: The Parallax View; Three Days of the Condor; Robert Ludlum novels; The Pelican Brief; The X-Files.

name: Political Thriller
description: Thriller built around governmental power — assassination plots, electoral conspiracies, succession crises. Domestic-political setting.
exemplars: Frederick Forsyth's The Day of the Jackal; Seven Days in May; House of Cards; Allen Drury's Advise and Consent.

name: Domestic Thriller
beats: First crack — small lie or anomaly
Survival or destruction within the home
description: Thriller set within a marriage, family, or household — the menace comes from intimate proximity. Claustrophobic setting; betrayal among supposed loved ones.
exemplars: Gillian Flynn's Gone Girl; Paula Hawkins's The Girl on the Train; Liane Moriarty's Big Little Lies; Rebecca (du Maurier).

name: Psychological Thriller
description: Thriller in which the engine is the protagonist's psychological state — paranoia, gaslighting, unreliable perception. Threat is partly internal; reader cannot trust the viewpoint.
exemplars: Gaslight (1944); Shutter Island; Black Swan; Patricia Highsmith's The Talented Mr. Ripley; Memento.

name: Serial Killer Thriller
description: Thriller centered on the pursuit of a serial murderer — often paired with psychologically scarred investigator who must enter the killer's mind. Ritual-of-killing patterns and forensic-psychological investigation.
exemplars: Thomas Harris's Red Dragon and The Silence of the Lambs; Jeffery Deaver's Lincoln Rhyme; Karin Slaughter; Mindhunter; Hannibal.

name: Whydunit
description: Mystery in which the criminal's identity is known or revealed early; the question and investigation focus on why — motive, history, psychology. Emphasis on understanding rather than capture.
exemplars: Lionel Shriver's We Need to Talk About Kevin; modern literary thrillers; The Killing season 1; I Saw the Devil.

name: Locked Room Heist
description: Heist set within a single, enclosed location — bank vault, museum, casino. Compressed setting; the team must operate within tight spatial and temporal constraints.
exemplars: Inside Man; The Bank Job; portions of Ocean's Eleven; Money Heist (extended).

name: Procedural Drama (general)
description: Episodic drama centered on the routines of a profession (medical, legal, police, scientific) where each episode features a self-contained case while a serialized arc plays out across episodes.
exemplars: Law & Order; ER; Grey's Anatomy; House M.D.; Bones; NCIS.

name: Medical Mystery
description: Mystery in which the puzzle is a baffling medical condition — a rare disease, an unexplained outbreak, an undiagnosed patient. The detective is a doctor; the criminal is biology.
exemplars: House M.D.; Berton Roueché's Eleven Blue Men; Atul Gawande essays; Lisa Sanders's Diagnosis column.

name: Treasure Hunt
beats: Each clue leads to the next
description: Quest narrative organized around a hidden valuable — gold, artifact, document — guarded by clues, traps, and rivals. Cipher-puzzle mechanics.
exemplars: Stevenson's Treasure Island; Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade; National Treasure; H. Rider Haggard's King Solomon's Mines.

name: Spy Procedural / Tradecraft Narrative
beats: Resolution through bureaucratic and operational means
description: Spy narrative emphasizing the bureaucratic, methodical work of intelligence services — agent runners, analysts, debriefings — over Bond-style action. Realism and institutional texture.
exemplars: John le Carré's George Smiley novels; The Americans; Charles McCarry's Paul Christopher series.

name: Conspiracy of Silence narrative
beats: Community reckons (or not) with what was hidden
description: A small community or institution maintains a shared silence around an old wrong — death, injustice, secret — and the protagonist's investigation threatens to break the silence.
exemplars: Tana French's In the Woods; Kate Atkinson's Jackson Brodie novels; Donna Tartt's The Secret History; Mare of Easttown.

name: Detective Memoir
beats: Series of cases, each a chapter
description: First-person narrative of a real or fictional detective's career, structured as remembered cases. Retrospective autobiographical voice.
exemplars: Vincent Bugliosi's Helter Skelter; The Spy Who Loved Us (Bashford); fictional detective frame in The Maltese Falcon's narration.

name: Heist-Gone-Wrong
beats: Tragic outcome — death, betrayal, or capture
description: Heist narrative whose pleasure is the failure of the plan — at some point the elaborate setup unravels, and the rest of the story is the consequences.
exemplars: Reservoir Dogs; Dog Day Afternoon; Killing Them Softly; the Coen Brothers' Fargo (variant).

name: Crime of Passion narrative
beats: Aftermath, attempt to flee or hide
description: Crime committed in sudden emotional storm — jealous love, betrayed loyalty, witnessed cruelty. Unplanned, single-event character; the genre's question is moral attribution.
exemplars: Camus's The Stranger (variant); Dreiser's An American Tragedy; Patricia Highsmith novels; In Cold Blood's perpetrator psychology.

name: High Fantasy
description: Fantasy set in a fully invented secondary world with its own geography, history, languages, and metaphysics. Total imaginative immersion.
exemplars: Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings; Robert Jordan's Wheel of Time; Brandon Sanderson's Stormlight Archive; Le Guin's Earthsea.

name: Sword and Sorcery
beats: Hero introduced in a specific corner of a magical world
description: Fantasy focused on a wandering hero (often a barbarian or rogue) confronting magical antagonists in self-contained adventures. Smaller scale, looser world-building.
exemplars: Robert E. Howard's Conan stories; Fritz Leiber's Fafhrd and Gray Mouser; Michael Moorcock's Elric; Joe Abercrombie's Best Served Cold.

name: Portal Fantasy
beats: Discovery or accidental crossing of portal
description: Fantasy in which protagonists from the everyday world cross into a magical world through a specific portal — wardrobe, rabbit-hole, mirror. The crossing itself is structural.
exemplars: Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland; C.S. Lewis's The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe; The Wizard of Oz; Spirited Away; Neil Gaiman's Coraline.

name: Grimdark Fantasy
description: Fantasy that systematically subverts heroic conventions — protagonists morally compromised, victories pyrrhic, world brutal. Fantasy's complicity with violence brought into focus.
exemplars: George R.R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire; Joe Abercrombie's The First Law; Mark Lawrence's Prince of Thorns; The Witcher (Sapkowski).

name: Urban Fantasy
beats: Investigation through occult and mundane means
description: Fantasy set in modern urban environments where magic, supernatural creatures, or hidden worlds operate alongside ordinary life. Contemporary setting, noir-influenced register.
exemplars: Jim Butcher's Dresden Files; Ben Aaronovitch's Rivers of London; Neil Gaiman's American Gods; Charlaine Harris's Sookie Stackhouse; Buffy the Vampire Slayer.

name: Romantasy (Romance + Fantasy)
beats: Lovers meet across faction or species
description: Hybrid combining fantasy world-building with central romantic plot. Romance gets equal or primary weight.
exemplars: Sarah J. Maas's A Court of Thorns and Roses; Rebecca Yarros's Fourth Wing; Naomi Novik's Spinning Silver; Holly Black's Cruel Prince.

name: Court Intrigue Fantasy
description: Fantasy centered on royal courts — succession, scheming, marriage politics, advisers' rivalries. Magic often present but secondary to political maneuvering.
exemplars: George R.R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire; Jacqueline Carey's Kushiel novels; Katherine Addison's The Goblin Emperor; The Lions of Al-Rassan (Kay).

name: Dark Fantasy
description: Fantasy with horror's atmosphere and stakes — gothic darkness, body-horror creatures, ambiguous magic. Distinct from horror by its fantasy structure; from grimdark by supernatural-rather-than-cynical register.
exemplars: Clive Barker's Imajica; Glen Cook's Black Company; Berserk (Miura); Susanna Clarke's Piranesi.

name: Fairy Tale Retelling
beats: Climactic event in conversation with source
Resolution that reveals what the original concealed
description: Modern reworking of classical fairy tale — often inverting, complicating, or contemporizing. Pleasure is recognition and revision of an inherited tale.
exemplars: Angela Carter's The Bloody Chamber; Gregory Maguire's Wicked; Robin McKinley's Beauty; Once Upon a Time (TV).

name: Mythopoeia
beats: Original gods, heroes, or first beings
description: Original myth-creation — fiction that invents new mythology rather than retelling existing ones. Mythic register and ambition.
exemplars: Tolkien's Silmarillion; Lord Dunsany's The Gods of Pegana; Neil Gaiman's American Gods (variant); C.S. Lewis's Narnia.

name: Dying Earth
beats: Search for meaning at the end
description: Fantasy set in a world at the very end of its time — sun dimming, magic fading, civilizations collapsed into ruin. Melancholy register and end-of-the-world atmosphere as constant.
exemplars: Jack Vance's Dying Earth sequence; Gene Wolfe's Book of the New Sun; Clark Ashton Smith's Zothique stories; M. John Harrison's Viriconium.

name: Mythic Fiction
beats: Encounter that reveals myth's continuing power
Climactic event that fulfills or revises the myth
description: Modern fiction that explicitly draws on mythic structures and figures, often setting them in contemporary context. More reverent treatment of myth than urban fantasy.
exemplars: Madeline Miller's Circe and Song of Achilles; Susan Cooper's The Dark Is Rising; Charles de Lint.

name: Fabulism
description: Short fiction in the mode of fable — talking animals, allegorical figures, magical events — but composed for adult audiences with modern sensibility.
exemplars: Italo Calvino's Cosmicomics and Invisible Cities; Jorge Luis Borges; Aimee Bender's stories; George Saunders's Fox 8.

name: Progression Fantasy
beats: Iterative cycles of training and breakthroughs
description: Fantasy emphasizing the protagonist's continuous, measurable progression in skill, magical power, or rank — often related to Eastern xianxia/cultivation but in Western worlds.
exemplars: Will Wight's Cradle series; Andrew Rowe's Arcane Ascension; Travis Baldree's Legends & Lattes (variant); web-fiction progression-fantasy generally.

name: Chivalric Romance (Medieval)
beats: Combat with monsters or rival knights
Test of courtly love and chivalric virtue
description: Medieval European narrative form featuring noble knights on quests of honor, courtly love, and religious devotion. Specifically medieval-Christian context.
exemplars: Chrétien de Troyes's Arthurian romances; Sir Gawain and the Green Knight; Le Morte d'Arthur (Malory); The Romance of Tristan.

name: Arthurian narrative
beats: Specific knight introduced or sent on quest
Test of virtue, often involving Otherworldly figures
Implication for the larger fall of the Round Table
description: Vast cycle of narratives concerning King Arthur, the Knights of the Round Table, and the Matter of Britain. Distinct sub-cycle within chivalric romance with its own conventions.
exemplars: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia; Chrétien's Yvain, Erec, Perceval; Le Morte d'Arthur; T.H. White's The Once and Future King.

name: Folk-Tale (general European)
beats: Encounter with magical helper or obstacle
description: Pan-European folk-tale form: short, formulaic narrative with stock figures, magical objects, and didactic close. Oral-traditional register.
exemplars: Brothers Grimm collections; Charles Perrault; Hans Christian Andersen; Italian Calvino's Italian Folktales; Russian Afanasyev.

name: Historical Fantasy
beats: Real historical setting established with care
Magical element woven into the period
Protagonist navigates both real and magical
Climactic event that touches both registers
description: Fantasy set in a real historical period with magic added — Tudor England with witches, Imperial Rome with gods, Napoleonic Europe with dragons.
exemplars: Naomi Novik's Temeraire; Susanna Clarke's Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell; Guy Gavriel Kay's historical fantasies; Outlander (Gabaldon).

name: Faerie / Fae narrative
beats: Strange and binding rules of Faerie
Return to mortal world, transformed or trapped
description: Fantasy centered on the Fae — beautiful, dangerous, alien, bound by strange laws. Faithfulness to specific folkloric conventions (Celtic and Germanic).
exemplars: Holly Black's The Cruel Prince; Susanna Clarke's Jonathan Strange; Catherynne M. Valente's In the Night Garden; Neil Gaiman's Stardust.

name: Sword and Planet
beats: Encounter with princess or noble figure
Quest involving sword and creature combat
Becomes hero of the alien world
description: Hybrid SF/fantasy: Earthling protagonist transported to alien planet engages in sword-and-sorcery-style adventure. Distinct from sword-and-sorcery by extraterrestrial setting.
exemplars: Edgar Rice Burroughs's A Princess of Mars (foundational); Otis Adelbert Kline; Leigh Brackett; John Carter (film).

name: Wainscot Society fantasy
description: Fantasy in which a hidden community lives within or behind the structures of mundane society — borrowers in walls, secret magic schools, hidden wizard governments. The masquerade is structural.
exemplars: Mary Norton's The Borrowers; J.K. Rowling's Wizarding World; Men in Black; Tom Holt's novels; Terry Pratchett's The Bromeliad.

name: Comic Fantasy
beats: Genuine fantasy stakes that don't break the comedy
Resolution that affirms both fantasy and joke
description: Fantasy whose primary register is humor — satirizing high fantasy conventions, playing with genre tropes, mixing absurdity into world-building. Laughter as structural payoff.
exemplars: Terry Pratchett's Discworld; Tom Holt's novels; Christopher Moore's fantasy-comedy; The Princess Bride (Goldman).

name: Romantic Fantasy
beats: Climactic threat to lovers and world
description: Older variant of romantasy: fantasy adventure in which a romance arc is central but not necessarily commercially-engineered. Less formula-driven, often deeper world-building.
exemplars: Mercedes Lackey's Valdemar series; Anne McCaffrey's Pern; Robin Hobb's Farseer trilogy.

name: Quiet Fantasy / Cozy Fantasy
description: Low-stakes, contemplative fantasy. World is magical but conflicts are small: opening a coffee shop with magical animals, growing potion herbs, mending the village. Comfort rather than adventure.
exemplars: Travis Baldree's Legends & Lattes; Becky Chambers's Monk and Robot; Heather Fawcett's Emily Wilde; Howl's Moving Castle.

name: Saga Fantasy (multi-generational)
beats: Family curse, prophecy, or duty across generations
Final generation reckons with the inheritance
Closure (or perpetuation) of the family line
description: Fantasy that follows multiple generations of a family, dynasty, or line — each generation a major arc. Familial-temporal sweep.
exemplars: Robin Hobb's Realm of the Elderlings; Le Guin's Earthsea (across decades); García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude (variant).

name: Body Horror
beats: Identity threatened by the body's change
description: Horror grounded in the violation, transformation, or grotesque alteration of the body. Visceral, embodied focus. What the body can become.
exemplars: David Cronenberg's films (The Fly, Videodrome); Junji Ito's manga; Annihilation (VanderMeer); The Thing (Carpenter).

name: Slasher
description: Horror centered on a killer (often masked, often supernatural) systematically eliminating victims — usually young people. Highly conventionalized ritual unfolding of violence.
exemplars: Halloween; Friday the 13th; A Nightmare on Elm Street; Scream (meta-slasher).

name: Found Footage Horror
beats: Beginning of the recording — normal life
description: Horror presented as if assembled from real recordings discovered after the events — handheld camera, security tapes, smartphone video. Documentary-fictional structure.
exemplars: The Blair Witch Project; Paranormal Activity; REC; Cloverfield; Host (2020).

name: Folk Horror
beats: Outsider arrives in remote rural community
Realization of the cult's true nature
description: Horror rooted in landscape, isolated communities, and ancient pagan or folk practice. Rural and pre-Christian register; terror from older orders the present has not erased.
exemplars: The Wicker Man (1973); Midsommar; The Witch (Eggers); Penda's Fen.

name: Possession narrative
description: Horror in which a person's body is invaded and controlled by a malevolent supernatural entity. Spiritual rather than physical horror; loss of self to outside will.
exemplars: The Exorcist; The Conjuring; Hereditary (in part); pan-cultural possession-narrative tradition.

name: Survival Horror
description: Horror grounded in protagonist's struggle to survive in environment systematically hostile — limited resources, lurking threats, attrition. Resource-management and endurance over confrontation.
exemplars: Alien (Ridley Scott); The Descent; Resident Evil (game); A Quiet Place; The Mist.

name: Psychological Horror
beats: Confrontation with the source (real or psychological)
Resolution that may collapse all earlier interpretation
description: Horror grounded in mental disturbance — paranoia, dread, dissociation, unreliable perception. Interior register; threat may be internal or ambiguous.
exemplars: Shirley Jackson's The Haunting of Hill House; Kubrick's The Shining; Polanski's Repulsion; James's The Turn of the Screw.

name: Vampire Narrative
beats: Vampire defeated, escapes, or seduces protagonist
description: Horror or fantasy centered on vampires — undead bloodsuckers with their own conventions. Aversion to sunlight and crosses, transformation through bite, eternal life, predatory romance.
exemplars: Bram Stoker's Dracula; Anne Rice's Interview with the Vampire; Let the Right One In; True Blood; Buffy the Vampire Slayer.

name: Werewolf / Lycanthropy Narrative
beats: Curse, bite, or inheritance triggers first change
Trying to control or hide the condition
description: Horror centered on humans who transform into wolves or wolf-like creatures — through curse, bite, or family inheritance. Body-transformation horror and dual-nature theme.
exemplars: An American Werewolf in London; The Wolf Man (1941); Ginger Snaps; Patricia Briggs's Mercy Thompson novels.

name: Zombie Narrative
description: Horror centered on the dead returning as mindless flesh-eaters. The zombie has become a dominant horror metaphor for various societal anxieties.
exemplars: George A. Romero's Night of the Living Dead; The Walking Dead; Max Brooks's World War Z; 28 Days Later; Train to Busan.

name: Haunted House
description: Horror in which the threat is the house itself — its history, its spirits, its inability to let people leave. Setting-as-antagonist structure.
exemplars: Shirley Jackson's The Haunting of Hill House; The Amityville Horror; House of Leaves (Danielewski); The Conjuring; Hereditary.

name: Splatterpunk
description: Extreme horror distinguished by graphic violence, gore, and transgressive content. Visceral, body-explicit register.
exemplars: Clive Barker's Books of Blood; Edward Lee; Jack Ketchum's Off Season; Hostel; Saw franchise.

name: Quiet Horror
beats: Final image that confirms but does not explain
description: Horror that operates through suggestion, atmosphere, and what is NOT shown rather than gore or shock. Restraint and psychological depth.
exemplars: Robert Aickman's stories; Shirley Jackson generally; Picnic at Hanging Rock; M.R. James's ghost stories; The Haunting (1963).

name: Cult Horror
beats: Outsider or new member encounters group
description: Horror in which the threat is an organized group — religious cult, secret society, hidden community — pursuing collective dark purpose. Human-collective threat.
exemplars: The Wicker Man; Rosemary's Baby; Midsommar; Stephen King's Children of the Corn; The Sacrament.

name: Witch Narrative
description: Horror or fantasy centered on witches — old crones, hidden covens, accused women. Spans victim narratives (Salem-style) and supernatural-power narratives (Macbeth-style). Specifically gendered horror history.
exemplars: Arthur Miller's The Crucible; The Witch (Eggers); Suspiria (Argento and remake); The Witches (Dahl/Roeg); Practical Magic.

name: Demonic Possession Horror
beats: Demon defeated, draws back, or wins
description: Horror sub-form: demonic-specific (vs ghost-possession) variants. Specifically Christian-demonological register with priest as exorcist.
exemplars: The Exorcist; The Conjuring franchise; Paranormal Activity; The Last Exorcism.

name: Eco-Horror
description: Horror in which the threat is nature itself, often as response to human ecological transgression — forests that fight back, animals that rebel, environments that consume.
exemplars: Daphne du Maurier's "The Birds"; The Happening (Shyamalan); Annihilation (VanderMeer/Garland); The Ruins; Old (Shyamalan).

name: Gothic Romance (genre fusion)
beats: Innocent young woman arrives at gloomy estate
description: Hybrid of gothic horror and romance — atmospheric mansion, dangerous Byronic love interest, family secret, bride in peril. Romance gets equal structural weight.
exemplars: Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre; Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca; Victoria Holt; Mary Stewart; Crimson Peak (del Toro).

name: Sci-Fi Horror
beats: Confrontation through technical and physical means
description: Horror in science-fiction settings — alien parasites, malevolent AI, body-snatcher infiltration. Rational-scientific grounding of the horror element.
exemplars: Alien; The Thing (Carpenter); Event Horizon; Annihilation; Invasion of the Body Snatchers.

name: J-Horror (modern Japanese horror)
beats: Encounter with cursed object/medium (videotape, phone, internet)
Confrontation reveals trauma at its root
description: Modern Japanese horror genre centered on technological haunting, female ghosts, slow-build psychological dread. Distinct from classical kaidan by media-and-technology setting.
exemplars: Hideo Nakata's Ringu; Takashi Shimizu's Ju-On; Kiyoshi Kurosawa's Pulse; Dark Water.

name: Korean Horror (modern)
beats: Family secret or social wound revealed
Resolution often acknowledges that some wounds don't heal
description: Modern Korean horror genre combining family/social horror, supernatural elements, and political subtext. Korean-specific cultural texture (Confucian family pressure, shamanic elements, han).
exemplars: The Wailing (Na Hong-jin); Train to Busan (zombie variant); A Tale of Two Sisters; I Saw the Devil.

name: Slow-Burn Horror
description: Horror that develops dread gradually across an extended runtime — minimal jump scares, accumulated unease, climactic payoff that earns the wait. Patience as structural feature.
exemplars: Hereditary (Aster); The Witch (Eggers); It Follows; The Babadook; A Ghost Story.

name: Found Document Horror (epistolary)
beats: Document collection introduced (often by frame editor)
Documents grow stranger and more disturbed
Final entries fragment or break off
description: Horror told through documents — letters, diaries, transcripts, computer files. Reader assembles the story from fragments.
exemplars: Bram Stoker's Dracula (proto-form); Mark Z. Danielewski's House of Leaves; World War Z (Brooks); Carrie (King's epistolary frame).

name: Existential / Cosmic Dread Horror
description: Horror grounded in protagonist's confrontation with meaninglessness, mortality, or cosmic indifference. Philosophical-existential rather than alien-encounter.
exemplars: Thomas Ligotti's stories; Robert Aickman; True Detective season 1 (in part); The Seventh Seal (Bergman).

name: Body Snatcher / Replacement Horror
description: Horror in which familiar people are replaced by hostile imitations — pod people, doppelgangers, possessed loved ones. Paranoia-of-the-known register.
exemplars: Jack Finney's The Body Snatchers; Invasion of the Body Snatchers; The Faculty; Get Out (race-coded variant).

name: Apocalyptic Horror
description: Horror tied to civilizational end — the last days, final judgment, cosmic curtain. The apocalypse itself is the horror, not just its aftermath.
exemplars: The Mist (King); Cabin in the Woods (in part); The Seventh Sign; Knowing; many religious-horror narratives.

name: Slasher (procedural/franchise)
description: Procedural slasher in which killer's mythology is the primary content (Freddy, Jason, Michael) and victim-cycle structure is iterated across sequels. Killer-as-franchise.
exemplars: Halloween (Michael Myers); Friday the 13th (Jason); A Nightmare on Elm Street (Freddy); Scream (Ghostface).

name: Horror Comedy
beats: Horror situation set up with comic register
Real danger that comedy doesn't dispel
Climactic moment that is both terrifying and funny
description: Hybrid where horror's conventions are played for laughter without abandoning real horror beats. Genuine horror stakes alongside comedy.
exemplars: Shaun of the Dead; Tucker & Dale vs Evil; What We Do in the Shadows; Cabin in the Woods; Sam Raimi's Evil Dead (II onward).

name: Contemporary Romance
description: Romance set in the present day with realistic settings — workplace, dating apps, modern friendship circles. Now-context.
exemplars: Emily Henry's novels; Jasmine Guillory; Beth O'Leary's The Flatshare; modern rom-com films.

name: Historical Romance
beats: Historical setting and social position established
Union (or tragic separation) within period constraints
description: Romance set in a specific historical period — period's social rules and constraints integral to the romantic obstacle. Careful period detail.
exemplars: Diana Gabaldon's Outlander; Eloisa James; Beverly Jenkins; The English Patient (variant).

name: Regency Romance
beats: Hero of higher status (often duke) appears
description: Specific historical romance set in British Regency period (~1811-1820): balls, country estates, marriage market, proper-and-improper rules. Highly conventionalized.
exemplars: Georgette Heyer's foundational novels; Julia Quinn's Bridgerton; Lisa Kleypas; Stephanie Laurens.

name: Paranormal Romance
beats: Human meets supernatural lover (or two supernaturals meet)
description: Romance with one or both partners as supernatural — vampires, werewolves, demons, witches. Romance gets equal or primary weight to fantasy.
exemplars: Stephenie Meyer's Twilight; Sherrilyn Kenyon's Dark-Hunter; J.R. Ward's Black Dagger Brotherhood; Charlaine Harris.

name: Romantic Comedy (Rom-Com)
description: Romance with comedy as primary register — meet-cute, mismatched personalities, comic complications, ending in committed union.
exemplars: Nora Ephron's When Harry Met Sally; Notting Hill; Bridget Jones's Diary; Crazy Rich Asians; Emily Henry novels.

name: Enemies to Lovers
description: Romance trope-based form: two characters begin in genuine antagonism that gradually transforms into love. Antagonism must be real, not feigned.
exemplars: Sally Thorne's The Hating Game; Casey McQuiston's Red, White & Royal Blue; Pride and Prejudice (proto); When Harry Met Sally (in part).

name: Friends to Lovers
beats: Catalyst that makes one notice the other newly
Friendship becomes love without losing what it was
description: Romance in which existing friends gradually realize romantic feelings. Slow recognition register; no enemies-to-overcome, only friendship's transformation.
exemplars: When Harry Met Sally; Jenny Han's To All the Boys I've Loved Before; many YA romances; The Office (Jim and Pam).

name: Second Chance Romance
description: Romance in which former lovers reunite years later — past relationship's failure and present-day reconciliation are equally central. Carries weight of accumulated history.
exemplars: Nicholas Sparks's The Notebook; Emily Henry's People We Meet on Vacation; Persuasion (Austen — original).

name: Marriage of Convenience
beats: Cohabitation reveals each to the other
Real love acknowledged; arrangement becomes real marriage
description: Two characters marry for non-romantic reasons (citizenship, inheritance, scandal-prevention) and gradually fall in love within the practical arrangement. Wedding first, love after.
exemplars: Helen Hoang's The Heart Principle (variant); many regency romances; The Proposal (Bullock); Sandra Brown novels.

name: Fake Dating
beats: Real feelings emerging beneath the act
Pretense exposed or moment of truth
description: Two characters pretend to be in a relationship for some external reason and develop real feelings during the performance. Highly conventionalized rom-com staple.
exemplars: To All the Boys I've Loved Before; The Proposal; The Wedding Date; 10 Things I Hate About You.

name: Slow Burn Romance
beats: Long period of restraint or denial
Each chapter or episode adds incremental closeness
Consummation that has been earned by accumulated weight
description: Romance whose pleasure is the extended development of feeling — sometimes across multiple novels or seasons — with delayed consummation. Commitment to deferral.
exemplars: Pride and Prejudice (canonical); Persuasion; many TV-series romances (The Office, Bones).

name: Workplace Romance
beats: Resolution: pursuit of relationship even at career cost
description: Romance set in a shared workplace — colleague dynamics, professional ambition, the workplace's rules complicating the relationship.
exemplars: Sally Thorne's The Hating Game; The Office (Jim and Pam); many romance novels and films.

name: Star-Crossed Lovers
beats: Cosmic-scale obstacle (warring families, opposing kingdoms, fate)
description: Romance whose external impossibility is woven into the universe itself — fate, family feud, war, religious schism. Cosmic-fatalistic register.
exemplars: Romeo and Juliet; West Side Story; Tristan and Iseult; The English Patient.

name: Fated Mates
description: Romance (typically paranormal) in which two characters are cosmically destined for each other — recognition is biological, magical, or supernatural. Inevitability premise.
exemplars: Many shifter romance novels; J.R. Ward's Black Dagger Brotherhood (variants); Maya Banks; Nalini Singh's Psy-Changeling.

name: Forbidden Love (deeper sub-form)
beats: Choice: relationship at career/social cost, or end
description: Love forbidden by specific institutional or social structure — student-teacher, priest-parishioner, employer-employee — with the prohibition itself becoming the structural drama.
exemplars: The Reader (Schlink); Notes on a Scandal; Y tu mamá también; Lust, Caution (Ang Lee).

name: Love Triangle
beats: Choice made; one interest left behind
description: Romance with three principals where the protagonist must choose between two romantic interests. Specific three-corner structure — choice itself is the genre's content.
exemplars: The Hunger Games (Peeta/Gale); Twilight (Jacob/Edward); Bridget Jones's Diary; The Age of Innocence.

name: Hate-to-Love
description: Specific enemies-to-lovers variant where antagonism is initial and dramatic but transformation faster and more passionate. Accelerated arc, intense register.
exemplars: Christina Lauren's novels; Tessa Bailey; many shorter romance novels and films.

name: Sweet / Clean Romance
description: Romance without explicit sexuality and graphic content — typically targeted at religious, conservative, or younger audiences. Register of restraint.
exemplars: Bethany House Christian romance; Hallmark Channel films; Karen Kingsbury's novels; Amish romance subgenre.

name: Bodice Ripper / Old-School Historical Romance
beats: Hero's love revealed beneath the dominance
description: 1970s-80s historical romance with sexual content treated as central — often featuring rakes, pirates, captive heroines. Now somewhat dated; the genre has evolved.
exemplars: Kathleen Woodiwiss's The Flame and the Flower (1972 foundational); early Johanna Lindsey; early Bertrice Small.

name: Erotic Romance
description: Romance with explicit sexual content as central to the relationship's development. Distinct from generic romance by foregrounding sexuality; from erotica by romance arc remaining primary.
exemplars: E.L. James's Fifty Shades of Grey (controversial); Christina Lauren; Lauren Blakely; Lisa Renee Jones.

name: Queer Romance
beats: Attraction develops with possible identity stakes
External or internal conflict (family, religion, self-acceptance)
description: Romance featuring same-sex or LGBTQ+ partners. Specific cultural and identity context; sub-conventions vary by sexuality.
exemplars: Casey McQuiston's Red, White & Royal Blue; Becky Albertalli's Simon vs. the Homo Sapiens Agenda; T.J. Klune's The House in the Cerulean Sea; Alice Oseman's Heartstopper.

name: Office Romance / Bossy Boss
beats: Choice — leave job, leave love, or change power dynamic
description: Specific workplace-romance variant with power asymmetry between boss and employee. Forbidden-power register within professional setting.
exemplars: Fifty Shades; many Harlequin Presents novels; Suits (Mike and Rachel).

name: Romance with Disability / Chronic Illness
beats: Protagonist's life and condition established without pity
Committed relationship that integrates the condition
description: Romance in which one or both partners has a disability, chronic illness, or neurodivergence. Specific stakes around accommodation, vulnerability, dignity.
exemplars: Helen Hoang's The Kiss Quotient (autism); Talia Hibbert; Jojo Moyes's Me Before You (controversial); The Fault in Our Stars.

name: Mafia / Dark Romance
beats: Heroine's danger as liability or asset
description: Romance with criminal antihero — mafia, mobster, dangerous outlaw — as romantic lead. Morally compromised hero and dark register.
exemplars: Penelope Sky; Sylvia Day's Bared to You; many "dark romance" indie novels; The Godfather's romantic subplots (proto).

name: Polyamorous / Reverse Harem Romance
beats: Second partner enters; jealousy or compatibility
description: Romance with multiple romantic partners in non-monogamous arrangements — reverse harem (one woman, multiple men) or genuine polyamory. Multi-partner structure.
exemplars: Various indie romance novels; Quinn Loftis novels (variants); polyamorous-focused romance subgenre.

name: Spy Thriller / Espionage
beats: Operative introduced with their distinctive method
Mission resolved — at moral or personal cost
description: Espionage narrative featuring intelligence operatives, double-crosses, and geopolitical stakes. Sub-types: glamorous (Bond), morally ambiguous (le Carré), procedural (Deighton).
exemplars: Ian Fleming's Bond novels; John le Carré's The Spy Who Came in from the Cold; Len Deighton's The IPCRESS File; Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy.

name: Legal Thriller
beats: Lawyer protagonist takes on the case
description: Thriller centered on legal stakes — courtroom, firm, case. Adversarial structure; justice contested through legal mechanics.
exemplars: John Grisham's The Firm, A Time to Kill; Scott Turow's Presumed Innocent; Robert Traver's Anatomy of a Murder.

name: Medical Thriller
beats: Medical setting with patient or specimen
description: Thriller in medical settings where stakes are biological — outbreaks, dangerous treatments, hospital conspiracies. Doctor as detective.
exemplars: Robin Cook's Coma; Michael Crichton's The Andromeda Strain; Tess Gerritsen's medical thrillers; The Constant Gardener (le Carré).

name: Heist narrative
beats: Target introduced and its impossibility established
Theft completed (or fails) — often with twist
description: A team of specialists plans and executes an elaborate theft. Highly structured genre with established conventions. Plan-meets-reality is the structural pleasure.
exemplars: Ocean's Eleven; The Sting; Topkapi; Heat; Inception (heist-shaped); Money Heist (La Casa de Papel).

name: Disaster narrative
beats: Multiple character introductions before the disaster
Aftermath — what is rebuilt, what is lost
description: Narrative organized around large-scale catastrophe — natural disaster, plague, accident — and a cast of characters facing it. The disaster itself, multi-perspective.
exemplars: The Towering Inferno; Titanic (Cameron); Contagion; Sebastian Junger's The Perfect Storm.

name: Action Thriller
description: Thriller foregrounding physical action — chases, shootouts, fights — with plot at the service of set-pieces. Kinesthetic sequences.
exemplars: Lee Child's Jack Reacher novels; Vince Flynn's Mitch Rapp; Mission: Impossible franchise; Bourne franchise.

name: Eco-Thriller
description: Thriller in which environmental crisis drives the action — climate disasters, pandemics, ecological warfare. Environmental causality.
