exemplars: Michael Crichton's State of Fear; Daniel Quinn's Ishmael; The Day After Tomorrow; Geostorm; Robinson's eco-fiction.

name: Hostage Thriller
description: Thriller in which a hostage situation drives the entire narrative — limited setting, ticking clock, negotiation as primary action. Spatial-temporal constraint.
exemplars: Dog Day Afternoon; The Negotiator; Inside Man; Phone Booth.

name: Disaster Thriller (prevention)
description: Thriller in which a large-scale disaster (natural, industrial, terrorist) is imminent or unfolding. Distinct from disaster narrative by thriller-pace and prevention-focus.
exemplars: Deep Impact; Armageddon; Sully; Apollo 13; Crichton's Sphere (variant).

name: Financial Thriller
description: Thriller centered on high-stakes financial maneuvering — markets, fraud, banking conspiracies, hostile takeovers. Specifically economic content.
exemplars: The Big Short (Lewis); Tom Wolfe's Bonfire of the Vanities; Margin Call; Wall Street (1987); John Grisham's The Firm.

name: Religious Thriller
description: Thriller in which religious texts, artifacts, conspiracies, or eschatology drive the plot. Often involves Vatican, Templars, ancient sects, or apocalyptic prophecy.
exemplars: Dan Brown's The Da Vinci Code and Angels & Demons; Umberto Eco's The Name of the Rose (literary variant); The Omen (horror variant).

name: Forensic Thriller
beats: Pattern reveals serial or organized criminality
description: Thriller foregrounding forensic science — crime scene analysis, autopsy, DNA, ballistics — as investigation's primary tool. Higher-stakes, more thriller-paced register than forensic procedural.
exemplars: Patricia Cornwell's Kay Scarpetta; Kathy Reichs's Tempe Brennan; Karin Slaughter; Bones (TV).

name: Cyber Thriller
description: Thriller in which the central crime, conflict, or threat is cyber — hacking, data theft, infrastructure attack. Digital register.
exemplars: Daniel Suarez's Daemon; Mr. Robot; Stieg Larsson's Dragon Tattoo trilogy (variant); Sneakers (1992).

name: Whistleblower Thriller
description: Thriller in which the protagonist is an insider exposing institutional wrongdoing — and is hunted for it. Action-thriller pace and pursuit register.
exemplars: The Insider (Wigand-Mann); Snowden (Stone); All the President's Men (variant); The Pelican Brief.

name: Survival Thriller
description: Thriller in which protagonist must survive in extreme environment or against ruthless pursuit — wilderness, ocean, post-apocalyptic terrain. Less supernatural than survival horror.
exemplars: 127 Hours (Aron Ralston); Jon Krakauer's Into Thin Air; Cast Away; The Revenant; Open Water.

name: Erotic Thriller
description: Thriller in which sexuality is woven into the danger — the protagonist's desire IS partly the threat. Distinct from erotic romance by menacing register.
exemplars: Basic Instinct; Body Heat; Fatal Attraction; Gone Girl (variant).

name: Domestic Noir
description: Crossover of domestic thriller and noir — middle-class home life with hidden darkness, unreliable narrators, twist endings. Noir-influenced literary style.
exemplars: Gillian Flynn's Gone Girl; A.J. Finn's The Woman in the Window; Paula Hawkins; Liane Moriarty.

name: Political Conspiracy Thriller
beats: Race to expose before being silenced
description: Sub-form combining political and conspiracy thrillers — a hidden political plot involving high-level officials. Specifically political-power conspiracy.
exemplars: Robert Ludlum's Bourne novels; The Manchurian Candidate; No Way Out; David Baldacci's political thrillers.

name: Adventure (sub-form)
beats: Climactic confrontation with environment or rival
Return (often with reduced team) carrying knowledge or treasure
description: Variant focused on physical exploration of dangerous geography — jungles, polar wastes, deep sea, mountains. Travelogue-with-stakes register.
exemplars: Jack London's stories; Jon Krakauer; H. Rider Haggard; Indiana Jones.

name: Survival Memoir
description: First-person account of an extreme survival experience told in memoir form — cancer, mountaineering accident, war, abuse. Non-fiction register.
exemplars: Jon Krakauer's Into Thin Air; Aron Ralston's Between a Rock and a Hard Place; Joe Simpson's Touching the Void; Ernest Shackleton's South.

name: Techno-thriller
beats: Cat-and-mouse with adversary using same tech
Resolution with implications for tech development
description: Thriller foregrounding high technology — military hardware, computing, biotech — as both setting and engine. Technical detail as feature.
exemplars: Tom Clancy's Hunt for Red October; Michael Crichton's novels; Daniel Suarez's Daemon; The Andromeda Strain.

name: Crime Thriller (general)
beats: Protagonist (criminal, victim, or detective) drawn in
description: Broad thriller form centered on criminal activity — crime planning, pursuit, or aftermath. Distinguished from procedural by thriller-pace.
exemplars: Don Winslow's The Power of the Dog; James Ellroy; Dennis Lehane's Mystic River; Heat.

name: Slow-Burn Thriller
beats: Aftermath that unsettles more than resolves
description: Thriller that develops menace gradually rather than through action set-pieces. Atmosphere-heavy, dread-driven register.
exemplars: No Country for Old Men (McCarthy/Coens); Prisoners; Wind River; Patricia Highsmith's literary thrillers.

name: Ancient World Historical Fiction
beats: Historical figure or invented protagonist embedded in real events
Climactic moment tied to real history
Implications for what we know happened
description: Historical fiction set in ancient civilizations — Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, Persia, China, India. Specific archaeological-historical detail.
exemplars: Mary Renault's The King Must Die; Robert Graves's I, Claudius; Steven Pressfield's Gates of Fire; Madeline Miller's Circe; Colleen McCullough's Masters of Rome.

name: Medieval Historical Fiction
beats: Protagonist within feudal or religious structure
description: Historical fiction set in the medieval period (~500-1500 CE) — knights, monasteries, plagues, courts, peasant revolts. Medieval-specific detail and worldview.
exemplars: Umberto Eco's The Name of the Rose; Ken Follett's The Pillars of the Earth; Bernard Cornwell's The Last Kingdom; The Saxon Stories.

name: Renaissance / Tudor Historical Fiction
description: Historical fiction set in European Renaissance and Tudor periods (~1400-1600). Court-intrigue heavy; era's politics, religion, art are central.
exemplars: Hilary Mantel's Wolf Hall trilogy (Cromwell); Philippa Gregory's The Other Boleyn Girl; C.J. Sansom's Shardlake mysteries.

name: Victorian / Edwardian Historical Fiction
description: Historical fiction set in Victorian and Edwardian eras (~1837-1914). Industrial-imperial setting, class anxieties, specific period social codes.
exemplars: A.S. Byatt's Possession; Charles Palliser's The Quincunx; Sarah Waters's Fingersmith; The French Lieutenant's Woman (Fowles).

name: WWI Historical Fiction
description: Fiction set during or around World War I (1914-18). Trench warfare register, lost-generation themes, modernist undertones.
exemplars: Erich Maria Remarque's All Quiet on the Western Front; Pat Barker's Regeneration trilogy; Sebastian Faulks's Birdsong; Testament of Youth (Brittain).

name: WWII Historical Fiction
beats: Specific war experience (combat, occupation, hiding, work)
description: Fiction set during or around World War II (1939-45). Largest historical-fiction subgenre by volume. Spans military, resistance, Holocaust, home-front, post-war.
exemplars: Anthony Doerr's All the Light We Cannot See; Markus Zusak's The Book Thief; Heller's Catch-22 (variant); Schindler's List (Keneally).

name: Holocaust Narrative
beats: Reckoning — for those who lived, and for those who didn't
description: Fiction or memoir set during the Holocaust (Shoah). Specific moral and historical weight; ethical conventions about representation are part of the genre.
exemplars: Elie Wiesel's Night; Primo Levi's If This Is a Man; Anne Frank's Diary; Imre Kertész's Fatelessness; Schindler's List.

name: Cold War Narrative
description: Fiction set during Cold War (1947-91), focused on ideological-geopolitical conflict between West and Soviet bloc. Spy thriller, political fiction, lived experience.
exemplars: John le Carré's Karla trilogy; Don DeLillo's Libra; Robert Harris's Archangel; The Americans (TV); Bridge of Spies.

name: American Civil War Narrative
beats: Loss, conflict over values, racial reckoning
description: Fiction set during or around the U.S. Civil War (1861-65). Specific North-South political and racial context.
exemplars: Stephen Crane's The Red Badge of Courage; Margaret Mitchell's Gone with the Wind; Charles Frazier's Cold Mountain; Beloved (Morrison, post-war variant).

name: Western (frontier narrative)
beats: Resolution: justice, exile, or ambiguous closure
description: Fiction set in the American West during frontier era (~1860s-1900s) — gunfighters, sheriffs, settlers, displaced Native peoples, ranchers vs farmers.
exemplars: Owen Wister's The Virginian; McCarthy's Blood Meridian and No Country for Old Men; Larry McMurtry's Lonesome Dove; True Grit (Portis).

name: Revisionist Western
beats: Climactic showdown that lacks moral clarity
description: Western that subverts traditional frontier mythology — Native dispossession, racial complexity, ambiguous heroism, costs of Manifest Destiny. Critical posture.
exemplars: McCarthy's Blood Meridian; Unforgiven (Eastwood); Dances with Wolves; The Sisters Brothers; Sergio Leone's Once Upon a Time in the West.

name: Imperial / Colonial Narrative
beats: Empire's continuation, decline, or recognition of guilt
description: Fiction set during European imperial-colonial expansion or its decline — colonizers' perspectives, colonial subjects' resistance, the colonial encounter's costs.
exemplars: E.M. Forster's A Passage to India; Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness; Adichie's Half of a Yellow Sun; Amitav Ghosh's Sea of Poppies.

name: Post-Colonial Narrative
description: Fiction by formerly-colonized peoples about colonialism's experience and aftermath. Writing from the subject of empire rather than its agents.
exemplars: Achebe's Things Fall Apart; Rushdie's Midnight's Children; Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's A Grain of Wheat; Dangarembga's Nervous Conditions; Kincaid's A Small Place.

name: Regency / Napoleonic Historical
beats: Napoleonic war as background or foreground
description: Specific period historical fiction set during British Regency / Napoleonic Wars (~1795-1820). Distinct from Regency romance by foregrounding the broader historical drama.
exemplars: Bernard Cornwell's Sharpe series; Patrick O'Brian's Aubrey-Maturin novels; Naomi Novik's Temeraire (fantasy variant).

name: Roaring Twenties / Jazz Age
beats: Protagonist's place within or outside it
description: Fiction set in the 1920s — boom, jazz, prohibition, modernism. Atmospheres of excess, hidden hollow, impending crash.
exemplars: F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby; Anita Loos's Gentlemen Prefer Blondes; Boardwalk Empire (TV); Babylon (Chazelle).

name: Great Depression Narrative
beats: Survival on the road or in the slum
description: Fiction set during the Great Depression (~1929-39). Poverty, displacement, labor. Often paired with social-realist register.
exemplars: Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath; James Agee's Let Us Now Praise Famous Men; Erskine Caldwell's Tobacco Road.

name: Civil Rights Era Narrative
beats: Protagonist's choice to engage or resist
description: Fiction set during the American Civil Rights Movement (~1954-68). Specific political-racial register and historical movement frame.
exemplars: Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird; Toni Morrison's novels (variant); Selma (DuVernay); The Help (Stockett, controversial); Whitehead's The Nickel Boys.

name: Vietnam War Narrative
description: Fiction set during or around Vietnam War (~1955-75). Jungle warfare, moral ambiguity, generational rupture, post-traumatic register.
exemplars: Tim O'Brien's The Things They Carried; Karl Marlantes's Matterhorn; Michael Herr's Dispatches; Apocalypse Now; Platoon.

name: Soviet / Eastern Bloc Narrative
beats: Risk of dissent or hidden truth
Survival or destruction within the system
description: Fiction set in Soviet Union or Eastern Bloc — gulag, surveillance, dissident underground, communal apartments. Specific totalitarian-state register.
exemplars: Solzhenitsyn's One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich; Bulgakov's The Master and Margarita; Kundera's The Unbearable Lightness of Being; Funder's Stasiland.

name: Reconstruction Era Narrative
beats: End of war and beginning of new freedom
Era ends in defeat and the long shadow forward
description: Fiction set during American Reconstruction (~1865-77) — post-Civil-War South, ex-slaves' freedom and its limits, reactionary backlash. Specific historical-political moment.
exemplars: Toni Morrison's Beloved; Edward P. Jones's The Known World; Whitehead's The Underground Railroad; Free State of Jones (film).

name: Stream of Consciousness Novel
beats: Associative chains rather than linear plot
Climactic moment of clarity or breakdown
description: Modernist novel form rendering unfiltered flow of a character's thought — associative, non-linear, sensory, syntactically experimental. Interior-mimetic register.
exemplars: James Joyce's Ulysses; Virginia Woolf's Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse; William Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury; Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time.

name: Modernist Novel
description: Early-20th-c. literary movement: experimental form, fragmented chronology, interior depth, skeptical of grand narratives. Formal innovation; coherent narrative ambition.
exemplars: Joyce's Ulysses; Woolf's Mrs Dalloway; Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises; T.S. Eliot's The Waste Land.

name: Postmodernist Novel
beats: Climactic gesture that may or may not be sincere
description: Late-20th-c. literary movement: ironic, metafictional, anti-foundationalist, often humorous. Self-conscious play with the conventions of fiction itself.
exemplars: Thomas Pynchon's Gravity's Rainbow; Italo Calvino's If on a Winter's Night a Traveler; Don DeLillo's White Noise; David Foster Wallace's Infinite Jest.

name: Maximalist Novel
beats: Resolution not through plot but through accumulated weight
description: Long, encyclopedic, dense literary novel that aims to encompass everything — culture, history, science, philosophy. Length, ambition, density.
exemplars: Pynchon's Gravity's Rainbow; Wallace's Infinite Jest; Roberto Bolaño's 2666; DeLillo's Underworld; Joseph McElroy.

name: Minimalist Fiction
description: Late-20th-c. literary movement: stripped prose, restrained emotional register, omitted subtext, economy as principle. More literary than dirty realism.
exemplars: Raymond Carver; Amy Hempel; Ann Beattie; Mary Robison; Frederick Barthelme.

name: Auto-Fiction
beats: Insight whose truth status is multilayered
description: Fiction in which author's biographical material is openly used while remaining fictional — line between novel and memoir is performatively blurred.
exemplars: Karl Ove Knausgård's My Struggle; Rachel Cusk's Outline trilogy; Sheila Heti's How Should a Person Be?; Ben Lerner's 10:04; Annie Ernaux.

name: Roman à Clef
beats: Characters obviously based on real figures
Plot follows real events at a fiction's distance
Insight or judgment about real figures
description: A novel in which real people appear as fictional characters — typically with names changed. Distinct from auto-fiction by depicting OTHERS rather than the author primarily.
exemplars: Truman Capote's Answered Prayers; Jacqueline Susann's Valley of the Dolls; Primary Colors (Joe Klein); Orwell's Animal Farm (allegorical variant).

name: Metafiction
beats: Climactic moment that uses metafiction structurally
description: Fiction that explicitly draws attention to its own status as fiction — author intrudes, narrative comments on itself, characters break the fourth wall.
exemplars: John Fowles's The French Lieutenant's Woman; Italo Calvino's If on a Winter's Night; Charlie Kaufman's Adaptation; The Princess Bride (Goldman).

name: Hysterical Realism
beats: Sense of meaning that may evade
description: Literary mode (named pejoratively by James Wood, 2000) characterized by manic energy, large casts, sprawling plots, conspiracy themes, information density.
exemplars: Zadie Smith's White Teeth; Salman Rushdie's The Ground Beneath Her Feet; Jonathan Franzen's The Corrections (variant); DeLillo's Underworld.

name: New Sincerity
beats: Earnest moment that risks looking foolish
description: Late-20th/early-21st-c. literary movement reacting against postmodern irony — embracing sincerity, earnestness, emotional directness. Post-ironic register.
exemplars: David Foster Wallace's later essays; Dave Eggers's A Heartbreaking Work of Staggering Genius; George Saunders's later fiction; Sally Rooney (in part).

name: Philosophical Novel
beats: Resolution through intellectual rather than plot mechanics
description: Novel whose primary content is philosophical inquiry — characters wrestle explicitly with metaphysical, ethical, or political questions. Foregrounds ideas as content.
exemplars: Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov; Sartre's Nausea; Camus's The Plague; Kundera's The Unbearable Lightness of Being; Iris Murdoch.

name: Existentialist Fiction
beats: Burden of choice without external grounding
description: Mid-20th-c. literary movement: protagonists confront meaninglessness, absurdity, burden of freedom. Specific existential framework.
exemplars: Camus's The Stranger; Sartre's Nausea; Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground; Kafka's The Trial (proto); Beckett.

name: Absurdist Fiction
beats: Characters carry on as if logic still held
Climactic full collapse of logical structure
description: Fiction grounded in recognition that human existence is absurd — meaningless or irreducible to logic. Leans into comedy and play rather than gravity.
exemplars: Kafka's stories and The Trial; Beckett's Waiting for Godot; Eugene Ionesco; Daniil Kharms; Catch-22.

name: Surrealist Fiction
beats: Image or event without rational connection
description: Fiction grounded in dream-logic, irrational juxtaposition, the unconscious. Specific Surrealist-movement aesthetics — Bretonian automatism, dreamlike imagery.
exemplars: André Breton's Nadja; Leonora Carrington; Bruno Schulz's The Street of Crocodiles; Haruki Murakami (proto-surrealist variant).

name: Magical Realism (literary, beyond LA)
description: Magical realism as a global literary mode — fantastic elements treated as ordinary within otherwise realistic settings. Distinct from Latin American specific genre as a transferred mode.
exemplars: Salman Rushdie's Midnight's Children; Toni Morrison's Beloved; Haruki Murakami's Kafka on the Shore; Yann Martel's Life of Pi.

name: Gothic Literary Fiction
beats: Hidden family or local secret hinted
Resolution that may not fully exorcise
description: Literary fiction drawing on gothic conventions — atmospheric darkness, family secrets, decaying houses, spectral presences — without committing fully to horror genre.
exemplars: Donna Tartt's The Little Friend; Wuthering Heights; Rebecca; Sarah Waters's The Little Stranger; Eleanor Catton's The Luminaries.

name: Campus Novel
description: Novel set in a university — students, professors, the politics of academia. Specific institutional setting and its peculiar mores. Often comic or satirical.
exemplars: Kingsley Amis's Lucky Jim; David Lodge's campus trilogy; Donna Tartt's The Secret History; Wonder Boys (Chabon); The Idiot (Batuman).

name: Künstlerroman (artist's novel)
beats: Encounter with art that calls them
Apprenticeship or struggle to develop voice
description: Specific Bildungsroman variant: novel of an artist's development — formation of the creative self. Foregrounds artistic vocation as the central arc.
exemplars: James Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man; Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time; Maugham's Of Human Bondage; Woolf's To the Lighthouse (in part).

name: Anti-Novel
description: Novel that systematically refuses or subverts the conventions of the novel — plot, character development, resolution. Specific anti-posture.
exemplars: Nathalie Sarraute's Tropisms; Alain Robbe-Grillet's Jealousy; Beckett's The Unnamable; David Markson's Wittgenstein's Mistress.

name: Verse Novel
description: A novel-length narrative composed entirely or primarily in verse. Formal hybrid: novel scope, poetry's compression and music.
exemplars: Pushkin's Eugene Onegin (foundational); Vikram Seth's The Golden Gate; Anne Carson's Autobiography of Red; Jacqueline Woodson's Brown Girl Dreaming.

name: Mystery Play (medieval)
beats: Biblical scene set up in vernacular
Closing with transition to next cycle
description: Medieval cycle drama dramatizing biblical episodes — Creation, Noah, Nativity, Passion, Judgment. Performed by guilds in towns. Religious-pageant register.
exemplars: York Mystery Plays; N-Town Plays; Towneley Plays; Coventry Mystery Plays.

name: Morality Play
beats: Search for companion to the grave
description: Late medieval allegorical drama in which Everyman or similar protagonist meets allegorical figures (Death, Goods, Knowledge, Mercy) and must make moral choices for salvation.
exemplars: Everyman (c. 1500, canonical); The Castle of Perseverance; Mankind.

name: Closet Drama
description: Drama written for reading rather than performance — often verse, philosophically dense, formally restrained. Non-performance ambition.
exemplars: Seneca's tragedies; Goethe's Faust (in part); Byron's Manfred; Shelley's Prometheus Unbound.

name: Verse Drama
beats: Action through speech rather than scene-mechanics
Verbal confrontation as the central event
description: Drama composed in verse rather than prose — highly artificial register that elevates speech. The Renaissance default; rare in modern drama.
exemplars: Shakespeare's plays; T.S. Eliot's Murder in the Cathedral; Christopher Fry; Tony Kushner's Angels in America (in part).

name: Melodrama
description: 19th-c. theatrical genre featuring sensationalism, clear good-and-evil, music-underscored emotion, broad acting. Emotional excess as feature, not flaw.
exemplars: East Lynne; Uncle Tom's Cabin (theatrical adaptations); Way Down East; many silent-era films.

name: Well-Made Play
description: 19th-c. dramatic structure formalized by Eugène Scribe: tightly plotted, with planted secrets, reversals, and complex denouement-through-revelation. Mechanical precision.
exemplars: Scribe's plays; Sardou's plays; Ibsen's early structure; influenced later well-made cinema.

name: Naturalist Drama
description: Late-19th-c. drama applying naturalist principles to theater — characters determined by environment and heredity, ordinary people as protagonists, explicit social problems.
exemplars: Ibsen's Ghosts; Strindberg's Miss Julie; Hauptmann's The Weavers; Chekhov (variant).

name: Symbolist Drama
description: Late-19th-c. drama countering naturalism: dreamlike, mythic, emphasizing inner mood and spiritual truth over external accuracy. Anti-realist register.
exemplars: Maurice Maeterlinck's Pelleas and Melisande; Yeats's plays; Strindberg's A Dream Play (variant); some Synge.

name: Expressionist Drama
description: Early-20th-c. drama foregrounding subjective psychological experience — distorted reality, fragmented dialogue, inner truth made visible. Specifically Weimar / German register.
exemplars: Georg Kaiser; Ernst Toller; Eugene O'Neill's The Emperor Jones; Elmer Rice's The Adding Machine.

name: Theatre of the Absurd
beats: Apparent waiting for meaning that doesn't come
description: Mid-20th-c. drama in which existential meaninglessness is staged through breakdown of language, narrative coherence, and character logic. Post-WWII philosophical register.
exemplars: Beckett's Waiting for Godot and Endgame; Ionesco's The Bald Soprano; Edward Albee's The Zoo Story; Harold Pinter's early plays.

name: Epic Theatre (Brechtian)
beats: Audience provoked to think rather than feel
description: Bertolt Brecht's theatrical method: explicit anti-illusionism, Verfremdungseffekt (alienation effect), political analysis, episodic structure. Refusal of emotional immersion.
exemplars: Brecht's The Threepenny Opera, Mother Courage, The Caucasian Chalk Circle; Tony Kushner's Angels in America (Brechtian variant).

name: Theatre of Cruelty (Artaud)
description: Antonin Artaud's theatrical theory and practice: theater as ritual, sensory assault, transformative collective experience. Theater that wounds and heals.
exemplars: Artaud's The Cenci; later Jerzy Grotowski; Peter Brook's Marat/Sade; Living Theatre productions.

name: Postdramatic Theatre
beats: No clear narrative or character development
Image, sound, body as primary materials
description: Late-20th/early-21st-c. theatrical mode that abandons traditional dramatic structure — text, plot, character — in favor of performance, image, body, and event. Post-textual ambition.
exemplars: Robert Wilson's productions; Heiner Müller's late works; Forced Entertainment; The Wooster Group; Hans-Thies Lehmann's theorization.

name: Dramatic Monologue
beats: Tension between what's said and what's meant
description: Dramatic form (in theater or poetry) consisting of a single character's extended speech to implied or silent listener. Character's psychology emerges through what they reveal and conceal.
exemplars: Robert Browning's "My Last Duchess"; Beckett's Krapp's Last Tape; Eric Bogosian's monologue plays; Talking Heads (Alan Bennett).

name: Duologue (Two-Hander)
description: Drama for exactly two characters — sustained dialogue, intimate scope, no external relief. Tight structural constraint.
exemplars: Edward Albee's The Zoo Story and Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (variant); Pinter's The Dumb Waiter; Beckett's Krapp (one-hander variant).

name: One-Person Show
beats: Climactic moment of revelation or confrontation
description: Theatrical form featuring a single performer for the entire show — autobiographical, character-impersonation, or political. Single-performer constraint.
exemplars: Spalding Gray's monologues; Anna Deavere Smith's Twilight: Los Angeles; Eric Bogosian; Hannah Gadsby's Nanette.

name: Devised Theatre
description: Theatre created collaboratively by an ensemble through workshops and improvisation, often without a pre-existing script. Collective-creation method.
exemplars: Forced Entertainment; Complicité; Punchdrunk's Sleep No More; Mike Leigh's films (devised process).

name: Immersive Theatre
description: Theatre that abandons the audience-stage division — audience moves through environments, encounters performers individually, makes choices that affect what they see.
exemplars: Punchdrunk's Sleep No More; Then She Fell; Felix Barrett productions; some Robert Wilson.

name: Documentary Theatre / Verbatim
beats: Real-world event or community as subject
Audience encounters reality at theatrical distance
description: Theatrical work whose text is drawn entirely from real-world sources — interviews, court transcripts, news reports — performed by actors. Verbatim documentary commitment.
exemplars: Anna Deavere Smith's verbatim plays; The Laramie Project (Tectonic Theater Project); David Hare's Stuff Happens; Tricycle Theatre tribunal plays.

name: Play with Songs
description: Theatrical form combining spoken text with songs, distinct from full musical by less integrated song-structure. More theatrical-than-commercial commitment.
exemplars: Brecht-Weill's The Threepenny Opera (proto); Michael John LaChiusa; Adam Guettel's The Light in the Piazza; Sondheim's more theatrical works.

name: Epic Poem
description: Long narrative poem of heroic scale — wars, voyages, founding of nations, divine interventions. Sustained verse register and conventional epic features.
exemplars: Homer's Iliad and Odyssey; Virgil's Aeneid; Milton's Paradise Lost; Dante's Divine Comedy; Beowulf.

name: Mock Epic
beats: Apparent gravity given to small things
description: Epic-form poem applied to trivial subject — using high heroic register to magnify a quarrel over a lock of hair, a frog-mouse battle, etc. Parodic stance toward epic conventions.
exemplars: Pope's The Rape of the Lock; Pope's The Dunciad; Byron's Don Juan (variant); Boileau's Le Lutrin.

name: Heroic Poem (medieval romance)
beats: Adventures with monsters and rival knights
description: Medieval narrative poem of knightly adventure, courtly love, and chivalric virtue. More individualized hero and romance conventions than classical epic.
exemplars: Chrétien de Troyes's romances; Sir Gawain and the Green Knight; Ariosto's Orlando Furioso; Spenser's The Faerie Queene.

name: Ballad (narrative poem)
beats: Setting and characters in opening stanza
Climactic event (often death or tragic loss)
description: Short narrative folk poem, traditionally sung, in regular stanzas. Tells a single dramatic episode — often of love, death, war, or supernatural encounter.
exemplars: "Sir Patrick Spens"; "Tam Lin"; "Barbara Allen"; Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner; Bob Dylan's narrative songs.

name: Lay
beats: Brief setup of knight or lady
Closing — often with marvel as memory
description: Short medieval narrative poem, especially Breton lay — supernatural-tinged adventures, courtly love, fantastic creatures. Compact, literary courtly origin.
exemplars: Marie de France's Lais; Sir Orfeo; Chaucer's The Franklin's Tale.

name: Idyll
description: Short pastoral or idealized poem of rural life — shepherds, lovers, peaceful scenes. Idealized rural register.
exemplars: Theocritus's Idylls; Tennyson's Idylls of the King (Arthurian variant); Wordsworth's pastoral poems.

name: Eclogue
description: Pastoral dialogue poem — typically two shepherds in conversation. Specific dialogue structure.
exemplars: Virgil's Eclogues; Spenser's Shepheardes Calender; Pope's Pastorals.

name: Pastoral (broader form)
beats: Court or city established as compromised
description: Literary mode idealizing rural life as contrast to corrupt urban or court life. Spans poetry, prose, drama. Country-versus-city register.
exemplars: Sidney's Arcadia; Shakespeare's As You Like It; Goldsmith's The Deserted Village; Frost's pastoral poems.

name: Georgic
description: Poem about agriculture and rural labor — work of farming rather than its idealized leisure. Distinguished from pastoral by its labor focus.
exemplars: Virgil's Georgics; James Thomson's The Seasons; Wendell Berry's poems (modern variant).

name: Elegy
beats: Resolution: consolation, acceptance, or unresolved sorrow
description: Poem of mourning — lament for the dead, lost love, or fading time. Meditative, grief-driven register.
exemplars: Milton's "Lycidas"; Tennyson's In Memoriam; Whitman's "When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd"; Auden's "In Memory of W.B. Yeats."

name: Ode
description: Lyric poem of elevated address — to a person, thing, or abstract idea. Often public, ceremonial, or contemplative. Formal verse structure and high register.
exemplars: Pindar's odes; Horace's odes; Keats's "Ode to a Nightingale"; Wordsworth's "Ode: Intimations of Immortality"; Pablo Neruda's odes (modern).

name: Sonnet (narrative)
beats: Sestet or final quatrain + couplet: response/resolution
description: 14-line lyric poem with established rhyme scheme (Petrarchan or Shakespearean). Used for love, philosophical reflection, or compressed argument. Volta structure.
exemplars: Petrarch's Canzoniere; Shakespeare's sonnets; Donne's holy sonnets; Edna St. Vincent Millay; Terrance Hayes's American Sonnets.

name: Villanelle
beats: Meaning of refrains evolves through context
Climactic stanza brings both refrains together
description: 19-line poem with two refrains and only two rhymes — five tercets and a quatrain. The repeating refrains accumulate meaning.
exemplars: Dylan Thomas's "Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night"; Elizabeth Bishop's "One Art"; Theodore Roethke's "The Waking."

name: Sestina
beats: Six end-words established in first stanza
Three-line envoi compresses all six end-words
description: 39-line poem of six six-line stanzas plus a three-line envoi, where six end-words rotate through specific pattern across stanzas. Extreme formal constraint.
exemplars: Arnaut Daniel's foundational sestinas; Elizabeth Bishop's "Sestina"; Anthony Hecht; Algernon Charles Swinburne.

name: Ghazal
beats: Each successive couplet a self-contained meditation
Final couplet often signs poet's name
description: Persian/Arabic/Urdu poetic form: 5-15 couplets, each self-contained, ending with a refrain — often about unrequited or divine love. Couplet-autonomy structure.
exemplars: Hafiz; Rumi; Mirza Ghalib; Agha Shahid Ali (modern English ghazals).

name: Haiku
beats: Second image or thought completes the contrast
description: Japanese 17-mora poem (5-7-5) traditionally including a kigo (season word) and a kireji (cutting word). Extreme compression and seasonal-imagistic register.
exemplars: Bashō, Buson, Issa; Yosa Buson; modern English haiku poets (Cor van den Heuvel).

name: Tanka
beats: First three lines (5-7-5) set image or situation
Final two lines (7-7) develop or respond
description: Japanese 31-mora poem (5-7-5-7-7), longer than haiku. Used for love, lament, courtly exchange. Narrative compactness and emotional depth.
exemplars: Manyoshu anthology; Kokin Wakashū; Saigyō; Ono no Komachi; modern English tanka writers.

name: Free Verse Narrative
description: Narrative poetry without fixed meter or rhyme scheme. Distinguished from prose by line-breaks and rhythmic attention; from formal verse by non-formal structure.
exemplars: Walt Whitman's Leaves of Grass; T.S. Eliot's The Waste Land; Ezra Pound's Cantos; Allen Ginsberg's Howl; Adrienne Rich's Diving into the Wreck.

name: Prose Poem
beats: Prose paragraph opens with poetic compression
description: Composition that uses prose-paragraph form but operates with poetic intensity, compression, and imagistic logic. Lyric register; paragraph structure.
exemplars: Charles Baudelaire's Paris Spleen; Arthur Rimbaud's Illuminations; Russell Edson; Anne Carson; Claudia Rankine's Citizen.

name: Concrete / Visual Poem
beats: Words and shape together create meaning
description: Poem in which the visual arrangement of words on the page is essential to meaning. Typographic content.
exemplars: Eugen Gomringer's constellations; bp Nichol; Kenneth Patchen; Apollinaire's Calligrammes; e.e. cummings.

name: Confessional Poem
description: Mid-20th-c. poetic mode of intimate first-person disclosure — mental illness, family dysfunction, trauma. Personal exposure as the poem's content and ethic.
exemplars: Robert Lowell's Life Studies; Sylvia Plath's Ariel; Anne Sexton; W.D. Snodgrass.

name: Spoken Word / Slam Poetry
description: Poetry composed for live oral performance, often in competitive slam contexts. Performance-orientation, voice, rhythm, political register.
exemplars: Saul Williams; Patricia Smith; Sarah Kay; Nikki Giovanni (proto); modern slam poetry generally.

name: Dub Poetry
description: Performance poetry rooted in Jamaican reggae rhythms and political content — often anti-colonial, post-colonial, anti-racist. Specific musical foundation.
exemplars: Linton Kwesi Johnson; Mutabaruka; Benjamin Zephaniah; Jean "Binta" Breeze.

name: Aphorism / Maxim
description: Extremely compressed prose statement of insight or wisdom — often a single sentence. Compression and freestanding rhetorical force.
exemplars: La Rochefoucauld's Maxims; Pascal's Pensées; Lichtenberg; Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil; Cioran.

name: Chōka (Japanese long poem)
description: Classical Japanese long poem alternating 5- and 7-syllable lines, ending with two 7-syllable lines. Used for elegy, praise, narrative.
exemplars: Manyoshu anthology; Kakinomoto no Hitomaro; Yamanoue no Okura.

name: Memoir
beats: Reflection on what the life means now
description: First-person account of selected periods or themes from the author's life. Distinguished from autobiography by thematic rather than chronological focus.
exemplars: Mary Karr's The Liars' Club; Tara Westover's Educated; Michelle Obama's Becoming; Maya Angelou's I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

name: Autobiography (formal)
description: Comprehensive first-person account of one's life — typically chronological, more formal than memoir, designed for posterity.
exemplars: Benjamin Franklin's Autobiography; Frederick Douglass's Narrative; Malcolm X (with Haley); Obama's Dreams from My Father.

name: Biography
description: Long-form third-person account of another's life. Distinct from autobiography by its outside-perspective and from hagiography by its critical-analytical register.
exemplars: Robert Caro's The Years of Lyndon Johnson; Walter Isaacson's biographies; Stacy Schiff; Edmund Morris.

name: Ethnography
description: Long-form descriptive account of a culture or community based on direct fieldwork — anthropological, sociological, journalistic. Participant-observer methodology.
exemplars: Bronisław Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific; Clifford Geertz's The Interpretation of Cultures; Adrian LeBlanc's Random Family.

name: Travelogue
description: Narrative account of a journey — geographically grounded, often combining observation, encounter, and reflection. Secular orientation.
exemplars: Bruce Chatwin's In Patagonia; Paul Theroux's travel books; Bill Bryson; Pico Iyer; Robert Macfarlane.

name: Nature Writing
beats: Reflection that ties nature to broader meaning
description: Literary nonfiction grounded in close attention to the natural world — ecology, place, plants, animals, weather. Specific environmental focus and lyric register.
exemplars: Henry David Thoreau's Walden; Annie Dillard's Pilgrim at Tinker Creek; Aldo Leopold's A Sand County Almanac; Helen Macdonald's H Is for Hawk; Robert Macfarlane.

name: Food Writing
beats: Climactic moment of taste or memory
description: Writing about food — its history, preparation, eating, social significance. Spans memoir, journalism, criticism, recipe-narrative.
exemplars: M.F.K. Fisher's The Art of Eating; Anthony Bourdain's Kitchen Confidential; Ruth Reichl's memoirs; Michael Pollan's books; Calvin Trillin.

name: Sports Writing (long-form)
beats: Sport or athlete framed with significance
description: Literary nonfiction about sports — players, games, the meaning of athletic competition. Literary scope and character depth.
exemplars: David Halberstam's The Breaks of the Game; Roger Angell on baseball; W.C. Heinz; Friday Night Lights (Bissinger); Gary Smith.

name: Music Criticism
description: Critical writing about music — performances, recordings, traditions. Specific aesthetic analysis register.
exemplars: Greil Marcus; Ellen Willis; Nat Hentoff; Robert Christgau; Pauline Kael's stylistic kin in music.

name: Film Criticism
description: Critical writing about cinema — individual films, directors, movements. Specific cinematic-aesthetic analysis.
exemplars: Pauline Kael; Andrew Sarris; Manny Farber; Jonathan Rosenbaum; J. Hoberman; Anthony Lane; Amy Taubin.

name: Art Criticism
beats: Implications for the artist or moment
description: Critical writing about visual art — exhibitions, artists, movements. Specific visual-aesthetic register.
exemplars: Clement Greenberg; Susan Sontag; John Berger's Ways of Seeing; Jerry Saltz; Roberta Smith; Hilton Als.

name: Cultural Criticism
description: Essays analyzing cultural phenomena — TV, movements, technology, public figures, political moments. Combines literary register with cultural-political analysis.
exemplars: Susan Sontag's essays; Joan Didion's cultural pieces; Zadie Smith's essays; Hilton Als; Ta-Nehisi Coates; Jia Tolentino.

name: Literary Criticism (essay)
description: Essay analyzing a literary work or writer. Distinct from academic criticism by being shorter, more accessible, more author-voiced.
exemplars: James Wood's How Fiction Works and reviews; Susan Sontag; Edmund Wilson; Cynthia Ozick; Adam Gopnik (variant).

name: Personal Essay
description: Short to medium-length essay using first-person experience as the engine for broader reflection. Essayistic compression; personal grounding.
exemplars: Montaigne's Essais (foundational); Joan Didion's essays; James Baldwin's essays; Annie Dillard; Phillip Lopate.

name: Lyric Essay
beats: Associative movement rather than linear argument
description: Hybrid form combining essay's argumentative shape with poetry's compression, image, and rhythm. Greater formal experimentation than personal essay.
exemplars: Anne Carson's The Glass Essay; Maggie Nelson's Bluets and The Argonauts; Eula Biss; Brian Doyle.

name: Hermit Crab Essay
beats: Personal content fitted to borrowed shape
Tension between form and content creates resonance
Climactic moment within the borrowed form
description: Essay that takes the form of another, non-essay genre — instruction manual, recipe, FAQ, list, syllabus — and uses that borrowed form for personal essay content.
exemplars: Brenda Miller and Suzanne Paola's writings; Jenny Boully's The Body; many contemporary creative-nonfiction pieces.

name: Investigative Memoir
description: Hybrid of memoir and investigative reporting — author investigates their own family history, an unresolved death, a personal mystery. Dual personal-and-reportorial register.
exemplars: Patrick Radden Keefe's Say Nothing (variant); Alison Bechdel's Fun Home; Daniel Mendelsohn's The Lost; Sarah Polley's Stories We Tell.

name: Trauma Memoir
beats: First moment of agency or hope
description: Memoir centered on survival of trauma — abuse, addiction, illness, war, escape. Specific extreme experience as content.
exemplars: Cheryl Strayed's Wild; Mary Karr's The Liars' Club; Tara Westover's Educated; Hope Jahren's Lab Girl.

name: Spiritual / Recovery Memoir
description: Memoir centered on the author's spiritual journey or recovery from addiction. Specific religious-recovery register and structure.
exemplars: Anne Lamott's Traveling Mercies; Mary Karr's Lit; Caroline Knapp's Drinking: A Love Story; Augusten Burroughs's Dry; Twelve-step recovery memoirs.

name: Food Memoir
beats: Personal life events tied to food
description: Memoir whose primary frame is food — meals, cooking, family recipes, restaurant work. Food as structural through-line.
exemplars: Ruth Reichl's memoirs; M.F.K. Fisher; Anthony Bourdain's Kitchen Confidential; Madhur Jaffrey; Heat (Buford).

name: Public Intellectual Essay
description: Long-form essay by a public intellectual — combining argument, scholarship, and broad cultural-political address. Expert-voice authority and ambition for general audience.
exemplars: Hannah Arendt's essays; James Baldwin's longer essays; Susan Sontag; Edward Said; Cornel West; Ta-Nehisi Coates.

name: Polemic
description: Strong, often combative argumentative essay or book. Passionate, confrontational rhetorical register and explicit advocacy.
exemplars: Christopher Hitchens's polemics; Tom Paine's Common Sense; Frederick Douglass; bell hooks's polemic essays; Andrea Dworkin.

name: Diary / Journal (literary)
beats: Major life events recorded as they happen
Reader watches life unfold without retrospect
description: Day-by-day or entry-by-entry first-person record kept across time, sometimes published. Real-time, accumulative structure rather than retrospective shaping.
exemplars: Samuel Pepys's Diary; Anne Frank's Diary; Susan Sontag's journals; Virginia Woolf's diaries; Joan Didion's notebooks.

name: Letter (literary, public)
beats: Personal disclosure as part of argument
description: Open or published letter as literary form — addressed to a specific recipient but designed for public reading. Rhetorical-public ambition.
exemplars: Martin Luther King Jr.'s "Letter from a Birmingham Jail"; James Baldwin's "Letter to My Nephew"; Ta-Nehisi Coates's Between the World and Me.

name: Annotated Edition / Marginalia
description: Critical apparatus — extensive footnotes or commentary — that creates a parallel narrative alongside a primary text. Dialogue-with-text register.
exemplars: Vladimir Nabokov's Pale Fire (fictionalized variant); Pope's The Dunciad Variorum; Talmudic commentary; David Foster Wallace's annotated essays.

name: Wire Report
description: Brief, fact-focused dispatch from a wire service designed for syndication — fastest hard news. Extreme brevity and absolute factual register.
exemplars: AP and Reuters wire service reports; AFP dispatches; Bloomberg flash reports.

name: Beat Reporting
description: Sustained coverage of a specific topic-area (politics, courts, education) by a single reporter who develops sources and expertise. Topic-depth.
exemplars: Beat reporters at major newspapers; Politico's beats; specific political reporters (Maggie Haberman).

name: Enterprise Journalism
beats: Initial reporting confirms there's a story
description: Original, self-initiated journalism that goes beyond breaking-news coverage — typically discovering or framing a story not on the daily agenda. Initiative-driven.
exemplars: ProPublica investigations; NYT enterprise pieces; investigative team work at major outlets.

name: Solutions Journalism
description: Reporting that focuses on responses to social problems — what's working, what's being tried, with rigorous examination. Investigative rigor and attention to evidence.
exemplars: Solutions Journalism Network archive; Christian Science Monitor's solution-oriented reporting; YES! Magazine; NYT "Fixes" column.

name: Hyperlocal Journalism
description: Reporting at the level of a single neighborhood, community, or small town — covering local politics, schools, businesses, characters that wouldn't make regional or national news.
exemplars: Patch.com (early years); West Seattle Blog; Curbed; local weekly papers generally.

name: Data Journalism
description: Reporting in which data analysis IS the journalism — patterns in datasets reveal stories that would not be apparent through interview-based reporting.
exemplars: Nate Silver's election work; NYT's "The Upshot"; FiveThirtyEight; ProPublica's data investigations.

name: Constructive Journalism
description: Reporting that explicitly aims at productive outcomes — engaged democracy, problem-solving, audience empowerment — rather than just informing or critiquing.
exemplars: Solutions Journalism Network; YES! Magazine; some BBC and NPR civic series.

name: Slow Journalism / Long-Read
beats: Connections recognized that wouldn't appear in fast coverage
description: Reporting that takes weeks or months and publishes as long-form analysis or narrative. Temporal investment.
exemplars: Delayed Gratification magazine; The Atlantic's long features; New Yorker reportage; Granta.

name: Magazine Feature
description: 3,000-10,000 word feature article — bridges journalism and literary nonfiction. Mid-length and magazine-rhythm pacing.
exemplars: New Yorker features; Atlantic features; Vanity Fair; GQ features; Tom Wolfe's New Journalism.

name: Newsletter (modern)
description: Email-distributed personal or specialized publication — combining curation, analysis, and reporting in distinctive single-author voice. Direct-to-reader, voice-driven model.
exemplars: Substack newsletters generally; Stratechery (Ben Thompson); Letters from an American (Heather Cox Richardson); Slow Boring (Yglesias).

name: Press Release Narrative
description: Institutional announcement structured as if it were a news story — designed to be repurposed by journalists. Self-promotional but news-format register.
exemplars: Apple press releases; PR Newswire distributions; standard corporate-communications announcements.

name: Photo Essay
description: Story told primarily through photographs with minimal accompanying text. Images get structural primacy.
exemplars: W. Eugene Smith's photo essays in Life; Sebastião Salgado's projects; National Geographic photo essays; Robert Frank's The Americans.

name: Long-Form Podcast Narrative
beats: Closing episode reflects on the journey
description: Multi-episode podcast told as a single sustained narrative — investigative, biographical, or thematic. Serial-narrative structure.
exemplars: Serial; S-Town; The Daily; This American Life's longer projects; Slow Burn.

name: News Conference / Press Conference
description: Formal address by official to assembled journalists, followed by Q&A. Institutional ritual and adversarial dynamic.
exemplars: White House press briefings; corporate press conferences; sports press conferences after major games.

name: Sports Recap (game story)
beats: Lead with key result and stakes
description: Day-after report of a sporting event — score, key plays, quotes, implications. Specific game-event focus.
exemplars: Wire service game stories; ESPN game recaps; daily-newspaper sports sections.

name: Business Memo
description: Internal corporate communication to colleagues — concise, action-oriented, often template-formatted. Institutional brevity and operational register.
exemplars: Standard business memos; Amazon's six-page narrative memos (Bezos); McKinsey internal memos.

name: Cold Email Pitch
beats: Subject line that earns the open
Easy yes or specific next step
description: Outreach email to a stranger — sales, partnership, fundraising — designed to be opened, read, and answered. Extreme brevity and conversion-focus.
exemplars: Standard sales-development cold emails; founder-to-investor outreach; modern cold-outreach templates.

name: Investor Update
description: Monthly or quarterly email/letter from founder to investors — metrics, progress, challenges, asks. Accountability-with-momentum register.
exemplars: Standard YC and Sequoia-style investor updates; Andrew Chen's writings; modern startup founder convention.

name: Board Deck
description: Presentation prepared for a corporate board meeting — quarterly performance, strategic direction, key decisions sought. Formal-governance audience.
exemplars: Standard SaaS board decks; PE board materials; standard corporate-governance practice.

name: One-Pager / Executive Brief
description: Single-page summary of a complex situation or proposal designed for executive consumption — ruthless distillation. Severe brevity and decision-orientation.
exemplars: Pentagon brief format; consulting one-pagers; modern enterprise decision documents.

name: Business Plan
description: Comprehensive document outlining a business — market, product, strategy, financials. Formal-comprehensive structure.
exemplars: SBA business plan templates; traditional MBA-school format; banking-loan business plans.

name: Lean Canvas / Business Model Canvas
description: Compressed alternative to traditional business plan — single-page visual format covering customer segments, value proposition, revenue, costs, etc. Template-driven brevity.
exemplars: Alex Osterwalder's Business Model Canvas; Ash Maurya's Lean Canvas; Steve Blank's Customer Development.

name: Marketing Plan
description: Strategic document outlining how a product will reach its market — positioning, channels, campaigns, budget. Marketing-specific focus.
exemplars: Standard CMO documents; agency-prepared marketing plans; brand quarterly plans.

name: Strategic Plan
description: Multi-year direction-setting document for an organization — vision, goals, initiatives, capabilities. Long-horizon, organization-wide scope.
exemplars: Corporate 5-year strategic plans; nonprofit strategic plans; government agency strategic plans.

name: Vision Document
beats: What it looks like when achieved
description: Aspirational long-term articulation of where an organization wants to be — typically less operational than strategic plan, more inspirational.
exemplars: Built to Last (Collins) vision-discussions; founder vision letters; nonprofit vision statements; corporate purpose documents.

name: Mission Statement
description: Compressed statement of an organization's purpose — typically one to three sentences. Operational-aspirational hybrid.
exemplars: Patagonia's mission; Google's "to organize the world's information"; nonprofit mission statements generally.

name: RFP Response (Request for Proposal)
description: Formal proposal responding to a procurement request — typically agency or government. Compliance-driven structure: each requirement must be addressed.
exemplars: Federal contract proposals; agency responses to government RFPs; consulting RFP responses.

name: Earnings Call Q&A Narrative
description: The Q&A portion of an earnings call — analyst questions and management responses. Dynamic adversarial-collegial register.
exemplars: Standard earnings call Q&A format; Apple, Tesla earnings calls; sell-side analyst interactions.

name: Annual Report (full)
description: Comprehensive yearly publication summarizing financial performance, narrative, and strategic direction. More comprehensive than shareholder letter.
exemplars: Berkshire Hathaway annual reports; modern corporate annual reports; nonprofit annual reports.

name: Sustainability / ESG Report
description: Corporate report on environmental, social, and governance performance — alongside or separate from financial annual report. Non-financial accountability register.
exemplars: Microsoft's sustainability reports; Patagonia's environmental reports; SASB and GRI-aligned reports.

name: Bug Report
description: Documentation of a software defect — what went wrong, how to reproduce, expected vs actual behavior. Specific debugging-utility register.
exemplars: GitHub issues; Jira tickets; standard QA bug reports.

name: Feature Specification (spec)
description: Document describing a software feature in detail — for engineers, designers, and stakeholders. Operational, build-this-thing register.
exemplars: Standard product spec documents; PRDs (Product Requirements Documents); modern startup spec conventions.

name: RFC (Request for Comments)
description: Engineering proposal document inviting comment from teammates before implementation. Collaborative-review register.
exemplars: IETF RFCs (the original); modern engineering RFCs at Google, Stripe, GitLab; Rust RFCs; Python PEPs.

name: Technical Postmortem
description: Engineering analysis of an incident — outage, security breach, data loss — written for organizational learning. Blameless, systems-focused register.
exemplars: Google SRE blameless postmortems; AWS post-event summaries; GitLab incident reports; Stripe engineering blog incident write-ups.

name: API Documentation
description: Reference documentation for software APIs — endpoints, parameters, responses, examples. Strict reference-utility register and example-driven structure.
exemplars: Stripe API docs (gold standard); Twilio docs; GitHub REST API docs; OpenAPI specifications.

name: Changelog / Release Notes
description: Document recording what changed in a software release — features, fixes, breaking changes. Version-keyed structural register.
exemplars: Standard software changelogs; keepachangelog.com convention; npm package release notes; macOS/iOS release notes.

name: Engineering Blog Post / Deep Dive
description: Long-form technical blog post explaining how a system, problem, or solution works at depth. Narrative-explanatory register.
exemplars: Stripe Engineering blog; Netflix Tech Blog; Cloudflare blog; High Scalability posts; Hacker News-typical deep dives.

name: Open Source README
description: Project's primary documentation file — first thing visitors see on a code repository. Onboarding-utility register.
exemplars: Standard GitHub README files; popular OSS projects (React, Linux kernel, Rails); make a readme convention.

name: Postmortem (product)
description: Analysis of a product launch, feature, or campaign after the fact — what worked, what didn't, what to learn. Product-focus rather than technical.
exemplars: Standard product retrospectives; agile retrospectives; Fast Company product post-mortems; failure-celebration cultures.

name: Internal Engineering Documentation
description: Documentation for internal engineering teams — runbooks, architecture docs, system overviews, onboarding guides. Insider audience.
exemplars: Internal Confluence pages; Notion engineering wikis; runbooks; on-call documentation.

name: Review Article (academic)
description: Comprehensive synthesis of research on a topic, distinct from systematic literature review by its narrative scope and authorial perspective.
exemplars: Annual Review of Psychology articles; Trends in... journal articles; comprehensive review chapters in handbooks.

name: Systematic Review / Meta-Analysis
description: Methodologically rigorous review of all existing studies on a question, often combined with statistical meta-analysis. Explicit methodology and reproducibility.
exemplars: Cochrane systematic reviews; PRISMA-compliant reviews; meta-analyses in psychology, medicine, education.

name: Case Study (academic)
description: In-depth examination of a single case, organization, or situation — distinct from teaching case by being scholarly research rather than pedagogy.
exemplars: Robert Yin's case study methodology; sociological case studies; policy case studies.

name: Theoretical Paper
description: Academic paper advancing a new theoretical framework or refining an existing one — without empirical study. Original theory-building.
exemplars: Major theoretical papers in psychology, sociology, economics; foundational papers like Kahneman-Tversky's Prospect Theory.

name: Methodology Paper
description: Paper introducing a new research methodology, statistical technique, or instrument. Focuses on the how rather than the substantive findings.
exemplars: Papers introducing new statistical techniques; psychometric instrument validation papers; field-research-method papers.

name: Replication Study
description: Study explicitly attempting to replicate a previous finding — direct replication, conceptual replication, or pre-registered replication.
exemplars: Many Open Science Collaboration papers; Many Labs projects; modern psychology replication crisis literature.

name: Pre-Registered Report
beats: Stage 1: introduction, hypotheses, method, analysis plan
description: Research report whose method and analysis plan were submitted and accepted for publication before data collection — protecting against p-hacking and HARKing.
exemplars: Center for Open Science framework; Registered Reports in psychology and biology journals.

name: Critical Theory Essay
description: Academic essay applying a critical theoretical framework (Marxist, feminist, postcolonial, queer, deconstructive) to a text or phenomenon. Specific theoretical lens.
exemplars: Frankfurt School essays; Judith Butler's gender essays; Edward Said's Orientalism; bell hooks's essays.

name: Conference Paper Abstract
description: Brief (250-500 word) abstract submitted to a conference for review — must convey scholarly contribution in highly compressed form. Competitive-selection function.
exemplars: Standard academic conference submissions across disciplines; abstracts for AAAS, MLA, AMA conferences.

name: Tenure Case Narrative
description: Faculty member's case for tenure assembled as research, teaching, and service narrative — designed for committee review. Career-defining stakes.
exemplars: Standard tenure dossiers; tenure-and-promotion narratives across U.S. higher education.

name: Course Syllabus
description: Document outlining a course's content, structure, expectations, and policies — distributed to students at term start. Institutional-pedagogical register.
exemplars: Standard university course syllabi; K-12 course outlines; online-course descriptions.

name: Lesson Plan
description: Detailed instructor's plan for a single class session — objectives, activities, materials, assessment. Specific-session granularity.
exemplars: Standard K-12 lesson plans; Madeline Hunter lesson plan model; backwards design lesson plans (Wiggins/McTighe).

name: Curriculum Design Document
description: Long-arc document designing an entire course or program of study — sequenced learning, assessment, philosophy. Design-thinking scope.
exemplars: Common Core curriculum; IB program documents; school-level curriculum mapping; corporate training curricula.

name: Reading Comprehension Passage
beats: Passage with controlled length and difficulty
Main idea and supporting details embedded
description: Short passage designed for assessment of reading skills — typically followed by questions. Specific testing-instrument register.
exemplars: SAT, ACT, AP exam passages; standardized testing material; reading curricula.

name: Worksheet / Practice Set
description: Set of practice problems or exercises for student practice. Drill-and-practice register and progressive difficulty.
exemplars: Standard math worksheets; language-learning practice sets; standardized prep books.

name: Lab Report
description: Student's account of a laboratory experiment — protocol, observations, conclusions. Specific empirical-pedagogical register; pre-IMRAD training.
exemplars: Standard secondary and undergraduate lab reports; chemistry, physics, biology lab notebooks.

name: Field Trip Narrative
description: Student or teacher account of educational excursion — what was seen, learned, experienced. Specific outside-classroom learning register.
exemplars: Class trip writeups; museum education narratives; outdoor education program accounts.

name: Standardized Test Question
description: Single question on a standardized exam — multiple-choice, short-answer, or essay. Specific assessment-instrument register.
exemplars: SAT, ACT, GRE, MCAT items; Common Core assessments; psychometric instruments.

name: Essay Prompt / Writing Assignment
description: Instructional prompt asking students to write — typically with specific question, length, audience, and criteria. Meta-genre: a prompt that generates a genre.
exemplars: AP English exam prompts; college admission essay prompts; classroom writing assignments.

name: Children's Picture Book
description: Short narrative for young children combining illustration and text. Visual-textual integration and developmentally-appropriate register.
exemplars: Maurice Sendak's Where the Wild Things Are; Eric Carle's The Very Hungry Caterpillar; Mo Willems's books; Goodnight Moon.

name: Educational Children's Book (chapter)
beats: Vocabulary and concept teaching woven in
description: Chapter book aimed at independent young readers (~7-12) — narrative shaped to be both engaging and teachingly age-appropriate. Longer chapter-divided structure.
exemplars: Beverly Cleary's Ramona books; Jeff Kinney's Diary of a Wimpy Kid; Magic Tree House; Nikki Grimes.

name: Apology Letter
beats: Recognition of impact on the recipient
description: Direct written acknowledgment of wrong to a specific person, accepting responsibility and seeking repair. Specific accountability register.
exemplars: Personal apology letters; corporate apology statements (when honest); literary examples (Augustine to his mother).

name: Love Letter
beats: Account of feeling for the recipient
description: Written declaration of romantic love or longing to a specific person. Specific intimate-direct register, often with intentional poetic heightening.
exemplars: John Keats's letters to Fanny Brawne; Napoleon's letters to Josephine; Frida Kahlo's love letters; Beethoven's "Immortal Beloved" letters.

name: Dear John / Breakup Letter
description: Written end-of-relationship letter to a partner. Specific termination-with-explanation register.
exemplars: Personal breakup letters; literary examples (The Letter; many novels' epistolary breaks).

name: Resignation Letter
beats: Statement of resignation effective by date
description: Formal written notice of resignation from employment. Specific institutional-professional register.
exemplars: Standard resignation letter templates; corporate convention; public-figure resignation letters.

name: Cover Letter (job application)
beats: Salutation to specific person if possible
Position applied for and how learned
description: Letter accompanying a job application — introducing the candidate, stating interest, summarizing qualifications. Specific job-search rhetorical register.
exemplars: Standard job-application cover letters; modern targeted cover letters.

name: Recommendation Letter
beats: Comparison to others writer has known
description: Written endorsement of a person — for job, school, award. Third-party authority register; the writer's credibility transfers.
exemplars: Standard recommendation letters; faculty grad-school recommendations; corporate references.

name: Sympathy / Condolence Letter
beats: Specific memory of the deceased (if applicable)
description: Written expression of sympathy following another's loss. Specific compassion-without-fixing register.
exemplars: Standard condolence letters; Lincoln's letter to Mrs. Bixby; modern grief literature recommendations.

name: Thank You Note
beats: Specific thanks for what was given
description: Brief written expression of gratitude for a gift, service, or kindness. Specific concise-warm register.
exemplars: Standard thank-you notes; thank-you letters after job interviews; wedding-gift thank-yous.

name: Greeting Card Message
beats: Specific reflection on relationship or year
description: Brief celebratory message inside a greeting card. Specific warm-affectionate compressed register.
exemplars: Standard birthday card messages; Hallmark and modern card text; personal-customized notes.

name: Personal Vow (wedding, commitment)
beats: What love means in this commitment
description: Words of commitment spoken at a marriage or other ceremonial bond. Specific public-promise register.
exemplars: Personal wedding vows; modern vow-writing templates; literary examples.

name: Public Apology (Celebrity / Corporate)
description: Public statement of apology by celebrity or organization for action that drew public criticism. Public audience and image-management stakes.
exemplars: Domino's Pizza response (2009); Tiger Woods's public apology; many modern celebrity apologies (success and failure cases).

name: Personal Statement (admissions)
beats: Specific moment of formation or decision
description: First-person narrative submitted to admissions committees — college, grad school, fellowships. High-stakes self-presentation register.
exemplars: College admission essays; med school personal statements; fellowship applications (Rhodes, Marshall).

name: Last Letter (deathbed / parting)
beats: What the writer hopes for survivors
description: Letter written knowing the writer is dying or leaving permanently — addressed to family, beloved, or community. Terminal stakes register.
exemplars: Sullivan Ballou's letter before Bull Run; deathbed letters in literature; military "in case of my death" letters.

name: Personal Manifesto
description: Personal declaration of values, goals, and stances written for self-clarification (or sometimes public). Individual-life register.
exemplars: Personal manifestos in self-help literature; founder personal statements; year-end review documents.

name: Coming Out Letter / Statement
beats: Reflection on what it means to share this
What is hoped for in response
description: Written disclosure of LGBTQ+ identity to family, friends, or public. Specific identity-disclosure register and stakes.
exemplars: Coming-out letters in memoirs; published examples (Anderson Cooper's); modern coming-out support literature.

name: Reality Competition Show
description: Competition format with elimination across episodes — cooking, design, dating, athletic. Specific competitive-elimination structure.
exemplars: Survivor; Top Chef; RuPaul's Drag Race; The Bachelor; Project Runway.

name: Talk Show (interview-based)
description: Television format featuring host interviewing guests — late-night, daytime, news, or specialty. Host-guest dynamic structure.
exemplars: The Tonight Show; The Daily Show; Oprah; Hot Ones (modern variant).

name: Game Show
description: Television format with contestants competing in games for prizes. Specific game-mechanics structure.
exemplars: Jeopardy!; Wheel of Fortune; The Price Is Right; Family Feud.

name: Documentary Series (long-form)
description: Multi-episode documentary on a single subject — true crime, history, sports, biography. Serial scope.
exemplars: The Last Dance (Jordan); Tiger King; Making a Murderer; Wild Wild Country; The Vietnam War (Burns).

name: True Crime Documentary
description: Documentary series or feature specifically investigating real crimes. Specific genre commitment.
exemplars: Making a Murderer; The Jinx; Don't F**k With Cats; The Staircase; Conversations with a Killer.

name: Nature / Wildlife Documentary
description: Documentary about natural world — animals, ecosystems, geography. Natural-world subject and conservation-adjacent register.
exemplars: Planet Earth; Blue Planet; Our Planet; David Attenborough's productions; Tiger (Disneynature).

name: Cooking Show (instructional)
description: TV format demonstrating recipes and cooking techniques. Instructional non-competitive register.
exemplars: Julia Child's The French Chef; Good Eats (Alton Brown); Barefoot Contessa; many YouTube cooking shows.

name: Travel Show
description: TV format following host(s) traveling to destinations — culture, food, adventure. Host-as-traveler register and place-focused structure.
exemplars: Anthony Bourdain's Parts Unknown and No Reservations; Rick Steves's travel; Conan Without Borders; Stanley Tucci's Searching for Italy.

name: Home Renovation / Makeover Show
description: TV format featuring transformation of home, person, or space — before-and-after structure. Specific physical-transformation register.
exemplars: Queer Eye; Fixer Upper; Extreme Makeover: Home Edition; Tidying Up with Marie Kondo.

name: Sketch Comedy
description: TV format featuring multiple short comedic skits, typically 2-7 minutes each. Episodic-self-contained-bit structure.
exemplars: Saturday Night Live; Monty Python's Flying Circus; Key & Peele; I Think You Should Leave; Mr. Show.

name: Championship Run Narrative
description: Narrative tracking a team or individual's run through a championship season or playoff. Specific season-arc register with elimination stakes.
exemplars: The Last Dance (Bulls); coverage of any major championship run; Friday Night Lights (Bissinger).

name: Comeback Narrative
description: Sports story of athlete or team returning from injury, retirement, or defeat to triumph. Specific redemption-through-sport register.
exemplars: Tiger Woods's 2019 Masters; Andre Agassi's career arc; Rocky II; many sports comeback stories.

name: Athlete Career Retrospective
description: Long-form narrative of an athlete's complete career — origins, peak, decline, legacy. Specifically athletic frame.
exemplars: Andre Agassi's Open; David Maraniss's When Pride Still Mattered (Lombardi); Roger Kahn's The Boys of Summer; The Last Dance.

name: Single-Game Reconstruction
description: Detailed narrative of a single sporting event — moment by moment, with backstory and context. Book-length depth.
exemplars: Books on Game 7 of various series; The Boys of Summer's game accounts; Mark Bowden's Bringing the Heat; Friday Night Lights game chapters.

name: Sports Team Profile
description: Long-form portrait of a sports team — its players, coach, culture, season. Specifically team-as-character register.
exemplars: Friday Night Lights (Bissinger); The Boys of Summer (Kahn); David Halberstam's basketball books; The Last Dance.

name: Sports Rivalry Narrative
beats: Reflection on what the rivalry meant
description: Narrative tracking the long-running rivalry between two teams or athletes. Specifically multi-encounter, head-to-head structure.
exemplars: Bird-Magic rivalry; Federer-Nadal-Djokovic; Yankees-Red Sox; Real Madrid-Barcelona.

name: Coaching Memoir / Strategy Book
description: Coach's first-person account of methods, philosophy, and seasons. Specifically strategic-leadership register.
exemplars: Phil Jackson's Sacred Hoops; John Wooden's books; Bill Walsh's The Score Takes Care of Itself; Pat Summitt's memoirs.

name: Sports Documentary Feature
description: Feature-length documentary on athlete, team, or sporting event. Specific filmic-sports register.
exemplars: Hoop Dreams; When We Were Kings; O.J.: Made in America; Senna; Free Solo.

name: Underdog Sports Narrative
description: Sports story specifically of unlikely team or athlete defeating favored opposition. Sports-specific underdog arc.
exemplars: Hoosiers; Miracle on Ice (1980 USA hockey); Rocky; Leicester City's 2015-16 EPL title; Cool Runnings.

name: Adventure Sport / Extreme Memoir
beats: Climactic moment of danger or success
description: First-person account of extreme sport feat — climbing, ultra-running, sailing, free diving. Adrenaline-stakes register.
exemplars: Aron Ralston's Between a Rock and a Hard Place; Free Solo (Honnold); David Roberts; Joe Simpson's Touching the Void.

name: Founder Story
description: Long-form narrative of a startup founder — origin, struggles, breakthroughs. Book-length scope.
exemplars: Phil Knight's Shoe Dog; Howard Schultz's Pour Your Heart Into It; Walter Isaacson's Steve Jobs; Bad Blood (Holmes/Theranos — variant).

name: Career Pivot Narrative
description: Narrative of changing careers mid-life — abandoning one trajectory for another. Specific second-act register.
exemplars: Po Bronson's What Should I Do With My Life?; Cheryl Strayed's Wild; many Substack newsletter founder stories.

name: Quitting / Resignation Narrative
description: Public account of leaving a job, organization, or institution — typically with critique or stand-taking. Public-narrative register.
exemplars: Resignation essays in The Atlantic; Bari Weiss's NYT resignation letter; published whistleblower departures.

name: Performance Review (employee)
description: Manager's structured assessment of employee performance — typically annual. Specific evaluation-development register.
exemplars: Standard corporate performance reviews; 360 reviews; modern continuous-feedback variants.

name: 360-Degree Review
description: Performance review gathering input from manager, peers, direct reports, and self. Multi-source structure.
exemplars: Modern corporate 360 review processes; coaching applications of 360 feedback.

name: Self-Assessment / Self-Review
description: Employee's own structured assessment of their performance — accompanies or precedes manager review. First-person professional reflection register.
exemplars: Standard self-review documents; corporate self-assessment forms.

name: Promotion Case
description: Document advocating for an employee's promotion — combining manager case, employee accomplishments, peer evidence. Specific advancement-advocacy register.
exemplars: Standard promotion-case documents in modern tech; FAANG promotion convention; consulting-firm partner cases.

name: Resume / CV
description: Compressed document listing professional history, education, and skills. Highly conventional, scannable structure.
exemplars: Standard resume templates; CV formats (academic); LinkedIn profiles (modern variant).

name: LinkedIn Post / Professional Reflection
description: Short professional reflection or update posted on LinkedIn — career milestone, lesson, opinion. Specific platform-conventionalized register.
exemplars: Standard LinkedIn long-posts; "3 things I learned" format; modern professional thought-leadership content.

name: Interview Story (job interview)
description: Narrative-format interview answer — STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) or similar structure. Specific demonstration-of-competency register.
exemplars: Standard behavioral-interview answers; modern interview-prep frameworks (STAR, CAR).

name: Onboarding Narrative
description: First-person account of joining an organization — first weeks, learning the culture, finding footing. Specific entry-into-institution register.
exemplars: Modern onboarding-experience blog posts; First, Break All the Rules onboarding chapters; "my first 90 days at..." Substack posts.

name: Exit Interview Narrative
description: Structured conversation with departing employee — capturing institutional learning. Specific candor-at-departure register.
exemplars: Standard HR exit interviews; published exit-interview essays; modern offboarding practices.

name: Career Coaching Conversation
description: Structured coaching dialogue focused on career direction — distinguished from generic mentorship by specifically career-trajectory focus.
exemplars: Standard executive coaching career conversations; career-counselor sessions; Designing Your Life (Burnett/Evans) framework.

name: Networking Pitch / Elevator Pitch
beats: What makes it interesting or unique
What I'm looking for / next step
description: Compressed self-introduction designed for networking events, conferences, or chance encounters — typically 30-60 seconds. Specific concise self-presentation register.
exemplars: Standard elevator pitches; networking event introductions; conference badge-up small-talk; modern "tell me about yourself" answers.

name: Divorce Narrative
description: Memoir or essay processing the experience of divorce. Specific dissolution-of-marriage register.
exemplars: Nora Ephron's Heartburn; Rachel Cusk's Aftermath; Eat Pray Love (in part); many divorce memoirs.

name: Grief Memoir
beats: Reconfiguration of life without the person
description: First-person narrative of mourning a specific loss — spouse, child, parent, friend. Specific bereavement-process register.
exemplars: Joan Didion's The Year of Magical Thinking; C.S. Lewis's A Grief Observed; Joyce Carol Oates's A Widow's Story; Helen Macdonald's H Is for Hawk.

name: Diagnosis Narrative
description: Narrative of receiving a serious medical diagnosis — illness named, life reorganized, treatment begun. Specific medical-life-pivot register.
exemplars: Susan Sontag's Illness as Metaphor; Paul Kalanithi's When Breath Becomes Air; Anatole Broyard's Intoxicated by My Illness; Audre Lorde's The Cancer Journals.

name: Recovery Narrative (health)
beats: New relationship with body and mortality
description: Narrative of recovery from serious illness, injury, or surgery. Medical-physical register distinct from spiritual recovery.
exemplars: Atul Gawande's essays; Christopher Reeve's Still Me; My Stroke of Insight (Bolte Taylor); cancer recovery memoirs.

name: Addiction / Recovery Memoir
description: Memoir of substance addiction and recovery. Specific addiction-substance register.
exemplars: Caroline Knapp's Drinking: A Love Story; Mary Karr's Lit; Augusten Burroughs's Dry; James Frey's A Million Little Pieces (controversial).

name: Mental Health Memoir
description: First-person narrative of mental illness, treatment, and integration. Specific psychiatric-experience register.
exemplars: William Styron's Darkness Visible; Kay Redfield Jamison's An Unquiet Mind; Susanna Kaysen's Girl, Interrupted; Andrew Solomon's The Noonday Demon.

name: Trauma Recovery Narrative
description: Narrative of processing and recovering from trauma — abuse, assault, accident. Specific trauma-integration register.
exemplars: Lucy Grealy's Autobiography of a Face; Sherman Alexie; Roxane Gay's Hunger; Chanel Miller's Know My Name.

name: Caregiver Narrative
beats: Specific challenges and moments of grace
description: First-person account of caring for a sick, aging, or dying family member. Specific caregiver-position register.
exemplars: Roz Chast's Can't We Talk About Something More Pleasant?; Atul Gawande's Being Mortal; Sue Miller's The Story of My Father.

name: Adoption / Birth Family Search Narrative
beats: Question or longing for biological identity
